items.title: Microsoft Fabric Retail Demo
items.text:
Download release 1.3.0

These docs describe release 1.3.0. Deploy from the release, not from main: main carries unreleased changes that may not match these docs.

Download 1.3.0 (.zip) Download 1.3.0 (.tar.gz) Release notes

To use Git instead, clone the release tag: git clone --branch 1.3.0 https://github.com/amattas/retail-demo.git

items.title: About this demo
items.text:
This demo brings a retailer's sales, inventory, customer, marketing, fulfillment, and supply-chain data together in Microsoft Fabric. All records are synthetic, so demonstrations do not expose real customer or company data.

Historical sales and operations data lives in a Lakehouse and is presented through Power BI. Optional live events go to Eventhouse, where you can query them with KQL (Kusto Query Language).

Machine-learning outputs add forecasts and risk estimates. An ontology maps business relationships, and Data Agents answer natural-language questions over the deployed data.

items.title: What the demo contains
items.text:
Business capability What you can demonstrate Main Fabric area Sales and margin analysis Compare stores, products, channels, and periods Lakehouse and Power BI Inventory and replenishment Review movements, stockout signals, reorder activity, and current position Lakehouse, Eventhouse, and Power BI Omnichannel fulfillment Follow online demand and fulfillment events alongside store sales Lakehouse, Eventhouse, and Power BI Marketing and customer analysis Explore campaigns, attribution, customer segments, and churn risk Lakehouse, machine learning, and Power BI Optional live operations Query recent generated events and operational summaries Eventhouse and KQL Business context and questions Navigate Store, Product, Customer, and Receipt concepts or ask grounded questions Ontology and Data Agents

The base historical contract contains seven dimensions, twenty-one fact tables, and ten Gold aggregates. The live driver declares and emits twenty-two business event types; KQL adds an unknown_event catch-all for unexpected event types. The active Power BI semantic model contains 44 tables. Optional machine learning, ontology, dashboard, rule, and agent experiences have separate readiness checks so that an optional failure does not silently invalidate required reporting.

items.title: Agentic application
items.text:
The optional local application places chat beside an embedded Power BI report. An orchestrator routes questions to Fabric data services or to operations agents that draft replenishment and retention proposals.

The Fabric data platform and the optional local application have different trust boundaries. The app can run synthetic replay, uses operator credentials for live calls, and delivers an embed token to the browser. Its approval store is local and its Eventhouse telemetry is best-effort, not durable production audit. Check the environment's readiness report before using live features. See decision boundaries.

For the underlying streaming, Lakehouse, Eventhouse, and semantic-model architecture, see Architecture overview.

items.title: What it is, and why it's useful
items.text:
The app uses the deployed retail-demo workspace to answer business questions and prepare local action drafts:

  • It routes metrics to the semantic model, named-entity relationships to the ontology, and supported live-sales questions to recent event data. A trace records the selected route and reason.
  • When a user requests an action, an operations agent reads the deployed synthetic data, applies business rules, and drafts a proposal for human review.
  • It attempts to send recommendations and approvals to Eventhouse. Ingestion failures can be suppressed, so verify delivery separately from the UI state.

The data platform uses one Fabric workspace; the local app, browser, identity, and router remain additional trust and cost boundaries. The same Gold tables feed the report, the agents, and the ML models. Eventhouse holds live sales and successfully delivered agent telemetry.

items.title: 1. The app surface: report + chat, side by side
items.text:
The app is a small FastAPI backend serving a single-page front end with three pages:

  • Dashboard places the Power BI report and chat side by side, using about 70% and 30% of the space. The report uses user-owns-data embedding: the backend obtains a Microsoft Entra ID token from the developer's az login session. The demo does not require a separate app registration or service principal.
  • Agent Operations refreshes an approval-funnel dashboard from Eventhouse agent_actions, with KPI cards, an events-per-minute timeline, a per-agent funnel, and a feed of ingested recommendations and approvals.
  • Ontology Explorer displays business entities and their relationships.

The orchestrator chooses the data source for a question.

items.title: 2. The orchestrator: which brain answers?
items.text:
An LLM intent router (gpt-4o-mini on Azure OpenAI, authenticated through Microsoft Entra ID) classifies each question into a route:

Route Goes to Example question Metric, ranking, trend, or ML rollup Data Agent over the semantic model "Top 10 stores by net sales, YoY %" Single named entity, in context Ontology MCP over the business graph "What segment and churn risk does loyalty member LC012304678 have?" Recent sales Live-sales shortcut over event data "Top products in the last 15 minutes" Decision or action Operations agent "Stock is low. What should we do?"

The live-sales shortcut currently uses a fixed 15-minute store-sales query. It does not guarantee the product grain or time window requested in a question. See the routing specification for gate order and fallback behavior.

To use Claude for routing, set RETAIL_LLM_PROVIDER=anthropic and RETAIL_ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. The trace names the model used. If the LLM call fails, a deterministic keyword router selects the route. The Data Agent and ontology can fall back to each other when one cannot answer.

items.title: 3. The two MCP servers: Data Agent and Ontology
items.text:
The app calls both Fabric services through Model Context Protocol (MCP). Each call is a JSON-RPC POST to a streamable-HTTP endpoint, authenticated with a Fabric bearer token:

  • Data Agent MCP (.../dataagents/{id}/agent) answers aggregates, rankings, trends, and ML rollups over the semantic model. Fabric translates natural language into DAX and returns the answer without the generated query.
  • Ontology MCP (.../items/{id}/ontologyEndpoint) exposes the business graph. It connects a named entity's profile with related data, such as a customer's segment and churn prediction. Fabric translates the question into a graph query and returns rows with a natural-language summary.

Use named-entity graph lookups for relationships such as Customer → ChurnPrediction. Route broad aggregations and deep scans to the semantic model, and verify graph paths before presenting them.

You can connect to both MCP servers from VS Code. See the VS Code MCP setup for the .vscode/mcp.json setup.

items.title: 4. The operations agents: perceive, reason, recommend, log
items.text:
When a user requests an action, the orchestrator selects an agent that runs app-authored DAX. The trace can show these queries in full.

Inventory & Replenishment reads stockout-risk predictions, checks fact_reorders for SKUs without an open reorder, and joins dim_products for prices. It applies a 14-day inventory-cover rule and drafts reorders with Approve and Dismiss controls.

Customer Retention reads churn predictions, joins customer_segments for lifetime value, and selects a ranked campaign cohort. It adds cross-sell suggestions from the market-basket model and drafts a win-back campaign with Approve and Dismiss controls.

Both agents estimate a proposal's value and require human review. Local approval does not place an order or execute a campaign.

items.title: 5. The closed loop: write-back to the Eventhouse
items.text:
The app attempts to log drafts and approvals in Eventhouse agent_actions, alongside live sales events. Successfully ingested events feed the Agent Operations approval funnel and can be queried with KQL:

agent_actions
| where action_ts > ago(1h)
| summarize count() by bin(action_ts, 1m), action_status
| render timechart

Successfully ingested events are queryable inside Fabric. The source app/backend/eventhouse.py logs on daemon threads and suppresses failures; durable audit, authenticated per-user approvals, and production actions need the additional controls under THREAT-009 / SEC-012.

items.title: Under the hood: transparency and which model thinks
"Show me how the agent got the answer"
items.text:
The collapsible how I reached this trace below an answer records the source, router model, decision reason, and exact MCP tool call and arguments. For ontology results, it reconstructs an entity path from the returned columns and shows a row preview. For operations agents, it shows the app-authored DAX.

Fabric's Data Agent and Ontology services generate queries server-side and do not return the query text. Their traces show the request and returned evidence, not the hidden query.

items.title: Which model is doing the thinking?
items.text: The application controls the intent-routing model, which defaults to Azure OpenAI gpt-4o-mini and can be changed to Claude with an Anthropic key. Fabric controls the models that translate natural language into DAX and ontology queries. The application cannot replace those models.

items.title: Why this matters
items.text:
The application lets a presenter move from a report value to a question and then to a reviewable local proposal using the same retail data. Pricing, logistics, and marketing agents remain proposed extensions; see the decision experience specification.

For presentation steps, see the CIO walkthrough.

items.text:
flowchart LR
    D[setup-01<br/>seed dictionaries]
    M[setup-02<br/>dimensions and date]
    S[setup-03<br/>sales and fulfillment]
    O[setup-04<br/>online orders]
    K[setup-05<br/>marketing]
    R[setup-06<br/>returns and promotions]
    A[setup-07<br/>store activity]
    I[setup-08<br/>inventory]
    T[setup-09<br/>attribution]
    P[setup-10<br/>publish Silver and run log]
    G[setup-11<br/>Gold]
    Silver[(ag Silver)]
    Gold[(au Gold)]

    D --> M & O & K
    O --> S
    S --> R & A & I
    S & O & K & R --> T
    M & S & O & R & A & I & T --> P --> Silver
    Silver --> G --> Gold

This is the supported new-workspace historical path. Setup-03 waits for setup-04 because ship-from-DC online lines draw the DC stock that store reorders also use, so at most five setup notebooks run at once. Every setup notebook regenerates the same deterministic dimensions from the seed and anchor_date; only setup-10 publishes them. Setup-11 runs in ml-required and holds the gold writer lock (see Writer locks).

Generation runs in each store's local time and publishes true UTC timestamps. dim_stores.TimeZone and fact_receipts.local_hour carry the store-local view. The logistics incident model (incidents.py) and the DC stock simulation (dc_supply.py) run inside setup-08 and publish fact_logistics_incidents, fact_logistics_incident_stores, planned and actual truck arrivals, and fact_dc_inventory_txn.

items.title: Live Eventhouse path
items.text:
flowchart LR
    Silver[(ag Silver dimensions and ledgers)]
    State[(ag._stream_state_* tables)]
    Stream[stream-events]
    Event[(22 typed Eventhouse tables)]
    Views[KQL functions and materialized views]
    Query[Queryset / manual dashboards / rules]

    Silver -->|seed: store ops, stock as of start| Stream
    State <-->|read as of batch N-1, write batch N| Stream
    Stream -->|Spark Kusto connector| Event --> Views --> Query

The Spark Kusto connector writes groups of rows from the optional stream notebook directly to Eventhouse KQL tables, one write per table every 60 seconds. Each micro-batch is generated inside foreachBatch from the same models as history (traffic calendar, customers, baskets, prices, payments, attribution, incidents). State that spans micro-batches lives in versioned Lakehouse Delta tables: store open/closed state, in-progress visits and online orders, store stock, pending loads, shipments and trucks, and the batch clock (_stream_state_stores, _visits, _orders, _inventory, _logistics, _meta). Batch N reads each entity as of batch N-1 and replaces its own versions, so a replay emits the same events and applies nothing twice. A new checkpoint incarnation seeds store state from Silver fact_store_ops and store stock from the Silver ledger as of its start. The stream plans the same logistics incidents as history and emits logistics_incident_started and logistics_incident_resolved once each; an outage holds its DC's dispatches. See the live event contract.

unknown_event is a KQL catch-all table, not a generated business event type.

items.title: Optional Eventhouse-to-Lakehouse projection
items.text:
flowchart LR
    KQL[(Eventhouse KQL)]
    Bronze[cusn Eventhouse shortcuts]
    S[03-streaming-to-silver]
    Silver[(ag Silver)]
    G[04-streaming-to-gold]
    Gold[(au Gold)]

    KQL --> Bronze --> S --> Silver --> G --> Gold

This path uses ag._watermarks. Its schedule is enabled by schedules.streaming_data_load, which defaults to stream.start_after_deploy. The Silver notebook defines the schema and routes for the streaming-only fact_online_order_status table. The manifest records its downstream exception, and Delta maintenance includes it in the table inventory. That inventory also includes the ag._watermarks, ag._job_locks, and ag._stream_state_* control tables.

Notebook 03 is incremental: each source replays a three-hour overlap from its watermark, attribution reconsiders only new purchases and late arrivals, and truck lifecycles read only the replay window's departures and their arrivals. DC stock moves (inventory_updated rows without a store) go to fact_dc_inventory_txn, and both incident events feed fact_logistics_incidents (one row per incident, MERGEd on resolution) and fact_logistics_incident_stores. Notebook 04 and setup-11 build Gold from one definition, generation/gold_rules.py.

items.title: Writer locks
items.text:
Pipelines on independent schedules write the same Delta tables. Writers hold leases in ag._job_locks (generation/job_locks.py, copied into each notebook):

Lock Holders Behavior when held silver 03, 90 03 skips the run after 10 minutes; 90 fails gold 04, setup-11 04 skips; setup-11 fails after an hour, then its activity retries ml:<table> the six required ML producers the producer waits 30 minutes, then fails and its activity retries

Notebook 05 claims each table's lock without waiting and skips locked tables. Leases last 15 minutes and a heartbeat renews them, so a crashed writer's lock expires. fabric/pipelines/README.md explains how to clear a lock by hand. The locks coordinate cooperating notebooks; they are not an access control, and a writer outside these notebooks ignores them.

items.title: Operational state
items.text:
Operational evidence comes from:

  • setup_run_log
  • ag._watermarks
  • ag._job_locks (current writer leases)
  • stream checkpoint incarnation records and ingest tags
  • Fabric notebook/pipeline history
  • Eventhouse ingestion state
  • ML model output metadata where present

retail-setup verify queries these sources through one bounded, redacted report. Required historical, Reporting, ontology, Data Agent, and task-flow evidence has been exercised live. The remaining IMP-013 boundary is recent evidence from the intentionally manual stream.

items.title: Ownership
items.text:
• Base Silver/Gold columns and types: utility/src/retail_setup/generation/schemas.py
  • Live event payload mapping: utility/notebooks/templates/driver-05-stream.py
  • Eventhouse tables: fabric/kql_database/01-create-tables.kql
  • Active semantic-model tables: fabric/powerbi/retail_model.SemanticModel/definition/model.tmdl (TMDL, or Tabular Model Definition Language, is the text format used to define the Power BI semantic model)

For exact columns, types, and mappings, see the historical data contract, event contract, and semantic-model specification.

items.title: Naming reality
items.text: New columns use snake_case (lowercase words separated by underscores), but the current physical contract includes PascalCase and mixed-case columns retained for existing TMDL bindings. schemas.py is authoritative for those exceptions.

items.title: Business event tables
items.text: receipt_created, receipt_line_added, payment_processed, inventory_updated, stockout_detected, reorder_triggered, customer_entered, customer_zone_changed, ble_ping_detected, truck_arrived, truck_departed, store_opened, store_closed, ad_impression, promotion_applied, online_order_created, online_order_picked, online_order_shipped, online_order_line_added, online_order_delivered, logistics_incident_started, and logistics_incident_resolved. The last two carry the logistics incident model's starts and resolutions; they are sporadic (a few per DC and year).

items.title: Other KQL tables
items.text:
• unknown_event
  • anomaly_alerts (written by 16-persist-anomaly-alerts)
  • anomaly_detection_runs (one row per detection run)
  • pricing_recommendation_created (PENDING rows written by 14-ml-dynamic-pricing)
  • pricing_recommendation_approved
  • pricing_recommendation_rejected

The KQL scripts define six core materialized views (including mv_truck_delay_hourly) and two pricing decision metric views. fn_pending_recommendations() derives current pending state across the recommendation, approval, and rejection event tables. fn_rule_thresholds() holds the store-type-dependent rule thresholds that the deployment writes for the deployed store type, and fn_active_incidents(), fn_incident_impacted_stores(), and fn_lane_delays() read the logistics incident and truck delay tables.

items.title: Dimensions (7)
items.text: dim_geographies, dim_stores, dim_distribution_centers, dim_trucks, dim_customers, dim_products, dim_date.

items.title: Facts (21)
items.text:
fact_receipts, fact_receipt_lines, fact_payments, fact_store_ops, fact_foot_traffic, fact_ble_pings, fact_customer_zone_changes, fact_marketing, fact_marketing_attribution, fact_promotions, fact_promo_lines, fact_online_order_headers, fact_online_order_lines, fact_reorders, fact_truck_moves, fact_truck_inventory, fact_dc_inventory_txn, fact_store_inventory_txn, fact_stockouts, fact_logistics_incidents, fact_logistics_incident_stores.

Silver timestamps are UTC; dim_stores.TimeZone converts them to store-local time and fact_receipts.local_hour keeps the store-local hour.

items.text:
• setup_run_log
  • streaming-only ag._watermarks
  • owned streaming-only output fact_online_order_status
  • writer leases ag._job_locks (lock_name, owner, acquired_at, expires_at)
  • live stream state ag._stream_state_stores, _visits, _orders, _inventory, _logistics, and _meta: versioned rows of (incarnation, batch_id, entity_key, payload, deleted); see the live event contract

The solution manifest validates its named downstream exception, and the Delta maintenance inventory includes this table and the control tables.

items.text:
The Direct Lake model has 44 active tables. Direct Lake is a Power BI connection mode that reads Delta/Parquet data from OneLake directly, without a separate import copy or DirectQuery round trip:

  • 10 Gold aggregates
  • 6 ML outputs: churn_predictions, customer_segments, demand_forecast, stockout_risk, product_recommendations, price_elasticity

items.title: Resource ownership
items.text:
Terraform provisions or resolves the Fabric workspace, Lakehouse, Eventhouse, KQL database, and optional custom Spark pool. fabric-cicd (Microsoft's open-source Python library for deploying source-controlled Fabric item folders) publishes supported workspace items. KQL schema application runs separately with the operator identity.

Terraform ignores changes to the Lakehouse description and folder_id and the Eventhouse folder_id (lifecycle.ignore_changes in deploy/terraform/main.tf). Later deploy steps own them: fabric-cicd publishes the manifest description and workspace_folders moves each item to its type folder. Without this, every Terraform plan reported drift and reset both, and the next steps restored them.

items.title: Current item layout
items.text:
Location Items Notebooks All selected notebooks, including setup, live driver, ML and case preparation; reset excluded Pipelines All pipelines, including setup-pipeline Reports Main report and connected twins Semantic Models Direct Lake semantic model ML Experiments ML experiment shells Data Agents Semantic-model and ontology agents, automatically published after ontology creation in full-demo Lakehouses Lakehouse and its managed SQL endpoint Eventhouses Eventhouses and their managed KQL databases KQL Querysets Bundled KQL queryset Ontologies Ontology and any service-managed children Fabric Apps Merchandising & Replenishment (retail-approvals), Promotion Studio (retail-promotions), and any service-managed backing items

The deployment folder policy also covers independently movable graph models, SQL databases, Operations Agents and Plans. Fabric moves child items with their parent rather than allowing separate child folders. These managed exceptions are recorded in workspace-folder-report.json.

items.title: Pipeline topology
items.text: Pipeline Actual scope Schedule setup-pipeline Setup 01-10 as a dependency graph (02, 04 and 05 after 01; 03 after 04; 06-08 after 03; at most five at once) On demand; mandatory for Reporting profiles historical-data-load Retained historical-load notebook On demand streaming-data-load Streaming Silver then Gold; anomaly-alert persistence in parallel Every 30 minutes (UTC) when schedules.streaming_data_load is true (default: on only when stream.start_after_deploy is true) daily-maintenance Delta maintenance, demand-forecast and stockout models, then the Operations Agent signal refresh Daily 00:00 Eastern when schedules.daily_maintenance is true (default on) ml-required Two waves: Gold (setup-11), demand forecast, market basket, promotion effectiveness and stockout risk; then segmentation and churn; then the contract validator. Producers and Gold retry once On demand; terminal Reporting gate ml-optional Promoted optional outputs Full-demo post-Reporting ml-experimental Experimental outputs Full-demo post-Reporting

items.title: External dependencies
items.text:
• Microsoft Fabric tenant and capacity
  • Terraform 1.8 or later, below 2.0
  • Azure CLI for guided setup and Terraform, or Azure PowerShell for Python clients with validated --skip-terraform outputs/provider credentials
  • fabric-cicd
  • azure-identity
  • azure-kusto-data
  • mssql-python on Windows/Linux, or Microsoft ODBC Driver 17/18 on macOS, for Lakehouse SQL readiness checks
  • Fabric Spark and Spark Kusto connector

Exact versions are pinned in the hash-locked utility/requirements-deploy.txt (currently fabric-cicd 1.4.0, azure-identity 1.27.0, msal 1.39.0, mssql-python 1.18.0, pyodbc 5.5.0, azure-kusto-data 6.0.4, and jsonpath-ng 1.7.0, which fabric-cicd 1.4.0 caps below 1.8) and in deploy/terraform/providers.tf with its lock file (microsoft/fabric 1.15.1).

items.title: Local deployment state
items.text: Each workspace name determines a local environment key. Its ignored environment overlay, Terraform input, backend state, Terraform data directory, fabric-cicd configuration, live outputs, and run journal stay under that key. Generation configuration lives at utility/config/environments/<env>.yaml, rendered notebooks at utility/out/<env>/, and every publication phase stages under deploy/.generated/<env>/workspace/. Different environments do not share these local paths. Operators must still serialize runs for the same Fabric target; path isolation is not a distributed lock.

items.title: Current constraints
items.text:
• The default full-demo inventory includes live-preflight-validated preview features; explicitly selected core and standard inventories are preview-free.
  • Task-flow deployment uses metadata behavior outside a stable Fabric item source-control contract.
  • Offline validation does not prove live workspace readiness. The separate profile-aware verifier queries Fabric, Kusto, and Lakehouse SQL. Prior full-demo evidence does not validate later changes. Collect fresh required-path and optional-stream evidence for each environment and run.

See deployment requirements and the operations backlog.

items.title: Purpose
items.text:
The demo has two data paths:

  1. Fabric-native historical setup through retail-setup and setup notebooks.
  2. Optional live Real-Time Intelligence (RTI): stream-events.ipynb writes directly to Eventhouse, where KQL (Kusto Query Language) queries the events.

items.title: Primary historical path
items.text: setup-01 through setup-11 seed dictionaries, generate dimensions and facts, publish Silver, and build Gold directly in the Lakehouse. Fact generation is split by domain into notebooks that run in parallel where the stage graph allows. This path does not require ADLS parquet shortcuts or the retained historical-load notebook.

items.title: Optional live path
items.text:
stream-events emits all twenty-two of its declared business event types to Eventhouse through the Spark Kusto connector, which is the Kusto software component for Apache Spark. It continues the generated history with the same models (volume, store-local hours, customers, baskets, prices, payments, logistics incidents) and keeps state that spans micro-batches (stock, trucks, open orders, visits) in versioned Lakehouse tables, ag._stream_state_*. KQL supplies the recent-event query path. Optional Eventhouse shortcuts and streaming transforms project events into Lakehouse Silver and Gold.

Direct Lake is the Power BI connection mode that reads Lakehouse tables directly from OneLake without importing a second copy.

items.title: Contract owners
items.text:
• Setup behavior: CLI specification
  • Deploy inventory: deployment framework
  • Base Lakehouse schema: historical data contract
  • Event envelope and payloads: live event contract
  • Eventhouse and Lakehouse analytics: Fabric analytics
  • Power BI: semantic model
  • Ontology and agents: ML and AI contracts

items.title: Current support boundaries
items.text:
• Deployment profiles select exact, dependency-checked groups. The destructive reset group is excluded from every automatic profile.
  • Dashboard and rule source files are not guaranteed deployable items.
  • The semantic model is Direct Lake and has 44 active tables, including six ML outputs.
  • Lakehouse writers on independent schedules coordinate through lease rows in ag._job_locks; see data flow.
  • fact_online_order_status is a streaming-only Silver output outside the base table contract.
  • Prior full-demo setup, ML, Reporting, ontology, agents, task flow, and readiness runs provide baseline evidence, not validation of subsequent changes. Validation of changed paths, alternate authentication, core/standard profiles, and recent optional streaming remains in the relevant module backlogs.

items.title: Identities
items.text:
• Python deploy-time operations use an Azure CLI or Azure PowerShell operator identity. Terraform uses Azure CLI or an explicitly configured provider-supported service-principal, OIDC, or managed-identity credential; it cannot consume an Azure PowerShell session.
  • KQL schema application runs from the local deploy process.
  • The streaming notebook uses its Fabric runtime identity and needs ingestion rights on the target KQL database.
  • Reports, KQL, ontology, and agents use assigned consumer permissions.

items.title: Data handling
items.text: All records are generated synthetic data for demonstration only. Production customer data is outside the supported boundary. Fabric workspace and item permissions control access; row-level privacy controls for generated records are not part of the default release.

items.title: Current controls
items.text:
• Local generation config and generated output are ignored.
  • Secrets are expected from identity, secret stores, environment variables, or ignored files.
  • KQL application is centralized.
  • Direct streaming requires pre-existing tables through FailIfNotExist.
  • Canonical public documentation is built only from reviewed docs/ content.
  • The default semantic model and agents may expose generated row-level detail to authorized workspace consumers.
  • Shared Lakehouse control tables (ag._stream_state_*, ag._job_locks, ag._watermarks) are protected only by workspace permissions. The stream state is versioned per incarnation and batch, and leases expire; neither is an access control (THREAT-012, SEC-015).
  • Deploy-time generation writes only typed numeric thresholds into fn_rule_thresholds(), and Data Agent snapshots are generated from the TMDL and the ontology builder with a CI drift check (THREAT-013, SEC-016).

items.title: Verification boundaries
items.text:
• Tenant-aware identity, bearer request handling, and target checks exist; alternate-authentication and renamed-target live proof remains IMP-001.
  • Required Eventhouse writes raise on failure so Spark cannot commit a failed micro-batch. Replay/checkpoint and deep-reconciliation code has local tests, but fresh injected-failure Fabric proof remains outstanding.
  • Environment-local configuration/render/staging and saved-plan guards do not replace operator review or serialize arbitrary remote writers.
  • Prior readiness reports do not verify subsequent changes; collect fresh live evidence for the revision being deployed.
  • The optional local app uses operator identity and browser token delivery for embedding; its proposal store is local and its Eventhouse telemetry is best-effort. See THREAT-009 before describing this as durable governance.

See access control and the security backlog.

items.title: Requirements ownership
items.text: Requirements define required outcomes, constraints, and acceptance criteria. Exact interfaces and workflows belong in specifications, current structure belongs in architecture, and risks and mitigations belong in security.

items.title: Stable IDs
items.text:
Prefix Owner REQ-CORE-* Cross-cutting demo behavior REQ-SETUP-* Bootstrap, configuration, and rendering REQ-DEPLOY-* Provisioning and publication REQ-GEN-* Historical synthetic data REQ-STREAM-* Live events and streaming transforms REQ-AN-* Eventhouse and Lakehouse analytics REQ-MLAI-* Machine learning, ontology, and agents REQ-BI-* Power BI semantic model and report REQ-OPS-* Readiness, monitoring, recovery, and CI REQ-SEC-* Security and governance outcomes REQ-DOCS-*, REQ-PUBLISH-* Documentation and publishing THREAT-*, SEC-* Security threats and controls IMP-* Improvement or implementation item tracked in a module backlog ENH-* Optional enhancement idea tracked in a module backlog

IDs are permanent. Retire an obsolete ID in traceability.md; do not reuse it for a different outcome.

items.title: Traceability states
items.text:
Only these states are allowed:

State Meaning proposed Draft outcome that has not been accepted. accepted Normative outcome; implementation is absent or incomplete. implemented Exact implementation evidence exists; verification is incomplete. verified Exact implementation and verification evidence exist. blocked The outcome cannot progress until a named external or upstream gate is resolved. retired The outcome is no longer required and its replacement or rationale is recorded.

items.title: Module ownership
items.text:
Each module has one requirements page and one backlog. A backlog contains only:

  • ## Open
  • ## Settled — do not reopen

Keep completed work out of backlogs. Git history and traceability.md retain the evidence.

items.title: Requirements traceability
items.text: This ledger records one row per stable requirement or threat ID. Use the states defined in Requirements ownership. Mark a row verified only when exact implementation and verification evidence exist.

items.title: Current remediation evidence boundary
items.text:
No fresh live deployments were performed in the recorded repair session. References below to prior full-demo runs, recovery, or hosted CI are historical baseline evidence, not verification of the repaired working tree. Generator implementation and independent review are complete. Pipeline, deployment-safety, Power BI, batch, package/cache/injection/build, and test/readiness code are complete in local scope. All five generated notebooks were rebuilt and drift checked; the ancillary review finding is resolved. Full Spark/filesystem/E2E and remote service/hosted release gates remain open.

New local environment isolation/resume/plan guards, Silver reconciliation, writer/cleanup safeguards, pipeline parameters, and KQL corrections have local validation evidence; no fresh live deployment is claimed. Existing test paths alone are not passing results. Preserve IMP-001, IMP-005, IMP-012, and IMP-013 external gates.

Recorded local results include 85 passing non-filesystem Spark tests and four passing Spark cases for the final holiday return-window correction. The utility non-Spark suite passed 391 tests; full utility Ruff and all five rebuilt notebook drift checks passed. The final post-fix root run passed 523 tests with one opt-in live test skipped. Final rebuilt wheel, notebook, dictionary-cache, and utility contract coverage passed 126 tests. The Windows CI marker selection executed three real Spark tests successfully. Notebook 12–14 metadata and DataAgent description contract blockers are closed. No live requirement is promoted to verified from these offline results.

The adversarial data review (PRs #451-#461) changed the historical contract (UTC timestamps, new columns and tables), the live event contract (new events, .alter table restatements, policies, checkpoint folders), the stream's internals (versioned state, incarnations), Lakehouse coordination (writer locks, ML waves, incremental Silver), consumers (rules, anomaly functions, measures, agent snapshots) and the ML notebooks. Their rows cite offline unit, contract, statistical and Spark tests; local runs and green hosted CI are recorded in each PR. None of it has run in Fabric. Rows whose behavior is only observable in a workspace stay implemented and name the pending live check; the live-acceptance run (setup re-run, KQL redeploy, a new stream incarnation) is tracked by IMP-005, IMP-013, and IMP-014.

PR #450 moved the deploy dependencies to fabric-cicd 1.4.0, azure-identity 1.27.0, msal 1.39.0, mssql-python 1.18.0, pyodbc 5.5.0, jsonpath-ng 1.7.0, and the microsoft/fabric Terraform provider 1.15.1, and made Terraform ignore the Lakehouse description and folder_id and the Eventhouse folder_id. Its recorded live evidence on retail-demo-kroger: fabric-cicd 1.4.0 publication succeeded, readiness passed with only the three optional-stream unknowns, mssql-python 1.18 queried the SQL endpoint, and a Terraform plan reported no changes after the ignore_changes fix. That run predates the data-review contract changes.
