items.title: Minimum deployment baseline
items.text:
Before a shared or customer-facing demo:

  1. Confirm the signed-in tenant and target workspace.
  2. Review workspace and item roles.
  3. Confirm generated files contain no credentials or operator-specific secrets.
  4. Confirm the workspace contains generated synthetic demo data only.
  5. Confirm monitoring and failure notifications are available.
  6. Validate that reset and recreate actions target the intended environment.

items.title: Supply-chain lock maintenance
items.text:
Change the owning input (requirements-*.in, utility/pyproject.toml, or deploy/terraform/providers.tf) before regenerating its reviewed lock:

python scripts/compile_locks.py

The script regenerates requirements-docs.txt, requirements-test.txt, utility/requirements-deploy.txt, utility/requirements-customize.txt (the opt-in Copilot SDK, constrained to the deploy pins), and utility/requirements-ci.txt. To regenerate only some of them, pass their paths. If uv is missing, the script installs uv==0.11.29 with pip. It passes the package index configured for pip to uv, including corporate feed proxies set in pip.ini/pip.conf or PIP_INDEX_URL. It then removes any non-SHA-256 hashes that a proxy publishes, so the locks stay SHA-256-only. Each lock header still records the plain uv pip compile command.

After changing the Fabric provider version, regenerate all supported platform checksums:

terraform -chdir=deploy/terraform providers lock `
  -platform=linux_amd64 -platform=linux_arm64 `
  -platform=windows_amd64 -platform=windows_arm64 `
  -platform=darwin_amd64 -platform=darwin_arm64

Miniforge version changes require updating every platform URL and SHA-256 value in scripts/setup.sh plus the exact winget version in scripts/setup.ps1.

items.title: Threat model
items.text: This document records the demo's security threats. See controls.md for mitigations and traceability for implementation and verification evidence.

items.title: Scope and assumptions
items.text:
• Microsoft Entra ID is the identity plane for Fabric access.
  • Operators use Azure CLI or Azure PowerShell for Python clients; Terraform requires a provider-supported identity.
  • GitHub Actions builds documentation and can run privileged automation.
  • Supported records are generated synthetic data. Production customer data is outside the demo boundary.
  • Preview Fabric features are not available in every tenant.
  • Generated configuration and output are not durable sources of truth.
  • The optional local app is a separate operator/browser boundary, not a hosted multi-user service secured solely by Fabric permissions. Live embedding sends an operator-derived Power BI token to the browser. Replay is not live query evidence.

items.title: Assets
items.text:
• Workspace roles, item permissions, and resource bindings.
  • Lakehouse, Eventhouse, semantic-model, ontology, and Data Agent access.
  • Deployment credentials, tokens, and environment-specific identifiers.
  • Run-history, freshness, approval, and verification evidence.
  • Lakehouse control state: live stream state (ag._stream_state_*), writer leases (ag._job_locks), and Silver watermarks (ag._watermarks).
  • Deploy-time generated artifacts: environment rule thresholds in fn_rule_thresholds() and the Data Agent datasource.json/ontology.json snapshots.
  • Canonical documentation and the public static site.

items.title: Trust boundaries
items.text:
flowchart LR
    Contributor[Contributor] --> GitHub[Repository and Actions]
    Operator[Deploy operator] --> Auth[Azure identity]
    GitHub --> Fabric[Fabric workspace]
    Auth --> Fabric
    Fabric --> Data[Lakehouse and Eventhouse]
    Data --> BI[Power BI, ontology, and agents]
    BI --> Consumer[Authorized consumers]
    Operator --> App[Local app]
    App --> Fabric
    App --> Browser[Operator browser and embed token]
    Operator --> Copilot[GitHub Copilot: business name only, during customize]
    GitHub --> Pages[Public Pages site]

items.title: Threats
items.text: ID Threat Impact Required controls Residual risk THREAT-001 Retired: workspace/model access exposes generated row-level customer-like data. Records are synthetic and demo-only. SEC-001, SEC-002 Row-level privacy controls for generated records are outside the release scope. THREAT-002 Credentials or tokens are committed, logged, masked incorrectly, or sent to the wrong endpoint. Unauthorized access or failed deployment. SEC-001, SEC-003, SEC-009 Request headers, tenant propagation, and redacted journals have local contracts; ontology-notebook token-host allowlisting is implemented without a dedicated test; alternate-auth/renamed-target live proof remains IMP-001. THREAT-003 Retired: an agent answers beyond its persona or returns generated row-level detail. Records are synthetic and demo-only. — Mandatory persona/prohibited-detail controls are outside the default release; richer experiences remain optional under ENH-003. THREAT-004 Mutable actions, plugins, or dependencies run with privileged tokens. Supply-chain compromise or unreviewed changes. SEC-007 Immutable repository references and locks have contracts; registries, OS package managers, and hosted runner images remain external trust roots. THREAT-005 Activity, deployment state, or freshness is not observable. Incidents or stale demo output go undetected. SEC-008 Readiness has historical baseline evidence; current cleanup/degradation consistency and fresh required/optional execution remain open. THREAT-006 Misbinding or unsafe reset targets the wrong tenant, workspace, or state. Cross-environment modification or destructive loss. SEC-001, SEC-009 Environment-local paths, fingerprinted resume, target validation, and saved-plan guards exist. They do not lock concurrent remote writers or replace operator review; live recovery drills remain outstanding. THREAT-007 Required streaming or deploy failures are treated as success. Lost integrity, advanced checkpoints, or false readiness. SEC-008, SEC-011 Required writes and progress fail closed in source; fresh Fabric failure/recovery proof remains open. Successful promotion with cleanup warnings must degrade, not falsely fail, readiness. THREAT-008 Public docs publish secrets, target-specific values, or temporary internal evidence. Disclosure and stale guidance. SEC-003, SEC-010 Review every source and built file, including files omitted from navigation. Zensical publishes non-nav files; inspect old tagged sites separately. THREAT-009 The optional app presents replay, local approval, or lossy telemetry as authenticated production action/audit evidence. False operational assurance, unauthorized future actions, or lost evidence. SEC-003, SEC-008, SEC-012 Proposals are local drafts and Eventhouse logging is best-effort. Per-user authorization, production adapters, durable audit, evidence validation, idempotency, and scope limits are not established by an approval button. THREAT-010 Notebook substitution executes configuration strings, or unverified/mismatched dictionary content is reused. Unintended statements or irreproducible data. SEC-007, SEC-013 Literal/JSON encoding, ref and cache checks, mutable refresh, and manifest-last publication are implemented; notebooks were rebuilt and drift checked. Explicit refs/fork overrides remain caller-selected; fresh live execution remains open. THREAT-011 A custom business layout carries injected instructions, unsafe text, real trademarks, or tampered dictionaries into notebooks, reports, or apps. Script/markup injection in themed artifacts, trademark misuse in demos, or data that differs from the reviewed layout. SEC-007, SEC-014 Copilot runs without built-in tools or permissions and output is schema- and text-validated; colors reach artifacts only as validated hex. The logo session's only tool is a read-only Wikimedia Commons search: Copilot's pick must be a returned file, the code downloads it from Wikimedia hosts only, and the SVG is sanitized and pinned by SHA-256 before it reaches reports or apps. Commons descriptions are untrusted model input; at worst they steer the choice among real search results, which the operator reviews in the preview. The fictionalization guard rejects only names the model declares or the business name itself, so the operator preview remains the final check for undeclared real brands. Copilot data handling follows the operator's GitHub Copilot terms. THREAT-012 Lakehouse control state (ag._stream_state_*, ag._job_locks) is edited, deleted, or left stale out of band, or a writer ignores the locks. The stream emits inconsistent events (negative stock, duplicate or missing trucks), two writers overwrite the same Delta table, or a stale lease blocks Silver, Gold or ML runs. SEC-008, SEC-011, SEC-015 Any workspace contributor can write these tables; the controls make normal replays, restarts and crashes safe, not tampering. Live Fabric behavior of the leases and the state tables is unverified. THREAT-013 Deploy-time substitution or snapshot generation writes unintended content into deployed definitions: non-numeric text in fn_rule_thresholds(), or Data Agent snapshots that drift from the model or select unintended fields. Broken or misleading alerting, KQL that fails to apply, or agents grounded on stale or unintended fields. SEC-013, SEC-016 Thresholds come from the operator's own environment configuration; the snapshots select every model field by design because the data is synthetic. Live re-export comparison of the deployed agents is outstanding.

items.title: Review triggers
items.text: Review when identities, public endpoints, agents, data classification, preview defaults, external action adapters, Lakehouse control tables, deploy-time substitutions, or documentation publication boundaries change. Prior Fabric runs do not validate changes made after those runs.

items.title: Specifications
items.text:
Specifications define exact behavior: interfaces, files, schemas, mappings, workflow order, state transitions, errors, compatibility, and current known divergence.

Requirements describe what must be true. Architecture describes where components sit. Security describes threats and controls. The guides turn these specifications into procedures.

items.title: Module owners
items.text:
Module Specification Cross-cutting conventions Core conventions Setup CLI and render contract Deployment Deployment framework Historical generation Data contract Live streaming Event contract Eventhouse and Lakehouse analytics Fabric analytics ML, ontology, and agents Model contracts; decision experience; application routing Power BI Semantic model Operations Runbook Security Access control Documentation Zensical site

These specifications replace the dated implementation plans and retired Docusaurus source.

items.title: Supported path
items.text:
Follow this setup sequence:

  1. scripts/setup.ps1, scripts/setup.sh, or python scripts/setup.py
  2. retail-setup configure
  3. retail-setup render
  4. retail-setup deploy or manual import
  5. setup notebooks 01 through 11
  6. optional stream-events

items.title: Configuration boundaries
items.text:
Location Ownership deploy/config/deploy.yml Shared deployment defaults deploy/config/environments/<env>.yml Ignored workspace target overlay utility/config/environments/<env>.yaml Ignored environment-specific generation configuration; legacy utility/config.yaml is a read fallback utility/out/<env>/ Environment-specific rendered notebooks deploy/.generated/<env>/terraform.tfvars Ignored Terraform input deploy/.generated/<env>/terraform.tfstate Ignored isolated Terraform state deploy/.generated/<env>/fabric-cicd/ Ignored publication config and rewrites deploy/.generated/<env>/ Ignored live outputs, run journal, and combined KQL deploy/.generated/<env>/workspace/ Environment-specific Fabric item staging

The workspace name determines the environment key. Select the environment explicitly for render and deploy. Local target and generated files are not authoritative project records.

items.title: Time and determinism
items.text:
• Use UTC timestamps with timezone-aware APIs.
  • Historical configuration is centered on months; the derived range ends yesterday.
  • Seeded generation uses deterministic hash-based draws suitable for Spark.
  • Event timestamps must preserve lifecycle order even when ingestion can be out of order.

items.title: Naming
items.text:
• New pipeline columns use snake_case.
  • KQL event tables use snake_case.
  • Presentation names may be user-friendly.
  • The current physical contract still contains PascalCase and mixed-case columns required by existing Tabular Model Definition Language (TMDL) bindings in the Power BI model. Those exceptions are explicit in schemas.py; documentation must not claim the current model is pure snake_case.

items.title: Support tiers
items.text: Tier Meaning Core Required for the supported historical demo Optional Supported only when explicitly selected and prepared Preview Requires tenant capability preflight and explicit consent Manual Source or template exists, but publication/configuration is not automated Proposed Backlog idea with no supported implementation claim

items.title: Documentation ownership
items.text: docs/ is the only site source. Requirements, specifications, architecture, security, and guides must link rather than duplicate normative content.

items.title: Purpose
items.text:
contracts/retail-demo.json defines shared metadata across the demo's modules. Its top-level sections are frozen at version 1.4.0:

  • metadata and version;
  • prerequisites and commands;
  • assets;
  • profiles;
  • readiness_expectations;
  • data_contracts, event_paths, and exceptions;
  • ml_contracts;
  • source_owners.

The resolver uses profile entries to select existing logical assets, notebook groups, pipeline folders, and Eventhouse KQL objects. Repository validation compares ML contract entries with producer notebook declarations, required runtime-validator declarations, and active TMDL projections.

items.title: Authority boundary
items.text:
The manifest defines stable IDs, logical ownership, support status, descriptions, source pointers, profile-to-existing-group/asset selection, dependency metadata, contract and path declarations, and explicit exceptions. It does not own item definitions or pipeline bodies. ML schema declarations are validated projections of their physical producer/TMDL sources, not a second unchecked physical schema.

Physical fact Authoritative source Available item types, notebook groups, and physical staging behavior deploy/config/deploy.yml and deploy/scripts/build_artifacts.py Event tables, fields, types, and JSON paths KQL DDL/mappings and driver-05-stream.py ENVELOPE/EVENT_PAYLOADS Historical Lakehouse tables, fields, and types utility/src/retail_setup/generation/schemas.py TABLES Active semantic-model tables and Direct Lake bindings model.tmdl references plus each table TMDL's executable schemaName/entityName partition ML output schemas Producer notebook ML_OUTPUT_CONTRACTS; active TMDL for the six Reporting outputs

Each physical inventory declaration specifies how to derive its members and which source to read. Validators calculate the inventory from that source. Do not copy item names, event fields, or table schemas into the manifest.

The live event extension follows the same boundary. The manifest stores the stable envelope/event/path IDs, business and dedupe keys, UTC event-time semantics, physical targets, terminal coverage, and named exceptions. Parsers derive fields, types, nullability, JSON paths, transforms, Gold outputs, and active TMDL bindings from the physical sources during every check.

Each event path must declare its own exact Silver, optional Gold, and optional semantic-model source pointers. Validation does not pool pointers across paths. The path mode, source/target asset roles, controlling contract IDs, and named terminal exception must agree with that path. The envelope declaration must select the ENVELOPE symbol owned by the event contract and share the physical driver source used for EVENT_PAYLOADS.

Every source pointer must resolve inside the repository. Validators parse selector-backed pointers using the declared selector. A pointer to a whole file or directory proves only that it exists and has an owner; it does not validate its contents. Contract checks use the declared selectors directly.

items.title: Readers and validation
items.text:
retail_setup.contracts provides the strict Pydantic loader and repository-aware validators. Validation checks:

  • the frozen schema, globally unique IDs, and internal references;
  • repository-local source existence and selectors;
  • profile references against existing artifact groups and pipelines;
  • profile dependency closure, deployment classification, group/asset agreement, exact item/KQL selection, staged counts, and workspace folders;
  • source .platform and staged item descriptions against manifest-owned asset descriptions;
  • source-derived inventory relationships;
  • Eventhouse DDL, ingestion mappings, and direct-writer field/type/path agreement;
  • all 18 emitted-event routes, the nine-field envelope, the operational unknown_event table, Silver/Gold transforms, and active semantic terminals;
  • each path's mode, asset/contract ownership, exact per-path sources, and semantic-or-exception terminal coverage;
  • the derived five-input marketing-attribution route;
  • every active TMDL table's executable Direct Lake binding, its agreement with sourceLineageTag, and the expected ag or au physical table;
  • representative wire fixtures, including nullable and unknown-event cases;
  • all 14 ML producer/source/schema/grain/temporal/lineage declarations;
  • required ML agreement across producer, validator, and active TMDL;
  • all 27 readiness check IDs, categories, profile applicability, and required/optional behavior against the unchanged runtime taxonomy;
  • declared inventory exceptions.

Run this read-only check from a repository checkout:

python scripts/check_data_contracts.py

It prints stable counts and source-derived streaming-only, historical-only, and operational boundaries. It never rewrites KQL, notebooks, schemas, or TMDL.

scripts/solution_manifest.py uses only the Python standard library. It exposes identity, prerequisites, canonical command examples, profile names and the default, publication counts/folders, manifest version, and a deterministic semantic SHA-256. Bootstrap reads it before installing dependencies; scripts/setup.py derives its --profile default from this view. Both readers reject primitive type coercion. Agreement and negative tests keep the projection aligned with the typed reader. Dry-run output, deploy journals, artifact inventories, and readiness reports carry the same manifest version/hash and resolved profile boundaries.

For the readable inventory, see the workspace and profile inventory.

items.title: Extension points
items.text:
Later work should populate existing sections rather than introduce parallel manifests:

  • profile execution belongs in profiles; separate live core/standard proof remains under IMP-012;
  • ML methodology and outputs belong in executable ml_contracts; the live required-ML/Reporting gate was completed under the settled IMP-008;
  • event fixtures and routes are implemented in data_contracts, event_paths, and exceptions; live Fabric evidence remains IMP-005;
  • readiness taxonomy metadata belongs in readiness_expectations; actual live evidence remains environment-local and the manual-stream boundary remains IMP-013;
  • live alternate-auth/renamed-target proof remains IMP-001, while core/standard profile proof remains IMP-012.

Add a source-derived inventory when physical membership is needed. Add an exceptions record for intentional divergence and remove it when the sources converge.

items.title: Eventhouse/KQL scripts
items.text:
Deployment applies numbered scripts in repository order:

  1. 01-create-tables.kql
  2. 02-create-ingestion-mappings.kql
  3. 03-create-functions.kql
  4. 04-create-materialized-views.kql
  5. 06-ml-anomaly-detection.kql
  6. 07-pricing-approval-tables.kql

Each source file is a standalone, fail-fast .execute database script with (ThrowOnErrors=true) batch. apply_kql.py removes that one leading wrapper from each selected source and emits one flat outer fail-fast script; embedded or repeated wrappers are rejected.

items.title: KQL object inventory
items.text:
• 22 typed business event tables
  • unknown_event
  • anomaly_alerts and its run log anomaly_detection_runs, written by 16-persist-anomaly-alerts in streaming-data-load
  • 3 pricing recommendation/decision tables; 14-ml-dynamic-pricing appends PENDING rows to pricing_recommendation_created
  • 6 core materialized views, including mv_truck_delay_hourly
  • 2 pricing decision metric materialized views
  • fn_pending_recommendations() for latest cross-event workflow state
  • fn_rule_thresholds() with the deployed store type's rule thresholds
  • fn_active_incidents(), fn_incident_impacted_stores(), and fn_lane_delays() over the logistics incident and truck delay tables
  • functions for attribution, truck SLA, anomaly detection, and related queries

Core materialized-view definitions are time-independent; seven-day retention is applied as a materialized-view policy. Anomaly functions build hourly series that start at the first event in the lookback and end at bin(now(), 1h), so the open hour is never scored. Counts default to zero; basket and payment-rate averages default to null and are filled with series_fill_linear. Inventory movement is scored per store, and only after ANOMALY_MIN_ACTIVE_HOURS (24) active hours; rows with a null store_id are dropped from every series. The functions then sort severity through a numeric rank while preserving the public result schema. Detector parameters come from calibration.py. fn_new_anomaly_alerts(lookback_hours, persist_hours, closed_end) keeps only closed hourly bins and alert ids not yet in anomaly_alerts, so the scheduled persistence is idempotent.

The direct live path writes typed tables and does not use the JSON ingestion mappings.

items.title: Lakehouse layers
items.text:
Layer Schema/location Role Live Bronze cusn shortcuts Read-only Eventhouse table references exposed to Spark; cusn is the demo schema used for these shortcuts Silver ag Typed dimensions, facts, and operational state Gold au Ten reporting aggregates and contract-tiered ML outputs

The primary historical path writes Silver/Gold directly through setup notebooks. The Eventhouse shortcut path is optional for incremental live projection.

items.title: ML output tiers and runtime validation
items.text:
contracts/retail-demo.json defines 14 executable output contracts. Each references its authoritative producer notebook and declares exact schema, grain, as-of and lineage fields, source tables, intended use, and limitations. The six required Reporting tables also reference their active TMDL projection. Repository validation fails when a producer, manifest declaration, validator, or TMDL projection disagrees.

The ML and AI contract lists all 14 outputs and their Required, Optional, or Experimental tiers.

15-validate-required-ml-contract runs after all required producers. It fails on missing or empty tables, incompatible schemas, null or duplicate grain keys, invalid probability/bound values, missing as-of or lineage values, and incomplete demand-forecast horizons. It does not create placeholder tables. Only its pipeline's terminal success permits Reporting publication.

items.title: Streaming-to-Silver behavior
items.text:
03-streaming-to-silver.ipynb reads Eventhouse shortcuts and replays a configurable interval from each per-source checkpoint in ag._watermarks. The default overlap is three hours to cover normal Eventhouse OneLake visibility latency. Once per day by default, a distinct per-source reconciliation checkpoint permits a bounded-cadence scan of older history. That scan anti-joins source dedupe keys against Silver and adds only missing rows to the same idempotent merge. Processing and reconciliation checkpoints advance only after the merge succeeds; null checkpoint timestamps still fail closed. Override the defaults with the REPLAY_OVERLAP_SECONDS and DEEP_RECONCILIATION_INTERVAL_SECONDS notebook parameters or environment variables.

The pipeline passes Lakehouse/schema notebook parameters and uses concurrency = 1 to prevent overlapping runs of that pipeline. Across pipelines and manual runs, 03 holds the silver writer lock in ag._job_locks and skips the run when it can't get it within LOCK_WAIT_SECONDS (see fabric/pipelines/README.md). The daily deep scan is cadence-gated, not a scan of all source history on every run.

Marketing attribution is incremental too. A run reconsiders only purchases newer than the marketing_attribution watermark (the newest purchase it has processed) minus the seven-day window and the replay overlap, plus purchases and journeys whose rows were merged this run with older event times (late arrivals and deep-reconciliation backfills). Touches, payments and promotions are read only for those candidates, from the earliest candidate minus the window. The first run, or a run whose late keys exceed ATTRIBUTION_LATE_KEY_LIMIT, reads full history. Journey IDs are trimmed when read instead of by table-wide UPDATEs, and the legacy store-operation casing repair runs once (recorded in _watermarks). If a run fails after merging a deep-reconciliation backfill but before attribution, those purchases are not revisited automatically. utility/tests/generation/test_streaming_silver_bounded_runtime.py checks that the candidate set stays the same when history grows tenfold.

Truck arrival/departure is handled as one lifecycle: Silver joins the two sources on truck, distribution center, store, and shipment before appending a completed fact_truck_moves row. A normal run reads departures from the replay window and their arrivals (up to a day earlier), and compares them with Silver lifecycles from the earliest candidate departure on. The daily deep reconciliation (and the first run) reads the whole retained truck sources, so delayed counterparts are not lost behind the watermark. tests/test_truck_dwell_contract.py verifies the cross-layer source contract; live Fabric execution remains a separate gate.

Live-specific behavior and divergences:

  • inventory_updated deterministically continues prior balances, orders deltas by event time and trace ID, and repairs legacy null-balance suffixes for affected store/product keys;
  • ad_impression rows are dated by impression_time (when a journey touch was shown) while the watermark follows ingest_timestamp (when it arrived with its purchase), so touches fall inside the replay window;
  • store operations are written as lower-case opened/closed, like history, and older upper-case rows are normalized once; promotion_applied.product_ids becomes the historical comma-separated, sorted ID list;
  • picked, shipped and delivered events populate ag.fact_online_order_status, and each run moves recent live fact_online_order_lines with their order (PICKED, SHIPPED, DELIVERED, or CANCELLED for zero-total headers);
  • inventory_updated rows without a store are DC stock moves and go to fact_dc_inventory_txn; lost sales keep their demand in requested_quantity and unfulfilled_quantity;
  • logistics_incident_started inserts one fact_logistics_incidents row and its fact_logistics_incident_stores rows; logistics_incident_resolved sets resolved_at once through a Delta MERGE;
  • fact_receipts.local_hour is derived from dim_stores.TimeZone;
  • fact_online_order_status is an owned streaming-only Silver contract: its exact schema and routes are declared in the Silver notebook, its terminal exception is validated from contracts/retail-demo.json, and 05-maintain-delta-tables.ipynb includes it and ag._watermarks in routine maintenance;
  • it is intentionally absent from schemas.py and the active semantic model because TABLES remains the historical contract;
  • live coverage is not equivalent for every historical fact.

Inventory also has runtime test coverage: utility/tests/generation/test_streaming_inventory_runtime.py executes the actual notebook transformation functions with real Spark DataFrames and windows. It covers prior-balance continuation, legacy-null repair, same-timestamp ordering by trace_id, and idempotent replay. The recorded local result is a pass on Spark 4.2 with a checksum-verified session-local JDK 17. Target-table lookup is stubbed; no live Delta MERGE, full Spark suite, or Fabric execution is proven by this test.

Watermark/replay behavior is fail-closed and contract-tested. The manifest declares all 22 emitted paths and derives the physical transform inventory from this notebook. python scripts/check_data_contracts.py fails if a route, terminal, mapping, key, or named boundary drifts.

items.title: Streaming-to-Gold behavior
items.text:
04-streaming-to-gold.ipynb and setup-11 build the ten Gold tables from one definition, utility/src/retail_setup/generation/gold_rules.py, which utility/scripts/build_notebooks.py copies into notebook 04. Sales tables count SALE receipts with an approved payment, online sales count orders with an approved payment, truck_dwell_daily has one row per completed shipment lifecycle dated by its arrival, and no source row at or after the Gold cutoff is used: the end of the generated history (local midnight after END_DATE, allowing 12 hours past UTC midnight) until streaming starts, then the build time. utility/tests/generation/test_gold_notebook_parity.py runs notebook 04's cells and gold.py on the same input and compares every table. 04 holds the gold writer lock and skips the run when setup-11 or maintenance holds it.

04-streaming-to-gold.ipynb writes each of the ten Gold candidates to a run-scoped staging schema. All ten must exist and pass row-count/schema validation before promotion. The notebook captures each prior Delta version; an attempted promotion failure restores pre-existing targets and drops newly created targets in reverse order. Rollback continues after individual restore errors and preserves staging when manual recovery is required.

Nine Gold tables have an emitted-event route. dc_inventory_position_current is rebuilt in batch from the DC ledger and is part of the named historical boundary, although the stream also appends DC stock moves to fact_dc_inventory_txn. The derived attribution path combines five Silver inputs and terminates at fact_marketing_attribution and campaign_performance_daily in the active semantic model.

items.title: Querysets
items.text: Checked-in KQL files are bundled as one KQLQueryset item with one tab per query. Deployment rewrites its cluster/database binding.

items.title: Dashboards and rules
items.text:
Dashboard JSON/templates and KQL rule definitions are source inputs, not guaranteed deployable items. They may require manual import and binding. Activator is Fabric's event-driven alerting and action service. Claims about five-minute schedules or deployed Activator actions are not current defaults.

Rule thresholds are calibrated from the generator (calibration.py), and utility/tests/generation/test_calibration.py fails when a rule, dashboard tile, anomaly function or TMDL literal drifts from them. Two thresholds depend on the store type: the zone-surge arrival count (the entrance arrivals of the largest store at the store type's busiest hour, weekday and month in the best weather, plus four Poisson standard deviations; 117 per 5 minutes for supercenter) and the high-value receipt (10 times the store type's avg_ticket_target, about one ticket in a thousand). They reach the rules through fn_rule_thresholds(). The checked-in function carries the reference store type's values; apply_kql.py --environment writes the deployed store type's values (custom layouts and the configured transactions per store-day included) as typed real/long literals and fails unless the function and each threshold appear exactly once. Every rule deduplicates on trace_id; the stockout and URGENT reorder rules raise one alert per store (or DC) and window, listing the products, and the incident-stockout rule one per incident. The dwell-breach rule keys on the departure's ingestion_time() through fn_truck_sla().departure_ingested_at. See fabric/rules/README.md for each rule.

items.title: KPI semantics
items.text: Current-state tables are overwrite snapshots. KQL and DAX use producer-aligned status labels, shared date slicing, source-correct grain, volume-weighted rollups, and hidden non-aggregatable technical fields. Repository contract tests guard those semantics.

items.title: Receipt repair utility
items.text: 90-augment-and-dedupe-receipts.ipynb materializes and validates candidates and backups before replacing receipt-grain targets. It records each attempted promotion before issuing the replacement statement. A server commit followed by a client exception therefore includes that target in reverse-order rollback, rather than silently restoring only earlier targets. tests/test_lakehouse_batch_ml_fixes.py exercises this failure window with executable mocks. Local batch work is complete; actual Fabric/Delta rollback execution remains a separate live gate.

items.title: Maintenance
items.text:
05-maintain-delta-tables.ipynb maintains every Silver table in schemas.TABLES, every Gold aggregate, every ML output, and the Silver control tables (_watermarks, _job_locks, the six _stream_state_* tables, fact_online_order_status, setup_run_log). It claims each table's writer lock without waiting and skips tables whose lock is held.

tests/test_maintenance_table_inventory.py keeps the lists and their ZORDER columns equal to those contracts. It skips genuinely absent optional tables, including optional ML/streaming state; missing required historical tables fail its base-inventory check. Checks and maintenance statements use fully qualified configured Lakehouse/schema/table names. Only genuine table absence is skipped: permission, catalog, and other real AnalysisException failures propagate rather than being reclassified as optional absence. Operation failures fail the notebook. Deployment supplies configured Lakehouse/schema parameters to pipeline notebook activities.

These changes are implemented locally. Fresh remote KQL, Silver/Gold, pipeline-concurrency, and maintenance smoke tests remain release gates.

items.title: Current order
items.text:
The supported deploy orchestrator is retail-setup deploy.

flowchart LR
    Resolve[Resolve manifest profile]
    Preflight[Validate profile preflight]
    Config[Generate environment config]
    TF[Terraform init/apply or resolve existing outputs]
    StageInfra[Stage infrastructure without Reporting]
    PublishInfra[Publish infrastructure]
    KQL[Build and execute ordered KQL script]
    Setup[Wait for setup-pipeline]
    RequiredML[Wait for ml-required + validator]
    StageReporting[Stage Reporting]
    PublishReporting[Publish Reporting]
    ExtendedML[Run selected post-Reporting ML]
    RefreshSQL[Synchronize Lakehouse SQL endpoint metadata]
    Validate[Validate publication]
    Ontology[Create or validate ontology]
    Agents[Publish Data Agents]
    TaskFlow[Deploy and read back complete task flow]
    FinalVerify[Verify complete readiness]

    Resolve --> Preflight --> Config --> TF --> StageInfra --> PublishInfra --> KQL
    KQL --> Setup --> RequiredML --> StageReporting --> PublishReporting
    PublishReporting --> ExtendedML --> RefreshSQL --> Validate --> Ontology
    Ontology --> Agents --> TaskFlow --> FinalVerify

Local and live preflight run before Terraform destroy/apply, item publication, or KQL changes. Local preflight validates source and state contracts. The orchestrator invokes it with --source-only to check committed notebook inputs before rendering; it does not require a prior rendered output set. Explicit rendered-output validation resolves utility/out/<env>/, not the shared legacy output directory. Live preflight uses documented Fabric APIs to validate tenant switches and capacity state, size/tier (SKU), region, and Spark sizing.

Deployment passes --resume-capacity to live preflight. Its active-capacity fast path is read-only; paused capacity may be resumed through Azure Resource Manager after resolving the configured capacity name. An explicit workspace.capacity_resource_id bypasses discovery. Otherwise, the configured subscription is searched, or all accessible subscriptions owned by the configured tenant are enumerated. All pages and subscription ownership must be validated, and exactly one capacity name match must remain. An inaccessible page or subscription cannot be skipped to produce an apparently unique match. Only Microsoft.Fabric/capacities F-SKU resources in Paused or Suspended are resumed, with API version 2023-11-01. Identity/name/subscription mismatches, inactive trial/Premium capacities, and ambiguous Fabric lookup results fail before the resume request. Fabric Inactive alone is not proof of an ARM paused state.

Resume uses a separate ARM token for the configured tenant/authentication mode, submits at most one POST, honors asynchronous operation headers and Retry-After, and polls resource and Fabric states with a bounded wait. HTTP 429 GET responses honor Retry-After within that deadline, including discovery and operation polling. POST retries are not introduced by throttling. Lost POST responses and conflicts trigger state reads, not blind repeat mutations. Polling URLs must remain on the trusted HTTPS ARM host. Resuming restarts billing; no scale, assignment, creation, or later automatic pause is performed. Default wait is 600 seconds. Standalone live preflight without the flag, deploy dry runs, and readiness remain nonmutating. deploy --resume reexecutes live preflight even when the prior run recorded it as successful, while retaining completed setup/ML steps. Before publication, target-access validation also proves that captured workspace IDs match managed state and resolve to the configured live workspace for the deployment operator.

The CLI saves terraform.tfplan and validates its JSON resource changes before apply confirmation. Review that file with terraform show; the plan guard captures its subprocess output rather than displaying a human-readable diff. Apply consumes that exact saved plan with -auto-approve; it does not recalculate an unreviewed plan. Deletion or replacement of fabric_workspace, fabric_lakehouse, or fabric_eventhouse fails the normal plan guard. Intentional destructive changes require the explicit --recreate workflow, including its destroy confirmation.

items.title: Custom business layouts
items.text:
When the environment selects a custom store type (custom-<slug>), the plan adds upload-custom-dictionaries after the infrastructure publication and before the setup pipeline. Report-staging build_artifacts runs receive --customization <spec>. Theming is applied to staged copies only and never changes source files. retail_setup.customization.theme.derive_theme turns the saved palette into tokens, adjusting lightness until text pairs meet WCAG AA (accent and muted text ≥ 4.5:1, headings ≥ 7:1 on white).

Surface Mechanism Main Power BI report Every hex literal, including colors inside the theme's embedded SVG page wallpaper, is remapped through fabric/powerbi/theme-color-roles.json; the registered custom theme gets brand dataColors; page headers are branded (below) Connected twins report Same remap and header branding, plus a registered BrandTheme.json custom theme; page backgrounds take a light brand tint Fabric Apps --cp-* CSS overrides appended to the staged main.css, a branded <title>, VITE_BRAND_NAME so in-app titles read " ", and the logo as staged src/assets/brand-logo.svg, which the app bundles for the sidebar and sign-in page when present Plan sheets Canvas wallpaper tinted with the brand surface color

Page headers are the *_header textboxes. Their title loses the trailing "— SmartRetail Live" or "— retail-twins" suffix. With a logo, the spec's logo.svg is registered as the BrandLogo.svg image resource and an image visual (<header>_brand_logo) fills the left of the header: as tall as the header, about 56 px of logo height, 56-180 px wide and at most a quarter of the header, scaled to fit. The title moves right by that width plus 16 px. Without a logo, the title starts with the business name in the brand accent color and a muted separator ("Kroger · Executive Cockpit"). Either way, a title whose estimated width no longer fits on one line is shrunk to fit, down to 14 pt. build_artifacts --customization reads logo.svg beside the spec and deploy_twins/deploy_fabric_app read it from the environment's customization folder; each verifies the recorded SHA-256 first.

The role map assigns each report color a role (accent, secondary, heading, muted, border, surface, data_1-data_8), a tint of a role (accent~0.86 is the accent blended 86% toward white; used for wallpaper and page backgrounds), or fixed (canvas white, black text, good/warning/bad status colors, and the wallpaper's alpha mask). A report color without a role fails staging, and tests/deploy/test_customization_theming.py fails when a report gains an unmapped color. Base Microsoft themes are not modified. Real-time dashboards are design-only query catalogs and are not themed.

items.title: Command modes
items.text:
Mode Exact behavior --dry-run Validates existing configuration and the Terraform/Python authentication boundary, then prints the plan without subprocess execution or live target access. With --skip-terraform, it also validates captured outputs. --yes Pre-confirms gated Terraform steps and existing-workspace handling; it never skips required pipeline gates. --skip-terraform Omits Terraform only after captured outputs match the selected environment, workspace, resource names, and non-placeholder IDs. --resume Reuses a compatible incomplete journal's contiguous SUCCEEDED prefix, then retries from the first other state. --recreate Deletes the Terraform-managed workspace (Fabric deletes its items with it), polls Fabric until the workspace name is absent (bounded at 180 seconds), then applies and publishes.

The recreate destroy first removes the Lakehouse, Eventhouse, Spark pool, Spark settings, and role assignments from Terraform state, and then destroys only fabric_workspace.main. Destroying those items one by one fails once other items depend on them. For example, Fabric refuses to delete an Eventhouse referenced by the ontology, Operations Agent, querysets, or shortcuts. Deleting the workspace removes everything at once. When the workspace is reused through existing_workspace_id, Terraform doesn't own it, so the managed items are destroyed individually as before. Terraform runs with -input=false.

--recreate and --skip-terraform are mutually exclusive. A normal interactive run detects an existing workspace by display name and offers update-in-place or recreate. --yes skips that prompt.

--resume cannot be combined with --dry-run or --recreate. The environment, targets, profile, manifest hash, ordered step IDs, and content/command fingerprint must match. The fingerprint covers deployment sources, selected configuration, dictionary files, and ordered commands. Legacy journals without the required plan/fingerprint fields are rejected; compatibility is never assumed. Failed, degraded, skipped, or pending steps do not extend the reusable prefix. Completed runs cannot be resumed. An interrupted recreate preserves its prior recreate target identity only when every prior step through deletion-wait succeeded. An unfinished destructive phase refuses automatic resume; explicit operator review and restart are required.

Pipeline gates persist one bounded evidence document immediately after a successful submission and before polling. The document contains only exact workspace/pipeline/run correlation, Location, status, and timestamps. A compatible RUNNING gate is resumed by polling that exact Location; the orchestrator never submits a replacement. Completed evidence is adopted, active evidence remains awaited, and terminal failure remains failure. Monitor timeout is a resumable local outcome and does not cancel or classify the remote Fabric run as failed. Ambiguous POST outcomes reconcile only one exact-pipeline run in the request window; zero or multiple candidates fail closed.

Before retrying a pending apply, resume regenerates and checks the saved plan. Before retrying a pending item-publication phase, it rebuilds that phase's staging, including post-ontology artifacts. A successful build record does not prove that temporary local files remain intact. Resume is not a substitute for live target validation or readiness evidence.

items.title: Operator recovery
items.text:
When deploy runs interactively (a terminal or the setup interface) without --yes, a failed step asks what to do next. Steps already running continue while the question is open; no new step starts until it's answered.

Step Choices Required Retry, Skip, or Stop Optional Retry, Continue, or Stop
  • Retry returns the step to PENDING and schedules it again.
  • Skip records the step as SKIPPED. Every step that depends on it, directly or through another blocked step, is then skipped with blocked_by naming the steps it was waiting for. The setup interface shows those steps as not runnable (BLOCKED). Steps that don't depend on the skipped step still run.
  • Continue keeps the optional failure, which leaves the run DEGRADED.
  • Stop lets running steps finish, starts nothing new, marks every pending step skipped, and exits with code 5.

Retry is withheld for a pipeline gate whose evidence can't be read or whose recorded Fabric run hasn't reached a terminal status (Failed, Cancelled, Deduped, or Skipped), because retrying could submit a second run while the first is still active. A skipped required step makes the journal FAILED, and deploy exits with code 6. Use --resume to run the skipped and blocked steps after fixing the cause. Under --yes, or without an interactive terminal, nothing is asked: a failed required step blocks its dependents, independent steps still run, and deploy exits with the failed step's code.

items.title: Workspace-scoped environments
items.text:
configure derives one environment key from the Fabric workspace name. It lowercases the name, converts punctuation and spaces to hyphens, and omits a leading retail-demo- prefix. For example, retail-demo-alice becomes alice.

Each key owns one ignored target overlay and one ignored generated directory. The overlay contains operator-specific tenant, capacity, workspace, and optional existing-item identifiers. The tracked deploy.yml contains shared defaults only. After Terraform, fabric-cicd targets the validated workspace ID rather than resolving a potentially duplicate display name.

items.title: Generated files
items.text:
Path Role Tracked deploy/config/environments/<env>.yml Workspace-specific target overlay No utility/config/environments/<env>.yaml Environment-specific generation settings; legacy utility/config.yaml is a read fallback No utility/out/<env>/ Rendered notebooks and render manifest No deploy/.generated/<env>/terraform.tfvars Terraform input rendered from merged YAML No deploy/.generated/<env>/terraform.tfplan Saved, guarded Terraform plan applied after confirmation No deploy/.generated/<env>/terraform.tfstate Local Terraform backend state No deploy/.generated/<env>/.terraform/ Terraform backend and provider data No deploy/.generated/<env>/fabric-cicd/config.yml Publication environment and item scope No deploy/.generated/<env>/fabric-cicd/parameter.yml Workspace, item, OneLake, KQL, and agent rewrites No deploy/.generated/<env>/terraform-output.json Captured live identifiers No deploy/.generated/<env>/database.kql Combined ordered KQL script No deploy/.generated/<env>/capacity-sizing.json Fresh, non-secret live capacity evidence and derived custom Spark pool bounds No deploy/.generated/<env>/deploy-run.json Atomic step/status journal for the latest deploy run No deploy/.generated/<env>/run-history/<hashed-run-id>.json Prior journal archived before a different new/resumed run replaces the latest journal No deploy/.generated/<env>/pipeline-evidence/<step-id>.json Bounded exact pipeline item/run/Location/status evidence used for reattachment No deploy/.generated/<env>/artifact-inventory-<phase>.json Validated manifest/profile/count/folder inventory for one publication phase No deploy/.generated/<env>/readiness-report.json Redacted profile-aware live evidence No deploy/.generated/<env>/workspace/ Staged Fabric items for every publication phase No

Terraform receives an environment-specific TF_DATA_DIR and local backend path. Parallel Terraform operations therefore cannot select or mutate another workspace's state. The orchestrator also isolates generation configuration, rendered output, and staging, including post-ontology staging, by environment. Do not run concurrent deploys against the same environment; different local paths are not a distributed lock on a shared Fabric target. Lower-level build helpers may retain legacy defaults, so use the orchestrator for isolation. The supported state path is a local backend; remote-backend coordination and distributed serialization across separate pipelines/manual writers remain external design and validation gates.

A legacy deploy/terraform/terraform.tfstate with no environment-local state fails preflight. The operator must verify its workspace ownership and move it to exactly one deploy/.generated/<env>/terraform.tfstate path.

If environment-local state exists, preflight reconciles its profile, resource, and target-output signals with terraform-output.json. Missing profile evidence, missing captures, or stale identities fail closed even when the state currently has no managed instances. A downgrade that would remove a profile-controlled Eventhouse or custom Spark pool requires explicit --recreate; absent evidence never authorizes deletion.

For custom-pool profiles, live preflight derives sizing from the resolved capacity SKU before Terraform configuration generation. Supported SKUs are F<n> and FTL<n>. Base Spark capacity is 2 vCores per CU; the framework reserves 25%, divides the remaining vCores across the root notebook producers in ml-required.DataPipeline, and uses 8-vCore Medium nodes. Per-session maximum nodes are floor(floor(CU * 2 * 0.75) / (producer_count * 8)), clamped to 2–16; the minimum is 2. A capacity that cannot provide a driver plus executor to every producer fails closed. Burst capacity is excluded from the calculation.

Config generation validates the evidence environment, configured capacity identity, SKU arithmetic, producer count, integer bounds, and deployment-run freshness. The journal stores the stable sizing identity. A resumed run regenerates and replans when sizing changes before apply; sizing drift after a successful apply requires a new plan and cannot be adopted by resume. Starter pool profiles do not require or consume capacity evidence.

items.title: Authentication boundary
items.text:
Azure CLI mode is shared by the Python clients and Fabric Terraform provider. The CLI tenant is validated before mutation, and Terraform receives an explicit tenant_id.

Azure PowerShell mode applies only to Python Fabric clients. Terraform apply/destroy is rejected before command execution unless exactly one provider-supported service-principal secret/certificate, OIDC, or managed-identity credential is configured. Otherwise the operator must use validated prior outputs with --skip-terraform. In this mode the provider's Azure CLI fallback is disabled, preventing an unrelated CLI context from being used silently; conflicting provider tenant variables are rejected.

items.title: Manifest authority and executable profiles
items.text:
contracts/retail-demo.json defines stable asset IDs/descriptions, support metadata, dependencies, profile-to-existing-asset/group selection, expected publication counts/folders, canonical commands/prerequisites, and readiness expectations. Physical item and schema definitions remain in deploy/config/deploy.yml, deploy/scripts/build_artifacts.py, and the source folders. Manifest source pointers are validated rather than used to duplicate physical schemas.

Resolution computes dependency closure and rejects unknown, cyclic, or unclassified selected assets. Pipeline selection is exact and independent of notebook references. All profiles exclude the destructive reset group.

Profile Assets Groups Pipelines KQL scripts Publication behavior core (explicit selection) 1 setup 0 0 Lakehouse shell and eleven rendered historical setup notebooks; no Eventhouse, Reporting, ML, stream, preview, task flow, or custom pool standard 8 setup, core, stream, ml-required 5 6 Supported real-time/streaming plus fail-closed required ML/Reporting path; starter pool and no preview features full-demo (manifest default for every entry point) 14 standard groups plus ml-optional, ml-experimental, ontology, utility 7 6 Required Reporting gate plus post-Reporting extended ML and advanced/preview features except reset

The exact initial infrastructure/Reporting counts are 5+0, 30+2, and 40+2 respectively. They and the workspace-folder sets are validated while staging; every staged .platform description is projected from the selected manifest asset. See the canonical workspace inventory. Checked-in Data Agent .platform files may retain nonempty agent-specific summaries distinguishing semantic-model and ontology scope. This source metadata exception does not change staging's manifest-description projection or exact description contracts for other artifact types. The prior IMP-008 profile blockers are removed because the required path is now executable and fail-closed. Full-demo checks Ontology/Data Agent tenant switches with the admin tenant-settings API and validates the selected capacity with the capacities API. Settings changes remain administrator-owned because Fabric publishes no tenant-settings update API.

The manifest marks full-demo as the default, so the guided wrappers, scripts/setup.py, and direct retail-setup commands all deploy it unless core or standard is selected explicitly. Configuration enables the connected twins report and the native Operations Agent by default for any Reporting profile; native Planning stays excluded unless include_plan is set. The operations-only publication step is non-required, so a Fabric rejection of the agent degrades the deployment instead of failing it.

Committed schedules stay disabled in source. Deployment configuration (schedules) switches them on when staging pipeline definitions, and readiness compares live schedules with that configured state. daily_maintenance defaults on; streaming_data_load defaults to stream.start_after_deploy, so a started stream is always moved to Silver before Eventhouse retention purges it. stream.start_after_deploy (default off) submits one stream-events run after readiness and never duplicates an active run. Dashboard templates and rule definitions remain manual sources even though full-demo classifies them in its logical inventory.

items.title: Two-phase Reporting publication
items.text:
For standard and full-demo, the orchestrator:

  1. stages and publishes infrastructure, notebooks, experiments, and pipelines without the Reports and Semantic Models folders;
  2. waits for setup-pipeline to complete;
  3. starts ml-required; Gold (setup-11) and four producers run first, segmentation and churn run once that wave finishes, and the validator joins all seven successful activities before the pipeline can complete;
  4. stages and publishes the semantic model and report only after status Completed;
  5. runs any selected optional/experimental pipelines after Reporting;
  6. synchronizes Lakehouse SQL endpoint metadata so newly written tables become visible to SQL and Power BI clients.

setup-pipeline, ml-required, ml-optional, and ml-experimental each declare concurrency: 1 to prevent overlapping duplicate runs. The required-ML producers and setup-11 retry once after 10 minutes: each is an idempotent overwrite that holds its writer lock in ag._job_locks, and the wait lets a crashed attempt's 15-minute lease expire. Activity retries stay inside the same pipeline run, so the deploy still adopts and awaits that one run. 15-validate-required-ml-contract keeps a bounded retry of two attempts at 120-second intervals and a one-hour timeout.

The required pipeline's final activity is 15-validate-required-ml-contract. A missing, empty, schema-incompatible, duplicate, invalid, or temporally incomplete required output fails the pipeline. Skipped, failed, cancelled, deduplicated, timed-out, or unknown run states all fail closed and leave Reporting unpublished. Optional and experimental failures mark the journal DEGRADED but do not retract required Reporting.

Phased Reporting profiles reject deployment.unpublish_skip: false. Unpublishing from a partial infrastructure or Reporting stage could otherwise delete healthy items absent from that stage. This setting is a configuration safety check, not permission to skip the required publication gates.

SQL endpoint metadata synchronization is also optional at the step level. A failure marks the journal DEGRADED; the later readiness check still fails closed if any required Reporting table is unavailable.

items.title: Workspace folder mapping
items.text:
Asset Workspace location All notebooks, including setup, stream, ML and case preparation Notebooks All Data Pipelines, including setup-pipeline Pipelines Reports, including connected twins Reports Semantic models Semantic Models ML experiment shells ML Experiments Data Agents (post-ontology only) Data Agents Lakehouses Lakehouses Eventhouses Eventhouses Bundled KQL querysets KQL Querysets Ontologies Ontologies Independently movable graph models Graph Models Fabric Apps Fabric Apps Independently movable SQL databases SQL Databases Operations Agents and Plans, when published Operations Agents, Plans

deploy/scripts/workspace_folders.py owns the shared object-type policy. Staging uses that policy, and the final deploy step reconciles native and Terraform-created items against the live folder inventory. Standalone publishers also reconcile after success. Those publishers run in parallel, so each reconciliation holds the per-environment deploy/.generated/<env>/.workspace-folders.lock file lock. Two publishers therefore never create the same folder or move the same item at once. If creating a folder still returns 409 Conflict (for example, a folder created in the portal meanwhile), the folder list is reread and the existing top-level folder is used. Moves preserve item IDs and task-flow bindings; they do not run notebooks or change data. Only empty retired Setup, Streaming, Reporting, and ML folders are removed.

Fabric requires managed child items to move with their parent. SQL endpoints therefore remain beside their Lakehouse, SQL database, or Fabric App; KQL databases remain beside their Eventhouse. Any additional children returned by the move API stay with their parent. They are reported as managed exceptions, not moved independently.

Terraform owns Eventhouse/KQL database resources. The staging process does not publish .platform-only Eventhouse shells. The reset notebook has a physical source but no automatic profile stages it.

items.title: Item types
items.text:
The resolver derives item_types_in_scope from the selected assets:

  • core: Lakehouse, Notebook
  • standard: core plus SemanticModel, Report, KQLQueryset, DataPipeline, and MLExperiment
  • full-demo: standard plus DataAgent

The configured broad list is an available-type allowlist, not an instruction to publish every type. A selected type absent from that allowlist fails resolution.

items.title: Parameter rewrites
items.text:
Generated parameter.yml rules rewrite:

  • OneLake and Direct Lake source identifiers;
  • KQL database item IDs and query URIs;
  • semantic-model connection IDs where configured;
  • Data Agent workspace, semantic-model, and ontology item IDs.

Pipeline staging replaces same-workspace notebook references with each notebook's deterministic logical ID and the default-workspace sentinel. fabric-cicd resolves those values natively during publication, avoiding generated per-notebook parameter rules.

Bulk publish is not enabled by default because the upstream bulk import API remains experimental. Since fabric-cicd 1.4.0, bulk mode also resolves dynamic replacement variables (such as the Data Agents' $items.Ontology.<name>.$id), so that is no longer a blocker; enabling it would still need a live full-demo post-ontology proof.

items.title: KQL application
items.text:
deploy/scripts/apply_kql.py concatenates only the ordered KQL files selected by the profile into one outer database-script payload and can execute it against the resolved KQL database with the Kusto Python SDK. Executing KQL without an environment/profile inventory is unsupported. Core selects no KQL.

The required target is the configured KQL database, not a hard-coded default. The current topology uses the default database created with the Eventhouse and therefore requires the same display name. Artifact staging rewrites only the known shortcut, ontology, stream, and queryset target names in generated copies. Both credential modes receive the configured tenant. Live Azure PowerShell and renamed-target verification are tracked by IMP-001.

items.title: Task flow and ontology timing
items.text:
The orchestrator supplies Terraform output to task-flow deployment, so the workspace, Lakehouse, Eventhouse, and KQL database bind by resolved ID. Published items not owned by Terraform still bind by type and display name. --workspace <name-or-id> remains an alternative target, but deployment still requires matching --environment and --profile full-demo; unscoped legacy task-flow deployment fails.

Ontology creation is separate from setup-pipeline and the required Reporting gate, but it completes automatically later in the same full-demo deploy. The orchestrator starts the deployed 30-create-ontology notebook on every full-demo deployment. The notebook updates an existing ontology in place or creates it when absent, requires the derived-graph definition rebuild to succeed, and then the orchestrator waits for both terminal notebook success and exactly one stable ontology item.

The next phase publishes both Data Agents and deploys the source-controlled task flow. Before mutation, source coverage must include every selected full-demo artifact. After mutation, the metadata service is read back and all 14 tasks, 60 item bindings, and 14 edges must match exactly.

The recovery command reruns the same idempotent phase:

retail-setup post-ontology --env <env>

This command creates the ontology when absent, rejects duplicate ontology items, stages and publishes Data Agents, deploys and reads back the task flow, and runs complete readiness verification.

Task-flow deployment fails before publication when any selected reference is unresolved; it never publishes a silently partial graph. Normal full-demo deployment and the recovery command use the same completion path.

Task-flow publication currently relies on Fabric/Power BI metadata behavior that is not a stable public source-control item contract.

items.title: Failure semantics
items.text:
• Required initial plan and ontology/task-flow completion commands fail their respective run.
  • Blockers, missing selected sources, invalid pipeline references, disabled tenant switches, unsuitable capacities, and unsafe profile downgrades fail before mutation.
  • For gated profiles, setup and required ML are mandatory exact-run terminal gates. --yes suppresses prompts but never skips either gate.
  • Post-Reporting optional/experimental ML failures are recorded and execution continues.
  • The orchestrator executes an explicit dependency graph with separate resource limits: one Spark-heavy step and up to four non-Spark/API steps by default. Required failures prevent descendants from starting; optional failures do not cancel independent siblings. Final task-flow publication, folder reconciliation, and readiness wait for every selected branch to become terminal.
  • SQL endpoint metadata synchronization failures are recorded as optional degradation. Required-table visibility is checked again by readiness.
  • Recreate polls every visible Fabric workspace page and fails closed on timeout or malformed pagination before Terraform apply.
  • deploy-run.json records PENDING, RUNNING, SUCCEEDED, DEGRADED, SKIPPED, and FAILED step states plus overall RUNNING, SUCCEEDED, DEGRADED, or FAILED. It stores no raw command output, environment variables, tokens, or tenant identifiers and redacts credential-like exception text.
  • Before a new or resumed run replaces the latest journal, the prior journal is atomically archived under run-history/, using the SHA-256 hash of its run ID as the filename. Latest-journal replacement happens only after that archive write succeeds. In-run status updates do not create history copies. Archive and latest files are separately atomic, not a distributed transaction.
  • Local deployment validation checks generated files only; it does not query live item, binding, run, or data readiness.

An overall DEGRADED result means the required workspace is usable, but one or more optional capabilities have failed or unknown evidence. Operators inspect the linked readiness report before presenting those optional capabilities. FAILED means a required capability is not ready.

Standard and full-demo run the profile-aware live verifier after their pipeline gates. Full-demo verification runs after automatic ontology, Data Agent, and exact task-flow completion. Verification is read-only: it does not trigger a second pipeline. Required failed/unknown evidence fails deployment; optional failed/unknown evidence marks the journal and linked readiness report DEGRADED. Operators may explicitly trigger the profile's post-publish pipeline only with retail-setup verify --env <env> --run-pipeline.

The verifier, report, and local contracts are implemented. Historical full-demo evidence predates these changes. Fresh readiness-consistency and remote smoke tests remain open, along with recent manual-stream evidence under IMP-013.

items.text:
• Canonical source: docs/

  • Generated output: site/
  • Publish branch: gh-pages
