  • Version publisher: scripts/publish_versioned_docs.py

website/ and Docusaurus are retired and must not return as a parallel current source. The version publisher may read their documentation from immutable historical tags when reconstructing an archived release.

items.title: Information architecture
items.text:
Navigation is explicit in zensical.toml:

  1. Home
  2. Start here
  3. guide index
  4. plain-language glossary
  5. getting started
  6. workspace profiles
  7. Explore the demo
  8. deployed walkthroughs
  9. presenter guides
  10. use cases
  11. Deploy and operate
  12. deployment
  13. operations
  14. Design Documentation
  15. Requirements
  16. Specifications
  17. Architecture
  18. Security

All nav targets must exist. Canonical Markdown uses relative links, Mermaid diagrams, and Zensical-compatible Markdown rather than MDX/React or Docusaurus-only metadata.

Task-focused guides live under docs/guides/. Technical requirements and contracts live under docs/design/, separate from setup and presentation instructions.

The Home and guide-index pages route readers by role and task. User-facing guides assume no source-code knowledge. They explain business meaning before implementation detail, define acronyms on first use, and link repeated terms to docs/guides/glossary.md. Formal requirements and specifications may use precise identifiers, but they still define domain-specific terms before relying on them.

Top-level navigation groups remain collapsible. Do not enable navigation.sections, which renders them as persistent sidebar groups on desktop.

items.title: Owner rules
items.text:
• Requirements: outcomes, constraints, acceptance, stable IDs, backlogs.
  • Specifications: exact interfaces, schemas, workflows, states, errors.
  • Architecture: current boundaries, deployment, dependencies, and flow.
  • Security: threats, controls, assumptions, and residual risks.
  • Guides: derived user procedures.
  • Root/component READMEs: concise local entry points and links.

Module backlogs contain only Open and Settled — do not reopen.

items.title: Temporary artifacts
items.text:
Keep dated plans, raw findings, generated context, and migration audits out of the published source tree. Move their lasting requirements, decisions, and unresolved work into the relevant technical pages before deleting the temporary files or replacing them with pointers.

The prior docs/superpowers/ implementation plans were removed after durable content was promoted. Temporary planning material must remain outside the published source tree.

The pinned Zensical version does not support exclude_docs or draft_docs (upstream tracking). Omitting a page from nav does not prevent publication or indexing. Do not add an unsupported exclusion setting as a security control.

The decision experience, ML/AI backlog, and THREAT-009 / SEC-012 replace the former root-level action and customer experience drafts. Routing has a specification; evaluation questions and the CIO walkthrough have dedicated guides. Raw response logs and generated HTML/diagram exports were removed after preserving unresolved ontology, model-quality, action, and security concerns. The action-framework URL remains a pointer for existing component links. No old response count, latency, or deployment claim is current verification.

tests/docs/test_documentation_boundary.py checks source publication boundaries, navigation, links, and requirement/threat ownership. Review the built output as well. Immutable historical versions use their tag's source; changing current docs does not retroactively validate or sanitize those sites.

items.title: Build
items.text:
python -m pip install --require-hashes -r requirements-docs.txt
python -m zensical build --clean

The build must succeed with no missing nav target or broken internal link. Generated output is written to the ignored site/ directory.

For a local preview:

python -m zensical serve

items.title: Maintainer checklist
items.text:
1. Update the canonical owner and all derived links in the same change.
  2. Preserve stable requirement, threat, control, improvement, and enhancement IDs.
  3. Keep module backlogs limited to Open and Settled — do not reopen.
  4. Use Mermaid for diagrams.
  5. Define unfamiliar acronyms and explain what an operational status means before listing internal field names or check IDs.
  6. Run python -m zensical build --clean.
  7. Check for broken links, missing navigation targets, stale website/ references, and dated plans that still own durable content.

items.title: Publishing workflow
items.text:
.github/workflows/docs.yml:

  • triggers from canonical docs/config changes;
  • fetches main plus the complete tag history;
  • checks out with an immutable action SHA;
  • installs Python, pinned Zensical, and the commit-pinned Zensical mike fork;
  • rebuilds the orphan gh-pages branch through mike;
  • uses contents: write;
  • does not request Pages OIDC permissions;
  • does not use Pages artifact deployment actions.

items.title: Published versions
items.text:
The version selector contains:

  • main, displayed as Latest and published at /latest/;
  • one entry for each stable SemVer major.minor line that has tags;
  • the highest numeric patch revision in each line, displayed as the normalized major.minor.patch value and published at /major.minor/.

Tags may use an optional v prefix. Pre-release tags and non-SemVer tags are excluded. Historical pages are built from the selected tag's own documentation source. Current pages always build with Zensical. Historical compatibility can read the repository's previous MkDocs and Docusaurus layouts so older release entries do not substitute current documentation.

Every publication reconstructs the generated branch from the currently tagged version set. The root page redirects to Latest.

Pull-request CI builds the current site and the complete version set without pushing, so tag selection, legacy-source compatibility, and selector metadata fail before publication.

items.title: External Pages setting
items.text:
The required GitHub repository settings are:

  • Source: Deploy from a branch
  • Branch: gh-pages
  • Folder: / (root)

After publishing, verify the Pages API and Docs workflow, the root redirect to /latest/, and selector metadata for Latest plus the selected stable minor lines. A clean local build does not establish the state of those external settings or published files.

items.title: Authority
items.text: utility/src/retail_setup/generation/schemas.py defines the base Lakehouse tables, columns, and types. engine.py orchestrates generation, invariants.py validates relationships across tables, writer.py publishes outputs, and gold.py builds the ten aggregates from gold_rules.py, the one Gold definition that notebook 04 also uses.

items.title: Dimensions
items.text:
dim_geographies, dim_stores, dim_distribution_centers, dim_trucks, dim_customers, dim_products, and dim_date.

dim_date uses ISO 8601 weeks: day_of_week runs Monday (1) to Sunday (7), and week_of_year is the ISO week (1-53; week 1 holds the year's first Thursday), so the first days of January can belong to week 52 or 53 and the last days of December to week 1. year stays the calendar year. Fiscal years run July to June and fiscal_year is labelled by the calendar year they start in: July 2025 to June 2026 is fiscal year 2025, and July is fiscal_quarter 1.

dim_products prices and names:

  • A base product sold by several brands keeps one title per brand: a title that starts with a brand name carries the SKU's own Brand; generic titles stay generic.
  • MSRP is the base price +/-15% and SalePrice equals it or a 5-35% discount from it, both at the nearest charm price (.49 or .99, a 9-cent ending below $1). Catalog base prices (dictionaries/catalog.py) take the nearest charm price inside their subcategory band, so sub-dollar and narrow bands keep their spread.
  • Cost leaves the department's gross margin band (pricing.DEPARTMENT_MARGINS, for example groceries 15-30%, electronics 10-25%, apparel 45-60%, jewelry 45-65%).

items.title: Facts
items.text:
fact_receipts, fact_receipt_lines, fact_payments, fact_store_ops, fact_foot_traffic, fact_ble_pings, fact_customer_zone_changes, fact_marketing, fact_marketing_attribution, fact_promotions, fact_promo_lines, fact_online_order_headers, fact_online_order_lines, fact_reorders, fact_truck_moves, fact_truck_inventory, fact_dc_inventory_txn, fact_store_inventory_txn, fact_stockouts, fact_logistics_incidents, and fact_logistics_incident_stores.

Each store is served by a DC in its own state, else its region, else any DC; among those the store goes to the DC serving the fewest stores so far, so DCs in one state share the load (network.assign_dcs). Geographies are sampled one city per state in turn, so the shared dictionary's skew (most cities in five states) does not concentrate stores and DCs. dim_trucks gives each DC one truck per daily delivery route (network.plan_routes, at least two trucks), plus a shared pool of about 15% of the fleet with a NULL DCID. A route is a set of the DC's stores in one time zone, each with a daily delivery slot in store-local time; slots on a route are spaced by the longest possible trip (load, the lane both ways, the maximum unload, a turnaround), so a truck on its route is never in two places at once. History and the live stream use the same routes and slots.

Online orders follow vocabulary.ONLINE_HOURLY_WEIGHTS over the UTC day (peaking in the US evening), and a BOPIS order is collected 1-24 hours after it is picked (delivered_ts); the stream uses the same parameters. Online orders are local, like the live stream (stream_events.plan_orders):

  • The customer is active on the order day and comes from a home-store pool drawn by store traffic, so an order belongs to the customer's home store.
  • One fulfillment mode serves the whole order (60% ship-from-DC, 30% ship-from-store, 10% BOPIS). Ship-from-store and BOPIS orders use the customer's home store as node_id; ship-from-DC orders use the DC that supplies that store.
  • Baskets are sized to the store type's avg_ticket_target like store receipts, lines follow the same shopping missions, and repeated SKUs merge into one line.
  • A cancelled or voided order has zero header totals and zero line ext_cents, and no payment.
  • 8% of shipped orders are backordered: they wait 3-14 days for stock between picking and shipping, then ship and deliver.
  • fulfillment_status and the stage timestamps are as of the end of history. Orders still in fulfillment then are PENDING, PICKED, or SHIPPED, with NULL timestamps for the stages still to come; no stage time is later than the end of history. The live stream does not continue these orders.

fact_logistics_incidents holds one row per logistics disruption (incident_type is DC_OUTAGE, LANE_DELAY, WEATHER, HOLIDAY_CAPACITY, or SUPPLIER_SHORT_SHIP), with resolved_at null while the incident is open at the end of history and store_id set only for a lane delay's store. fact_logistics_incident_stores lists every store each incident affects (the DC's stores, the lane's store, or a geography's stores), one row per incident and store. History and the live stream plan incidents with the same model (see Logistics incidents). fact_truck_moves carries planned_arrival_time, delay_minutes, delay_reason, and load_units.

items.title: Time convention
items.text:
Generation runs in each store's local wall-clock time: opening hours, the hourly traffic curve, store operations, and the inventory schedule are local. Silver stores true UTC, the same convention as the live stream:

  • dim_stores.TimeZone is the store's IANA zone, from its geography's state (generation/timezones.py, STATE_TIME_ZONES).
  • Every published timestamp column is UTC, and event_date is the UTC date of event_ts. An evening sale on the West Coast can therefore carry the next day's event_date.
  • Store events convert with their store's zone; receipt and promotion lines use the store encoded in receipt_id_ext. A shipment's whole lifecycle (truck moves, truck loads and unloads, and the DC rows that mirror the loads) uses the destination store's zone, so one shipment never mixes zones and DC balances follow UTC order.
  • Online orders and marketing impressions are not tied to store hours. They are generated directly in UTC and not converted. Attribution runs on UTC purchases.
  • fact_receipts.local_hour is the store-local hour (0-23) for hour-of-day reporting. Notebook 03 sets it for streamed receipts from dim_stores.TimeZone.

Invariants that depend on the local clock (operating hours) convert back with the store's zone. Existing environments must re-run setup after this change; Silver written before it has local timestamps and no TimeZone or local_hour.

items.title: Shared vocabulary and calibration
items.text: generation/vocabulary.py owns the names and formats both producers use: tenders and the decline model, the promotion catalog and per-line eligibility, BLE, ad, beacon, sensor, and campaign ID formats, zones, marketing channels and cost bands, device types, and fulfillment modes. generation/calibration.py owns thresholds that consumers repeat as literals: the 90-minute truck dwell SLA, stockout and reorder thresholds, the zone-surge count (sized from the stream's own visit rate at the store type's peak), the high-value receipt rule (10 x the store type's avg_ticket_target, about one ticket in a thousand), and the anomaly detector parameters. Contract tests fail when the stream, rules, KQL functions, or semantic model drift from them. The two store-type thresholds reach the rules through the Eventhouse function fn_rule_thresholds(), whose values the deployment's KQL step writes for the deployed store type (calibration.rule_thresholds).

items.title: Operational output
items.text:
setup_run_log appends a unique setup-attempt record, table-level completion records, and a final completion or failure record. Reusing an existing run_id is rejected so retries cannot create ambiguous duplicate history.

Setup-02 generates and validates dimensions without publishing them. Setup-03 through setup-09 regenerate the same deterministic dimensions and generate the facts as handoff tables. Setup-10 (setup-10-publish-silver) is the single Silver publication boundary. write_all stages every candidate under a run-scoped <schema>_stage schema, validates schema and row counts, captures existing Delta versions, then promotes. An attempted promotion failure restores pre-existing targets and drops newly created targets in reverse order.

Each Silver run's setup_run_log rows carry the generation_fingerprint of the configuration and dictionaries it published. Setup-10 drops the handoffs after a successful publication, so a retry (for example a pipeline activity retry after a timeout) finds none. When the latest completed Silver publication carries the same fingerprint and its tables still exist, the retry succeeds without publishing again; otherwise it fails on the missing handoffs and the generation notebooks must run first.

Publication is atomic for writers, not for readers. The Silver tables are promoted concurrently, each with its own CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE, so a query running during promotion can read some tables from the new generation and others from the old one. A failed promotion rolls every table back. Gold is built afterwards by setup-11 (setup-11-build-gold, in the ml-required pipeline); until it finishes, or if it fails, Gold describes the previous Silver. Consumers should not read during setup and should treat Gold as current only once setup-11 has completed for the same run.

Terminal publication states distinguish data recovery from staging cleanup: COMPLETED, FAILED, ROLLED_BACK, ROLLBACK_FAILED, COMPLETED_CLEANUP_FAILED, and ROLLED_BACK_CLEANUP_FAILED.

COMPLETED_CLEANUP_FAILED means data promotion succeeded: the writer returns success with a warning and logs retained staging artifacts. Readiness reports cleanup as degradation, not failed historical data. Rollback states still represent failed publication attempts even when restoration succeeded.

Historical Silver replacement is blocked once the configured <lakehouse>.<silver_db>._watermarks table exists, even if it has no rows. Stop writers and use coordinated Silver/checkpoint recovery before rebuilding history; deleting watermarks alone would allow replay to corrupt rebuilt data. The writer guard is not a distributed lock, so operators must serialize historical and streaming writers.

The retained historical loader must materialize the exact ordered TABLES field names and types, not sampled/inferred Parquet schemas. Synthetic fixture data must not silently stand in for a missing or incompatible historical source.

items.title: Gold output
items.text:
• sales_minute_store
  • top_products_15m
  • inventory_position_current
  • dc_inventory_position_current
  • truck_dwell_daily
  • online_sales_daily
  • zone_dwell_minute
  • marketing_cost_daily
  • campaign_performance_daily
  • tender_mix_daily

ML output tables are not part of this base contract.

Every Gold table is built from gold_rules.py: sales tables count SALE receipts with an approved payment, online sales count orders with an approved payment, truck_dwell_daily has one row per completed shipment lifecycle, and no source row at or after the Gold cutoff is used (see Fabric analytics).

The source-derived live-route check compares this inventory with declared event paths. Seven dimensions, fact_promo_lines, fact_truck_inventory, and dc_inventory_position_current are the named historical-only boundary. fact_dc_inventory_txn has a live route (the stream emits DC stock moves as inventory_updated rows without a store), as do fact_online_order_lines, fact_logistics_incidents and fact_logistics_incident_stores. The manifest records those targets and rationale; schemas.py continues to own their fields, types, nullability behavior, and mixed-case compatibility.

items.title: Generation order
items.text: The engine creates dimensions and date context, then candidate store demand. It resolves inventory-constrained fulfillment before publishing sales, returns, payments, promotions, attribution, sensors, and stock ledgers. Online orders, marketing, store activity, and Gold output retain their related contracts. Reusable intermediate data is cached where repeated calculations would otherwise recompute it.

items.title: Execution performance
items.text:
Generation is a dependency graph of stages (STAGES in generation/engine.py). Each stage names its inputs, its outputs, and the setup notebook that runs it:

Notebook Stages Waits for setup-03-generate-sales candidate receipts, fulfillment plan setup-04 setup-04-generate-online-orders online orders setup-01 setup-05-generate-marketing background impressions setup-01 setup-06-generate-returns-and-promotions returns, promotions setup-03 setup-07-generate-store-activity store operations, foot traffic, BLE setup-03 setup-08-generate-inventory inventory, logistics, and stockout ledgers setup-03 setup-09-attribute-marketing last-touch attribution setup-03 to 06 setup-10-publish-silver invariants and atomic Silver publication setup-02 to 04, 06 to 09

setup-pipeline follows the same dependency graph at notebook level; a test checks that the two graphs agree. Independent notebooks run in separate Spark sessions. At most five run at once, within the session concurrency that capacity sizing reserves for required ML. Setup-10 runs its invariant checks and per-table staging, validation, and promotion concurrently; every phase still completes for all tables before the next starts, and any promotion failure rolls back every table.

Gold (setup-11-build-gold) runs in the first ml-required wave with the demand forecast, market basket, promotion effectiveness and stockout models, before customer segmentation and churn, so the pipeline needs at most five sessions. Setup-11 holds the gold writer lock in ag._job_locks while it publishes. Inside a notebook, up to six ready stages run concurrently. A stage writes its own outputs one after another so related cached plans are never built concurrently. Completion order and the notebook split do not change the output; a test compares the notebook path with single-session generate_all row for row.

Stage outputs that a later notebook needs are written as gen__<stage>__<output> Delta tables in the Silver staging schema. Each records the generation fingerprint (a hash of the generation configuration and of the dictionary files generation reads) in its Delta commit, and loading a handoff produced for another configuration or other dictionary content fails. Setup-10 promotes single-handoff facts directly from their handoffs and drops every handoff only after publication succeeds, so a failed publication can be retried without regenerating. Within a notebook, other stage frames are checkpointed under Files/setup/_checkpoints/<notebook> in the Lakehouse rather than on executors. Later steps therefore do not depend on an executor's local data surviving autoscaling or executor loss. generate_all (local tests) runs the whole graph in one session with the same checkpoints, which stay on the executors when no folder is given.

Generation output never depends on Spark partitioning, so each notebook sizes spark.sql.shuffle.partitions to the configured receipt-line volume (about one million lines per partition, between 200 and 8,192) and lets adaptive execution coalesce small shuffles. Materializing each stage before dependants consume it also means later plans start from small leaves instead of re-analyzing the full upstream lineage on the driver. The inventory policy runs in Python workers through mapInArrow, which moves demand and events in Arrow column batches rather than pickling each row. BLE zone selection, ping sequencing, and zone changes are per-visit array operations, so the ping stream is never shuffled.

items.title: Retail behavior and calibration
items.text:
Historical store demand starts with open-hour visitors. A seeded negative-binomial count controls arrival variability; each visitor has a purchase decision using store/hour conversion propensity. Footfall uses this same visitor grid, not receipts divided by a fixed conversion percentage, and counts zone passages along the shared visit path (see Store profiles and derived defaults).

Visitors per store-day also follow the US holiday calendar and the local weather (generation/stream_calendar.py, shared with the live stream):

  • Holidays. holiday_dates lists New Year's Day, Presidents' Day, Valentine's Day, Easter Saturday and Sunday, Mother's Day, Memorial Day and the Saturday before it, Father's Day, July 3 and 4, Labor Day, Halloween, Thanksgiving eve and day, Black Friday and the Saturday after, Cyber Monday, Christmas Eve, Christmas, December 26, and New Year's Eve. Each holiday scales the day's traffic by the store type's class (store_class: general, grocery, hardware, or luxury, from the department mix and ticket size) and online orders by its own factor (HOLIDAY_EFFECTS). A factor of 0 closes the stores: Christmas for every class, Thanksgiving for all but grocers. Closed days have no receipts, store operations, or returns, and returns due on one move to the next day.
  • Weather. Each geography has a daily weather index: a weighted sum of the last 8 days' seeded shocks (weights 0.7 to the power of the age), so weather persists for days (lag-1 autocorrelation about 0.7). Its effect on traffic depends on the state's climate and the month (snow-belt winters, southern storm summers), within 0.4-1.2x and about 1 on average. An index of 2 or more marks a severe-weather day (severe_weather_column); the logistics incident model opens WEATHER incidents on those days.

Customer selection has persistent, long-tailed visit propensities and geography affinity. Continuous customer spending propensity and quick, regular, family, and bulk shopping missions shape basket sizes. Most lines share the trip's department preference; others permit cross-department shopping. Product popularity is persistent, price-sensitive, and uneven. Catalog selection excludes products not yet launched.

avg_ticket_target calibrates expected line counts against actual eligible catalog prices, category quantities, tax, and expected discounts. basket_lambda limits the nominal mean line count; neither setting changes catalog prices or forces every ticket to the target. One-line minimums and expensive catalogs can make a target unattainable. A target below the cost of one line produces only single-item receipts, so each store type's target must allow multi-item baskets: required market-basket recommendations depend on them. Report distributions and calibration error rather than truncating individual tickets. Consumables and durables use different geometric quantity distributions, with single units most common and no artificial four-unit maximum.

Promotion exposure precedes basket-size sampling and raises additional-item demand. Discounts still precede tax, and receipt/payment amounts reconcile in integer cents. Price response comes from the shelf-price schedule and the department elasticities, and product pairs from fixed complements (see Prices, baskets and promotions); both are synthetic designs, not models learned from real transactions.

The shared draw implementation uses Box-Muller normal draws and an exact integer-shape negative-binomial distribution (sum of geometric draws). All decisions retain stable key/seed salts, independent of Spark partitioning. The changed simulation intentionally produces different data from older code with the same seed; reproducibility requires the same code, dictionaries, configuration, and date window.

Dimensions depend only on the seed, the scale settings, and anchor_date, never on the run date. Product launch dates are placed around anchor_date, which retail-setup configure pins once per environment and render passes to the setup notebooks (it defaults to start_date). Rendering the same months configuration on a later day therefore regenerates identical stores, geographies, customers, and products; only the fact window moves. Each department's first product still launches before the history starts, even when the history begins before the anchor. Floating-point catalog weights are summed in product order, so they are bit-identical regardless of how Spark delivers rows.

items.title: Inventory feedback and unfulfilled demand
items.text:
The replenishment policy covers every selling store/SKU. It learns from past attempted demand, considers on-hand and pending deliveries/accepted restocks, and orders case-pack quantities against coverage and safety-stock targets. Each SKU starts from a prior of its expected daily demand at the first history day (store volume and multiplier, lines per basket, seasonal department weight, the SKU's popularity share of its launched department, units per line): the prior starts the demand estimate and sizes opening stock between the reorder point and the order-up-to target (4-8 days of cover). It never looks at generated demand, and it removes the start-of-history stockout wave a flat opening stock caused.

Each DC simulates one product for all of its stores at once (dc_supply.simulate_dc_sku), so DC stock is shared. Every SKU a store reorders when a day closes ships on its next open delivery slot as one load, which drives the lane and is received when unloading starts, 15 minutes after arrival. The DC ships the day's reorders from the stock it has, most urgent first; a reorder it cannot cover is short-shipped, so the store reorders again the next day and runs out if the DC stays empty. inventory.py packs each load into shipments of at most truck_capacity units in product order (_split_reorders_by_capacity; IDs SHP-<dispatch yyyyMMdd>-<store>-<leg>), splitting a SKU's receipt across legs when needed. Shipments go, in loading order, to a truck that is free for the whole trip (loading until it is back at the DC): the store's route truck for the first leg, the shared pool and then the DC's other trucks for overflow legs. Dwell is the unload model shared with the live stream (network.unload_minutes: base minutes plus units at the site's rate, slower in the store's busy hours and quicker at night, plus a door wait for a truck 30 or more minutes late; 30-180 minutes). Each load has a planned and an actual schedule (incidents.plan_delivery): moves before arrival show the plan in eta/etd with delay_minutes 0; from ARRIVED on they show the actual arrival, delay_minutes (actual minus planned_arrival_time) and delay_reason.

A candidate line is fulfilled in full only when its stock is available. Rejected lines are omitted from realized receipts; empty receipts disappear. Receipt totals, discounts, tax, payments, and refunds are reconciled against fulfilled lines. The return plan preserves sampled dates and identities while only actual fulfilled/refunded units can be restocked. Dependent promotions and attribution consume realized sales, not attempted demand.

items.title: Returns and payments
items.text:
About return_rate of sales are returned 1-14 days later, at a random time inside the store's hours (store-local), favouring baskets whose categories customers return more (returns.RETURN_CATEGORY_WEIGHTS: apparel and electronics far more than fresh food). A return is partial: each line of the receipt is returned with a probability that follows its category (at least one line), and a multi-unit line returns some or all of its units. The refund keeps the sale's customer_id, goes back to the tender that paid for the sale, and links it in fact_receipts.original_receipt_id_ext (NULL on sales). Refund cents are the returned share of each line's net with integer basis-point tax; return lines keep their own promo_code (receipt_type = RETURN marks them). Only returned units the store filled can be restocked.

Payments follow the shared decline model (vocabulary.payment_outcome_column): the first tender declines with its probability; 80% of declined shoppers retry on another tender (a DECLINED then an APPROVED payment), the rest walk away and the sale is voided, so it never becomes a receipt and takes no stock. A voided online order is cancelled (zero totals, no payment). Every receipt and placed order therefore has exactly one APPROVED payment, and its header tender is the approved one. Transaction IDs derive from the purchase ID and attempt (TXN-<receipt or order>-<attempt>), so they are unique.

fact_store_inventory_txn appends two long audit columns after the existing schema: requested_quantity and unfulfilled_quantity. LOST_SALE rows record rejected demand with zero physical quantity; they must not decrement stock. Store/DC/truck transfers share the fulfillment plan, and inventory positions exclude deliveries outside the requested history. Physical-stock invariants verify nonnegative balances, running-sum conservation, opening stock, receipt/refund mirrors, demand accounting, and transfer conservation.

Streaming replay preserves historical demand-audit fields. Older ledgers without these columns derive fulfilled requested quantities from negative SALE movements and use zero unfulfilled demand, because the older producer did not record lost sales. This is read-side compatibility only: writes still require the declared target schema. Regenerate historical setup or explicitly migrate the target before resuming streaming against an older table. Live sales carry requested_quantity; a live line the store cannot fill is a LOST_SALE with its demand in unfulfilled_quantity, as in history.

DCs keep their own stock (fact_dc_inventory_txn): an opening stock of 10-16 days of their stores' expected demand, supplier orders when the position (on hand plus open orders) falls to the reorder point (lead time + 1 + 4 safety days of smoothed demand, at least a case per store), received a stable 3-7 day lead time later at 04:00 DC time (INBOUND_SHIPMENT, short during a supplier short-ship), truck loads (OUTBOUND_SHIPMENT), and ship-from-DC online lines when they ship (ONLINE_SHIPMENT; units the DC lacks are EXPEDITED_RECEIPT just before). A DC stockout is a fact_stockouts row with DCID. The model does not optimize fleet routing. Overflow legs can only overlap a truck's earlier trip when they outnumber the shared pool. Historical online orders keep their own fulfillment statuses; do not read them as reservations against the store policy.

items.title: Logistics incidents
items.text:
incidents.plan_incidents lays out every disruption from the seed and the dates, the same way for history and the live stream:

Type Frequency Effect DC_OUTAGE 1.5 per DC and year, 6-36 hours no dispatches; loads leave at each store's next slot after it LANE_DELAY 4 per DC and year, 2-12 hours, one store trucks on the lane arrive 45-180 minutes late WEATHER severe-weather days, more often in the climate's rough season, 1-4 days lanes into the geography's stores run 60-240 minutes late HOLIDAY_CAPACITY Black Friday weekend and the days after Christmas, 70% of DCs loading starts 60-240 minutes late SUPPLIER_SHORT_SHIP 2 per DC and year, 3-10 days, one supplier group (a sixth of products) 20-60% of supplier orders arrive

Severity follows the delay (90/150 minutes), outage length (12/24 hours) or lost supply share (50/65%). Loads never arrive on a store's closure day, and traffic delays some runs (5-20% by lane length, more on Fridays) by 15-50% of the lane time. delay_reason names the largest cause of a delay (DC_OUTAGE, HOLIDAY_CAPACITY, LANE_DELAY, WEATHER, TRAFFIC); the live stream adds TRUCK_AVAILABILITY when a load waited for a free truck. Frequencies and ranges live in generation/calibration.py.

End-of-history incident. Every history also ends inside one prolonged DC_OUTAGE (incidents.end_of_history_incident), keyed only on the seed and the history's last day. The DC serving the most stores (a stable draw breaks ties) stops dispatching between 00:00 and 05:59 DC time two days before the last day, for 78-96 hours (END_OF_HISTORY_OUTAGE_*; longer than the random 6-36 hours on purpose, HIGH severity). Its cause is a warehouse system outage or a labor shortage. Its ID is the random outage ID with an -END suffix, for example INC-OUT-001-20250815-END. The DC's stores get no loads for the last three days, so their fast movers (about two units a day or more) really run low: at the as-of, some of them have under three days of cover, and some are empty. Slow movers keep at least a case (12 units) on the shelf and stay well covered. The incident lands in fact_logistics_incidents and fact_logistics_incident_stores with a NULL resolved_at. The live stream plans the same outage from END_DATE, starts it in its first batch and emits logistics_incident_resolved at its planned end, 6-54 hours after the last local day. Random incidents are unchanged.

items.title: Historical/live boundary
items.text:
The stream notebook embeds the shared basket/catalog/quantity code at build time. It emits a variable-length receipt-line array with matching item counts, promotion products, line discounts, tax, header totals, and payments. Live online orders use history's online promo codes, tenders, declines and destination tax. Missing store tax or an empty/missing eligible catalog is an error, not a synthetic $9.99 price.

Live catalog launch eligibility is snapshotted when the stream starts; restart the stream to pick up newly launched products or changed catalog/profile data. Live store visits continue the historical visitor-arrival process: the same hourly, daily and monthly weights in store-local time, the same traffic multipliers and operating hours, the same conversion model, and customers from the same ticket-weighted local pools (see the live event contract). Live store stock, trucks, DC stock, incidents and online order lifecycles are state machines that continue the history (see the live event contract); their state lives in ag._stream_state_*. A new stream incarnation reads store stock from the Silver ledger as of its start.

Live fact_store_ops rows use the historical lower-case opened/closed; notebook 03 lower-cases rows written by earlier stream versions. Live fact_marketing journey touches are dated by when they were shown (impression_time), not when they arrived, and live fact_promotions.product_ids is the same comma-separated, numerically sorted list as history.

items.title: Marketing and attribution
items.text: Background impressions cost real CPMs: $0.002-$0.03 an impression by channel and device (vocabulary.CHANNEL_COSTS), with cost to four decimals and cost_cents rounded at random so summed spend is unbiased. Each campaign rotates a small creative pool per channel (CRT<campaign>-<channel>-<n>, four creatives). Conversion follows exposure (attribution.py): an impression reaches the customer of its ad ID and converts with a small probability weighted by channel (search and email best, display worst) when that customer makes an eligible purchase within seven days; the probability is calibrated per run so the campaigns return about TARGET_ROAS (4x) their spend, which keeps conversions well under 1% of impressions. A journey is the converting impressions themselves, so its touches look like every other impression (same ID and creative formats, CRM-matched customer_id at the same rate) except for attribution_journey_id; every campaign family can convert, and each touch sits in its own campaign window. Last touch decides the campaign. The live stream attributes the share of eligible purchases that returns the same ROAS on its spend (attribution.live_journey_rate), with one to three touches built like background impressions.

items.title: Statistical acceptance
items.text: Use multiple seeds and short and multi-year windows. Check ticket and basket percentiles, customer purchase-frequency dispersion, SKU concentration, conversion variability, stockout duration/recovery, inventory conservation, and historical/live basket distributions. Keep legitimate price points, integer quantities, business constraints, and calibrated model-score plateaus; do not add jitter to hide them. Local synthetic calibration targets are demo assumptions, not claims about measured industry distributions.

items.title: Invariants
items.text:
Current invariant checks include:

  • key uniqueness and required foreign keys;
  • non-null event dates;
  • online-order header/line integrity;
  • pricing, tax, and promotion consistency;
  • seven-day last-touch uniqueness and impression/purchase linkage;
  • attributed revenue, discount, tax, total, and payment reconciliation;
  • stockout location exclusivity;
  • physical stock, transfer conservation, and explicit unfulfilled-demand accounting;
  • truck timing and inventory relationships;
  • sales only within each store's operating hours, evaluated in store-local time, and local_hour equal to the store-local hour of event_ts;
  • returns linked to their sale (same store and customer), posted after it (on a later store-local day, by construction), refunding no more than the sale;
  • exactly one approved payment per receipt and order, unique transaction IDs;
  • logistics incidents reference known DCs and stores and resolve after they start;
  • no receipt line sold before its product's launch date;
  • returns posted strictly after the originating sale (never same-day);
  • product lifecycle dates present (no degenerate lifecycles).

utility/src/retail_setup/generation/invariants.py enforces the shared live/batch invariants: operating hours, product launch eligibility, return timing, lifecycle presence, and validated profile controls.

items.title: Naming compatibility
items.text: New columns use snake_case, but current TMDL compatibility requires explicit legacy exceptions such as ID, StoreNumber, CustomerId, StoreID, ReceiptId, Source, Subtotal, and __index_level_0__. These exceptions are documented in schemas.py and must not be silently normalized in a transform.

items.title: Store profiles and derived defaults
items.text:
Supported profiles are supercenter, grocery, hardware, and luxury, plus per-environment custom business layouts (custom-<slug>, see the setup CLI customize contract). Custom layouts are built deterministically from a saved spec by the same catalog builder as the preset trees (retail_setup.dictionaries.catalog). Their products.json rows add explicit Taxability and Refrigerated values, which take precedence over the department/category name rules preset catalogs rely on. Their brand Category equals a department name, and branded titles use a brand from the product's own department.

A custom layout's department_weights are calibrated when its dictionaries are built (retail_setup.customization.calibrate). Copilot tends to answer with revenue-like shares, which, read as basket-line shares, leave a realistic ticket target buying about one item. When the ticket target affords fewer than min(basket_lambda, 2) items, the weights move toward line share (weight * expected_line_value ** -alpha) by the smallest alpha in [0, 1] that reaches it, or alpha = 1 when nothing smaller does. The ticket target and catalog are unchanged, the saved spec keeps Copilot's weights, and profile.json carries the calibrated ones, so batch, stream and estimates all use them. Dictionaries built by an older calibration are rebuilt automatically. Current derived defaults include:

  • silver_db = ag
  • gold_db = au
  • dc_count = max(1, store_count // 10)
  • customer_count = max(store_count * transactions_per_store_day * 365 * 1.0525 * (1 - anonymous_share) / (0.75 * v), 5000), where v is the profile's customer_visits_per_year (supercenter 8, grocery 9, hardware 6, luxury 2.5): about 14,000 customers per supercenter
  • anonymous_share = 0.45
  • annual_churn_rate = 0.20
  • annual_volume_growth = 0.03
  • transactions_per_store_day = the store type's profile value (see below)
  • online_orders_per_day = store_count * transactions_per_store_day * 1.0525 * s / (1 - s), where s is the profile's online_order_share and 1.0525 is the mean store traffic multiplier, so online orders are s of all orders
  • return_rate = 0.01
  • brands_per_product = 3
  • truck_capacity = 15000

Each store type's profile sets its store knobs. Presets declare them; custom layouts derive them:

Store type Receipts per store-day Operating hours Store formats Online share supercenter 400 6-22, 7-23, 24h hypermarket, superstore, standard 12% grocery 280 6-22, 7-22, 7-23 superstore, standard, neighborhood, express 15% hardware 180 6-21, 7-21, 7-22 superstore, standard, neighborhood 20% luxury 40 10-19, 10-20, 11-19 boutique 25% custom 400 * (85 / avg_ticket_target) ** 0.6, 20-1000 hours whose hourly weight reaches 10% of the peak (24h when that is all day) boutique at a $500+ ticket, else all other formats profile value

A store's format is drawn from those its volume class suits among the store type's formats. Every store follows its store type's operating_hours patterns ("24h" or "open-close"). Foot traffic, BLE pings and zone changes use the store type's zones (upper-cased), in history and in the live stream, and the same visit path (vocabulary.visit_zone_path): entrance, one to three department zones in random order, checkout (buyers) and exit.

fact_foot_traffic counts zone passages per store-hour, not shares of the visitors: the entrance and exit count every visitor of the hour, checkout counts the hour's buyers (so it is never below the receipts), and each department zone the visitors who browse it (on average two zones a visitor). Visitor totals and conversion use the entrance count; the semantic model's Foot Traffic Count does so unless a zone is filtered. Beacons detect a quarter of visits (BLE_DETECTED_SHARE), buyers and non-buyers alike. A detected buyer's pings run entrance, departments, checkout and exit, with the purchase in the middle of its checkout dwell; a non-buyer starts inside the hour and never passes checkout. Pings and zone changes stay inside store hours.

items.title: Customers and churn
items.text:
generation/customers.py gives every customer a lifecycle, as pure functions of the seed and their ID, shared by history and the live stream:

  • Home store. dim_customers.HomeStoreID is drawn in proportion to store traffic, and the customer lives in that store's geography. 85% of a customer's identified visits are at the home store; the rest are at another store, picked by traffic.
  • Anonymous shoppers. About anonymous_share (45%) of in-store receipts have no customer_id (cash and non-loyalty shoppers). Returns, BLE pings of anonymous visits and most marketing impressions also carry none. Every consumer filters or tolerates NULL customer_id.
  • Visit frequency. Each customer's yearly trip rate is lognormal around the profile's customer_visits_per_year, capped at three trips a week (156 a year), and replicated as selection tickets.
  • Acquisition. Customers who already existed when history starts are active from the first day; the rest sign up uniformly across the history, so first purchases keep arriving and the base turns over. The two groups are sized so acquisitions replace churn.
  • Churn. A customer's lifetime is exponential with a hazard driven by segment (budget and convenience shoppers churn sooner than brand-loyal and quality shoppers), trip frequency (infrequent visitors churn sooner) and basket budget (small spenders churn sooner). The base hazard is calibrated so annual_churn_rate (default 20%) of the customers active at a time churn within a year. 75% of churners taper: their visits fall linearly to 15% of their rate over the 60 days before they stop, the early-warning signal a churn model can learn. The rest stop abruptly.
  • Online orders and marketing. An online order's customer is active on the order day (the first of four tries; an order that finds none is not placed), and a CRM-matched impression's customer is signed up and not churned.

A receipt is identified with a calibrated probability, picks a ticket from its pool, and keeps that customer with their activity on the receipt's local date (1 while active, tapering before churn, 0 before signup or after churn); otherwise it is anonymous. Churn dates are not published: models learn them from purchase behavior.

items.title: Prices, baskets and promotions
items.text:
generation/pricing.py sets every SKU's shelf price per week, as a pure function of the seed, the SKU and the date, shared by receipts, online orders and the live stream:

  • dim_products.SalePrice is the list price at anchor_date. Regular prices follow a per-department inflation trend from there (for example grocery 3%, electronics -3% a year).
  • Every 13 weeks (each SKU on its own phase) a price review resets the regular price within 6% of trend; 30% of review periods carry a one-to-three week markdown of 10-35%. Regular prices end in .49 or .99 (9 cents below $1); markdown prices end in 9 cents and always undercut the regular price.
  • fact_receipt_lines.unit_cents and fact_online_order_lines.unit_cents are the shelf price on the sale's local date. No separate price-history table is published: reports read sale prices from the lines and catalog prices from dim_products.
  • Product choice responds to price: within a department, a SKU's choice weight scales with (price / trend price) ** elasticity, with department elasticities from about -0.8 (groceries, jewelry) to -2.5 (electronics), so markdowns sell more units.
  • Store traffic and online orders grow annual_volume_growth (3%) a year from the anchor date.

Store baskets (generation/baskets.py, shared with the stream) are built per receipt:

  1. Lines are drawn by department missions as before; 15% of lines bring along their complementary product, a fixed partner in the same department, so market-basket analysis finds real pairs.
  2. A SKU drawn twice becomes one line with the summed quantity.
  3. A receipt with an offer (the profile's promo_rate) gets one promotion code for the whole basket, drawn among the PROMO_CATALOG codes in season whose minimum (for example SAVE20 at $50, BFRIDAY40 at $100) the basket gross subtotal meets. Seasonal codes are three times as likely while in season. Each code discounts only the lines in its department scope (for example BACKTOSCHOOL20 on clothing, office and electronics); BOGO50 discounts every second unit of eligible lines with two or more units. A line carries at most one code, and fact_promotions has at most one row per receipt.
  4. Tax is integer basis-point math on each line's net amount, at the share of the store's combined rate its state's taxability rule sets (_shared/tax_rules.json, baskets.line_tax_cents). Taxable goods pay the full rate everywhere. Grocery staples (NON_TAXABLE) are exempt unless the state taxes food (for example Alabama, Mississippi, South Dakota, Tennessee at a reduced share). Clothing (REDUCED_RATE) pays the full rate unless the state exempts it (Minnesota, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Vermont) or exempts items under a price (New York under $110, Massachusetts under $175, Rhode Island under $250). Online orders apply the fulfilling store's state, or the customer's for ship-from-DC orders; returns refund at the original rule. Dictionary sets without the rules file use the defaults (groceries exempt, clothing taxed).

Fulfillment prices the basket again over the lines the store could fill, so a promotion whose minimum the filled basket no longer meets is replaced or dropped. The invariants check one code per receipt, met minimums, and no repeated SKU within a receipt.

items.title: Removed active-path behavior
items.text: Local FastAPI control, DuckDB persistence, parquet export, Blob upload, Event Hubs, outbox, dead-letter queue (DLQ), and Prometheus services are not part of the supported Fabric-native contract.

items.title: Decision experience and action boundaries
items.text: This specification defines the proposed action layer and Retail customer experience (CX). It replaces dated implementation plans; the Fabric profile manifest still defines deployment selections. REQ-MLAI-005 remains proposed: the presence of replay/app code does not prove the complete scenario, shared hosting, or production execution.

items.title: Current local application boundary
items.text:
app/backend/main.py routes questions to Fabric Data Agent and Ontology MCP services, and to inventory/retention tools in app/backend/agents.py. app/backend/replay.py supplies synthetic replay responses. Inspect the selected mode before presenting any answer as live.

Live proposals are local JSON records managed by app/backend/proposals.py. Approving a record changes its local status; it does not submit a purchase order, send a campaign, or call an ERP, CRM, pricing, or workforce system. app/backend/eventhouse.py sends telemetry on daemon threads and suppresses ingestion errors. It is best-effort telemetry, not a guaranteed audit trail. These limitations are tracked by THREAT-009 and SEC-012.

items.title: Native availability pack
items.text:
REQ-MLAI-006 covers a separate native experience, not a claim that the full proposed CX application is implemented. The deployment entry point is deploy/scripts/deploy_operations_planning.py; configuration and operator steps live in the deployment guide.

Configuration enables the pack by default whenever the profile provisions Eventhouse and a semantic model, with include_plan=false. Because Fabric can reject Operations Agent creation, an operations-only deployment step is non-required: its failure is journaled and the deployment continues. Readiness expects the Operations Agent as a non-required item, so its absence degrades rather than fails readiness. Explicitly including the Plan restores a required, fail-closed step.

operations_planning.include_plan=false selects Operations Agent and its draft notebook independently. It bypasses only unselected Planning prerequisites, not authentication or validation for a selected Plan. No model connection is changed and no fixed credentials are created. Agent instructions and notebook notes route human review to the Lakehouse draft table and existing SSO report instead of a nonexistent Plan. Readiness excludes the unselected Plan. Use this mode when organizational policy prohibits fixed credentials; native Planning is unsupported in that environment, not silently simulated.

The bounded Protect weekend availability scenario seeds a watchlist of at most 20 of the network's riskiest observed positions. Positions that meet an agent alert rule (stockout_probability >= 0.7 or days_of_inventory < 3) rank first, then the positions closest to one. Nothing is relabeled; when no position is at risk, the agent has nothing to alert on, so activation is refused: the report records activation_refused and alertable_signal_count: 0, and the agent stays stopped. Everything else is published, so the publisher exits 3 and the deploy journals the step DEGRADED without prompting; rerun the publication with --operations-only once the stockout or forecast outputs show an at-risk position. Slow-moving catalogs (for example home improvement, where a SKU reorders at a 12-unit case floor) often have no such position until logistics incidents or the live stream draw stock down. When the native Plan is selected, the watchlist stays inside the Plan's locked cohort (store IDs 1-5, product IDs 1-20) so every case can be reviewed there. The scenario takes current au.stockout_risk, keeps positions with a complete seven-day forecast from au.demand_forecast, and resolves product names through ag.dim_products. Missing, non-finite, negative forecast, duplicate-grain, out-of-scope, stale, and future evidence fail closed. A known negative stock ledger is not inbound supply; the available-stock measure has a zero floor. Every case's source_as_of is the risk snapshot's as-of time (stockout_risk.predicted_at), not the SKU's last ledger change, so an unchanged (often stocked-out) SKU is not dropped as stale by the agent's seven-day filter. The snapshot can precede the forecast's common source anchor. Both timestamps remain explicit; publication time does not replace either. Case identity includes store, product, and both source timestamps. Each signal also records plan_cohort, the cohort mode it was selected in. Risk retains its own risk_horizon_days (default three); it is not relabeled as seven-day risk. The Plan's additive Next 7 Days measures slice forecast dates rather than filtering horizon metadata: the demand model defaults to fourteen days. Existing full-horizon measures remain unchanged.

After every fresh setup the agent has an open disruption to act on. Each generated history ends inside the end-of-history DC outage (see the data contract): the DC serving the most stores has dispatched nothing for the last days of history, and the outage is still open at the risk snapshot. The store policy keeps four to eight days of cover, so outside an incident no position falls under three days. The outage really draws those stores' fast movers down through the simulation, and some reach days_of_inventory < 3 or zero stock. Their signals carry the outage as active_incident_id, active_incident_type (DC_OUTAGE) and active_incident_cause. Slow movers keep at least a case on the shelf, so a layout that sells almost nothing fast (a small luxury network, or the Plan's fixed product cohort when those products sell slowly) can still have no alertable case. The live stream resolves the outage at its planned end, 6 to 54 hours after history ends.

fabric/operations/01-availability-tables.kql owns ops_availability_signals and ops_case_actions. These are selected-pack tables, not the optional retail event stream. Seeding them must not satisfy stream watermarks, ingestion, or checkpoint freshness. The agent's canonical query (fabric/operations/availability.instructions.md) keeps the latest signal per store and product, so a refreshed case supersedes the older case for the same position, then left-anti joins ops_case_actions so a case with a DRAFT, APPROVED, or RESOLVED action never alerts again. deploy/scripts/_operations_scenario.current_alert_cases is the tested reference for those semantics. Historical reorder rows do not establish open commitments, confirmed inbound, reservations, or shared DC availability. Each signal also carries its supply context from Silver logistics: the store's DC (dc_id), its observed delivery lead time (lead_time_days), the units of the product on trucks to the store at the snapshot (inbound_units, planned to arrive at expected_inbound_ts), and the logistics incident affecting the store at the snapshot (active_incident_id, active_incident_type, active_incident_cause from fact_logistics_incident_stores and fact_logistics_incidents). The agent explains a shortage with these fields only; reservations and shared budget stay unverified.

The deploy seeds the signals once. 17-refresh-availability-signals reseeds them nightly in daily-maintenance after 06-ml-demand-forecast and 12-ml-stockout-prediction, using the same selection and validation (a test requires identical SQL and signals) and the plan_cohort recorded by the deploy. It skips cleanly when the pack is not deployed, and writes nothing when the Gold snapshot is older than seven days. Without new stream data the snapshot does not advance, so the readiness check freshness.operations_signals reports the signals UNKNOWN once they leave the agent's seven-day window.

retail-availability-operations publishes stopped with its KQL database and instructions. The REST publisher omits the empty playbook object so the UI can generate it. The public definition API rejects FabricJobAction, so the publisher follows item creation with the UI-native OA workload call and binds prepare-replenishment-case using itemArtifactId, itemWorkspaceId, and RunNotebook. It requires exact workload-service readback of one KQL source and one action. The public service may normalize a KQL source ID to all zeroes in definition readback; the workload readback is authoritative for configured source/action details. The public definition is published with shouldRun=false.

Saving the workload configuration makes Fabric generate the playbook (the agent's rules) from its instructions; GET configuration/behaviorModel returns HTTP 409 BehaviorModelGenerationInProgress until it finishes. When operations_planning.activate_agent is true (the default), the publisher waits up to 15 minutes for a playbook with at least one rule, then sets agentState=Active through PATCH configuration/settings and requires an Active readback. It never starts an agent without generated rules. A failed start leaves the agent stopped and records activation_warning in the report instead of failing publication. Running the agent sends recommendations only; every action still requires human approval, and deployment never enables autonomous purchasing. Teams destination review remains an operator step.

The prepare-replenishment-case action validates a selected case against live signals, freezes the inspected snapshot, and merges a DRAFT into <lakehouse>.ops.replenishment_cases. The deploy renders PLAN_COHORT into its parameters; the Plan's store/product bounds are enforced only when a Plan is published, so operations-only cases anywhere in the network are accepted. It never overwrites an existing case. Existing APPROVED or RESOLVED cases are not relabeled or audited as DRAFT. An idempotently tagged Kusto audit follows the durable Delta write. The two services are not an atomic transaction: failures propagate and a retry can finish the missing audit without duplicating the draft. Historical ag/au tables and external purchasing systems remain unchanged.

retail-replenishment is a native Plan, not another autonomous agent. Its supported PlanV1 definition binds the deployed semantic model through an explicitly supplied shared Power BI Semantic Model connection (PowerBIDatasets, OAuth2 or ServicePrincipal). Separately, the underlying Direct Lake-to-data connection must use fixed credentials, not Automatic/SSO. WorkspaceIdentity can be valid for that underlying hop but is not a supported substitute for the Plan-to-model connection. The deploy inspects both without automatically rebinding the existing model. The deploy must reject missing connection or unacknowledged billing before creating either component of a combined request. --operations-only is an explicit partial operation when configuration still includes the Plan. A persistent include_plan=false selection requires only the Operations components.

Native planning what-if inputs are assumptions until confirmed. There is no public run-Optimize API in this implementation and no automatic bridge from Plan writeback to an ERP, or from a case row into a new semantic-model table. The planner uses the case's store/product identifiers for the human handoff. Native application-database bootstrap, interactive model access, approval workflows, and SQL writeback need separate in-product acceptance. Plan creation/opening can start a non-cancellable 30-day billable session.

The source definitions are not added to unsupported fabric-cicd item types. Native item APIs perform idempotent name resolution, bounded long-running-operation polling, and definition readback. Duplicate names, untrusted polling hosts, denied requests, and mismatches fail explicitly. Supported existing task-flow bindings remain unchanged until native artifact-type support is established.

items.title: Responsibility split
items.text:
flowchart LR
    User[Question or decision] --> Router[Application orchestrator]
    Router --> Metrics[Semantic model: measures and broad aggregates]
    Router --> Graph[Ontology: named entities and relationships]
    Router --> Actions[Domain action tools]
    Metrics --> Evidence[Source, grain, time window, limitations]
    Graph --> Evidence
    Evidence --> Actions
    Actions --> Draft[Local proposal]
    Draft --> Human[Approve, dismiss, or scenario override]
    Human --> Package[Draft action package]
    Human -. best-effort telemetry .-> Eventhouse[Eventhouse]

Use semantic-model measures for rankings, period comparisons, conversion, velocity, margin, and prediction rollups. Use the ontology for named-entity context, serving-node/compatible-SKU paths, and evidence relationships. Do not substitute an unbounded graph scan for broad analytical queries. The active live generator writes directly to Eventhouse through Spark Kusto, not through Eventstream.

items.title: Proposed action roster
items.text:
Only inventory and retention have local action-tool implementations. The remaining domain tools and multi-agent composition require acceptance and verification under the ML/AI backlog.

Domain Evidence and decision Proposed draft Inventory Stockout risk, forecast, balances, and covering reorders; serving DC/truck path Reorder, expedite, rebalance, or safety-stock review Retention Churn, segment/LTV, purchase context, and market-basket cross-sell Cohort win-back brief and offer suggestions Pricing Elasticity, promotion discount, margin, and price recommendation Price/promotion review with quantified assumptions Store operations Velocity, conversion, checkout dwell, and anomalies Staffing, lane, investigation, or store task Fulfillment Predicted truck dwell, lane delays, fulfillment mix, and uncovered demand Dispatch/route/fulfillment review Merchandising Association lift/confidence, sell-through, spread, and returns Bundle, placement, assortment, or quality review

An actionable recommendation requires a quantified gap, a decision owner, and a reversible first step. Informational executive, channel, segment, forecast, journey, or association questions must not silently create actions. Composite opportunities include revenue-at-risk retention, stockout/sales protection, margin recovery, and a prioritized per-store action list. Illustrative financial impacts are assumptions, not realized savings.

items.title: Proposed guardrails
items.text:
Tier Meaning Required boundary before enabling execution T0 Inform without a write Identify source and uncertainty T1 Draft a local proposal Display evidence; human review before promotion T2 Reversible external execution Explicit authenticated approval and durable outcome record T3 High-impact price, offer, or large reorder Approval plus reason, limits, and audit evidence

Only the local draft/review boundary is in scope today. Future tools must validate IDs against source rows, use configurable numeric thresholds, check covering/repeated actions for idempotency, cap fan-out, and retain the asker, evidence, tier, approver, outcome, and decision time. These are proposed controls, not guarantees of the existing prototype.

items.title: Proposed Retail CX scenario
items.text:
The fictional Aster & Pine Outfitters scenario, Protect the Winner, follows Dana Reyes, a regional merchandising lead:

  1. A declining Performance Footwear category contains a growing Momentum Runner product family. Compare periods and store/channel contribution.
  2. Find named products/SKUs, stock snapshots, stores, regions, channels, and fulfillment nodes through explicit relationships.
  3. Activate sufficiently covered stores, replenish high-velocity constrained stores, and propose compatible transfers from slower excess-stock stores.
  4. Remove one source store with a required human reason; retain the original recommendation and recalculate candidates.
  5. Produce a draft transfer/replenishment list, activation brief, execution checklist, evidence bundle, owner, review date, and decision/override log.

Reserved inventory remains at its certified fulfillment-node/product grain. Never infer store allocation, SKU compatibility, or a relationship absent from source data. Separate selling, fulfilling, and source stores; use one inventory snapshot/as-of time, aggregate numerators and denominators before ratios, and align periods with the scenario's fiscal calendar. Distinguish observed facts, derived values, and recommendations; return unsupported when required evidence is missing.

items.title: Proposed experience and replay contract
items.text:
• Decision Cockpit: synthetic label, report or replay, morning brief, guided prompts, route badge, and evidence/query trace.
  • Story Studio: chapter navigation, Work/Fabric/Foundry/Web IQ cards, signal state, independent Question Lab, explicit action trigger, decisions, and links to the canvas and operations.
  • Decision Canvas: signal, diagnosis, certified-grain constraint, recommendation, override, draft package, owner, and review state.
  • Ontology Explorer: entities, properties, relationships, and highlighted paths used by the selected answer.
  • Agent Operations: proposal states, approvals/dismissals/overrides, modeled impact assumptions, evidence ownership, and live/replay provenance.
  • Walkthrough: capability explanation, validated click path, and fallback.

Replay and live modes must use the same response contracts and components. Replay must visibly say REPLAY — SYNTHETIC DATA and work without Fabric credentials. A versioned fixture must include KPIs, prompts, metric/graph answers, graph paths, cards, override response, action package, and telemetry. Do not silently present fixture data as a successful live query.

items.title: Proposed data and packaging
items.text:
Generate all records independently, never by copying, sampling, perturbing, or hashing customer records. Use fictional vocabulary and opaque keys; keep real contact details, credentials, environment identifiers, and customer response logs out of source, fixtures, and screenshots. Review generated content before publication (SEC-003, SEC-010, SEC-012).

The scenario package needs a fixed seed/date/scale run ID, source-separated JSONL or Parquet, file checksums, row counts, reconciliation results, and golden answers. It should intentionally exercise category decline/product growth, three high-velocity low-cover stores, four activation-ready stores, two excess-stock stores, an override, and an aggregate-grain DC constraint. These are scenario requirements, not changes to historical TABLES.

Potential future entities include ProductFamily, SKU, InventorySnapshot, FulfillmentNode, TradingSignal, DecisionScenario, Recommendation, Evidence, Decision, Override, and ActionPackage. Extend the authoritative model and ontology contracts before claiming these relationships exist.

Reuse the standalone app before considering hosted delegated-identity or Fabric Workload packaging. Keep backend/UI contracts portable; a new agent framework is optional, not a prerequisite. Shared hosting, service identity, secret management, durable approvals/audit, external adapters, and a native Fabric shell require separate design and tests.

items.title: Verification still required
items.text: Run the complete five-act story in replay without credentials, assert answers and override transitions, verify synthetic labels and no production writes, and exercise degraded live-service behavior. Separately validate live Fabric/model/ontology bindings and telemetry delivery with retained run evidence. Golden replay answers are not live readiness proof.

items.title: Pipeline sequence
items.text:
The deployment separates data setup, required Reporting dependencies, and extended ML:

  1. setup-pipeline runs setup notebooks 01 through 11.
  2. ml-required runs in two waves to avoid oversubscribing the shared Spark pool: Gold (setup-11), demand forecast (06), market-basket mining (07), promotion/elasticity analysis (10) and stockout (12) first; customer segmentation (08) and churn (09) once that wave finishes. Producers retry once and hold a writer lock on their output (ag._job_locks).
  3. 15-validate-required-ml-contract runs only after all six producers succeed, and validates all six required output tables.
  4. Reporting can publish only after that exact pipeline run reaches terminal Completed.
  5. full-demo runs ml-optional (notebooks 11 and 13) and ml-experimental (notebook 14, which consumes price_elasticity produced by the required run) after Reporting.

Optional or experimental failure cannot block required Reporting. Ontology creation is a separate preview phase after Reporting and extended ML, but full-demo executes it automatically. The task-flow metadata mirrors the runtime order as Required ML Reporting Gate -> Reporting -> Post-Reporting Extended ML.

items.title: ML contracts
items.text:
The repository includes demand forecast, market-basket, customer segmentation, churn, promotion effectiveness, journey, stockout, delivery, and dynamic pricing notebooks.

contracts/retail-demo.json records typed support tiers and one contract for each of their 14 outputs:

Tier Outputs Required demand_forecast, customer_segments, churn_predictions, stockout_risk, product_recommendations, price_elasticity Optional promoted product_associations, journey_patterns, zone_transitions, zone_dwell_stats, dwell_predictions Experimental promotion_lift, pricing_constraints, pricing_recommendations

Every contract identifies its producer and source tables, exact output schema and grain, as-of and lineage fields, intended use, and limitations. Producer notebooks declare the same schema and validate types and non-null constraints immediately before writing that exact physical target. Required contracts additionally reference the active Tabular Model Definition Language (TMDL) projection and the runtime validator. These checks keep the manifest aligned with the physical schema.

For all six required outputs, generated_at is the true Gold publication timestamp and model_run_id identifies that generation. Source/business cutoffs remain separate lineage: source_as_of for demand, segmented_at for segments, prediction_date for churn, and predicted_at plus inventory_as_of for stockout. product_recommendations and price_elasticity carry the same generated_at, model_run_id, and schema_version lineage columns as the original four; their business as-of remains computed_at. Readiness orders and ages generated_at from the same row as a nonblank run ID; it never treats a business as-of date as a generation timestamp.

The Reporting gate requires nonempty results from market-basket mining and promotion/elasticity analysis, alongside demand, segmentation, churn, and stockout outputs. This includes product_recommendations and price_elasticity in the required tier.

The runtime validator creates no tables. It rejects missing/empty required outputs, incompatible columns or types, null/duplicate grain keys, invalid probabilities or bounds, NaN or infinity in any floating output, missing as-of/lineage, and incomplete forecast horizons. It also rejects:

  • a table whose source as-of column (SOURCE_AS_OF_COLUMNS) holds more than one value, outputs whose source as-of values differ by more than MAX_AS_OF_SKEW_HOURS (default 6), and any source as-of that is ahead of the current Silver as-of or behind it by more than MAX_SOURCE_LAG_HOURS (default 24);
  • store, product and customer keys missing from dim_stores, dim_products or dim_customers (FOREIGN_KEYS);
  • category values outside ALLOWED_CATEGORY_VALUES, which include every literal the semantic model's measures filter on (HIGH stockout risk, High/Very High churn, Highly Elastic/Inelastic SKUs);
  • a demand mape at or above MAX_FORECAST_MAPE (default 1.0, the error of forecasting zero). Demand is the only required output that records a quality metric in its table; the other producers log theirs to MLflow.

tests/scripts/test_ml_required_logic_imp008.py checks the category values against the producers and the TMDL measures. Repository validation parses the validator's required grain, as-of, lineage, probability, and horizon rules and compares them exactly with the manifest.

Optional outputs may be empty when the business preconditions for a result do not exist. For example, sparse baskets can produce no association rules, and a delivery run can have no currently open arrivals to score. In those cases the producer overwrites the target with an empty table that still has the exact contract schema. Readiness accepts that empty snapshot only when the owning optional pipeline has exact, recent terminal-success evidence.

Demand evaluation freezes store/product eligibility at the training cutoff; current production inference selects its cohort independently. Churn and stockout partition on label-availability dates and purge 90-day and three-day forward-label horizons, respectively.

items.title: Shared source as-of
items.text:
Every required producer anchors on the same source as-of time: the latest event_ts in Silver fact_receipts. Each reads only source rows at or before it, so the six outputs describe one snapshot of Silver even when the stream adds rows between producers.

Demand counts SALE receipts only (returns never net units sold) and anchors on the last complete day, the day before the as-of date. The partial as-of day is not used for training, testing or the inference lags, and forecasts start on the as-of date, so forecast_date - to_date(source_as_of) runs from 0 to forecast_horizon_days - 1. A day with no receipts at all in the source (the gap between the end of history and a later live stream) is a source gap, not zero demand: the dense calendar flags it, gives it the combination's mean observed demand for the lag and rolling features only, and never uses it as a training label, calibration or test actual, or for eligibility.

Stockout scores current positions rolled forward to the as-of time. Each store/product keeps its last ledger balance (inventory_as_of is when that balance was recorded), while its demand windows end at the as-of time. A slow mover's months-old snapshot is therefore scored on today's demand, not the demand around its last ledger change. Ledger rows after the as-of time, such as scheduled deliveries, are ignored.

Segmentation and churn count every purchase of a known customer: store SALE receipts and online orders (fact_online_order_headers). Returns and anonymous purchases (null customer_id) never count. Segmentation produces one row per customer with at least one purchase. Churn scores a customer at a snapshot only when they purchased in the feature window before it, so never-active and long-lapsed customers are neither trivial training examples nor published predictions; an online order in the forward window keeps a customer active. Churn aggregates purchases to customer-days first and pairs each day only with the snapshots whose feature or label window contains it, so its work grows with activity rather than with customers times snapshots.

items.title: Stockout inventory semantics
items.text:
The inventory ledger retains signed balances; a deficit is not a negative number of available units. Notebook 12 selects the latest inventory event per store/product/day, then derives model current_inventory as max(balance, 0) for known balances. Both training and current inference use that same snapshot function, so derived days_of_inventory and inventory ratios remain nonnegative. This does not rewrite the underlying ledger.

Unknown balances remain null, and the producer rejects any null inventory balance before training. A null must never be converted to zero by Spark's greatest null-skipping behavior. Notebook 15 continues to reject negative inventory/demand/coverage, invalid classes/horizons/ranks, and inconsistent as-of timestamps. Its stockout error reports per-rule violation counts. utility/tests/generation/test_stockout_contract_runtime.py executes the producer feature functions and the downstream domain validator together.

items.title: Stockout model
items.text:
Stockouts are rare (about 0.4% of store/product days stock out within the three-day horizon), and most of the risk sits in the few low-stock positions. Notebook 12 therefore fits a Spark LogisticRegression on the physical driver of a stockout: log-scaled current stock, demand velocity, and stock cover over the horizon (current stock divided by expected horizon demand, capped at 999), plus demand trend and day of week. Day of month and week of year are excluded because, with about a year of history, they identify individual dates rather than a repeatable pattern. The held-out isotonic calibrator is unchanged.

The earlier depth-5 gradient-boosted ensemble memorized the few low-stock examples and calendar dates. Against observed history it scored a one-unit position at about 20% when roughly 60% stocked out within three days. On the same held-out window the logistic model is calibrated in every stock band and ranks better (AUC about 0.98 versus 0.93).

Churn retains hidden nullable is_churned_actual solely as a deprecated compatibility projection and always writes it as null. All formerly exposed required columns remain present, so a failed required-ML gate can leave the previous Reporting artifact query-compatible while Reporting publication stays blocked.

Optional and experimental corrections are also contract-bound:

  • recommendation support, confidence, and lift come from one singleton-pair market-basket rule counted over every SALE basket, single-item baskets included, so support and lift are relative to all baskets. A rule needs at least MIN_PAIR_BASKETS (default 20) co-purchases, MIN_CONFIDENCE (default 0.05) and lift above MIN_LIFT (default 1.0); each product keeps its MAX_RULES_PER_PRODUCT (default 5) best rules by lift. The generator's complementary products (baskets.with_complements) are what these rules recover.
