It also writes utility/out/<env>/render-manifest.json with the resolved generation window. All twelve notebooks default to that environment directory. An explicit render output override is an advanced path; normal deployment consumes the environment-scoped output.

Notebook JSON is parsed structurally. Code substitutions are allowed only inside ordinary Python string literals, then encoded with Python literal representation and parsed for syntax; remaining tokens outside supported literals fail. Metadata is substituted as data and the notebook is serialized with JSON encoding. Quotes, backslashes, or statement-like text in --ref therefore remain string data rather than executable statements.

Without --ref, render requires Git metadata resolving the checkout's full commit revision. Missing Git metadata fails closed instead of falling back to mutable main. Setup 01 downloads dictionaries from GitHub at that revision, so it must exist on GitHub:

  • If HEAD is on a remote-tracking branch, render uses HEAD.
  • If HEAD isn't pushed, render uses the newest pushed ancestor and prints a note. This happens only when utility/data/dictionaries in the working tree, including uncommitted and untracked files, is identical to that ancestor.
  • Unpushed dictionary changes fail with a message to push or pass --ref.
  • A clone with no remote-tracking refs keeps HEAD.

An explicit --ref remains accepted; operators should use an immutable revision for reproducibility.

items.title: Dictionary source and cache
items.text:
Setup 01 owns Files/setup/dictionaries/_dictionary_manifest.json. An immutable 40- or 64-hex revision is reused only when manifest version, repository owner/name, ref, store type, complete expected JSON-file inventory, recorded optional absences, sizes, and SHA-256 hashes match. Mutable refs always refresh, even when the prior manifest matches.

All downloads and JSON validation complete in staging before publication. Only a 404 for a declared optional file is accepted; other download/JSON failures stop the attempt. Publication invalidates the old manifest, replaces files, removes stale optional files, and atomically publishes the new manifest last. This is not an atomic directory swap or distributed transaction: interrupted publication cannot leave a manifest that marks partial data as valid. utility/tests/test_dictionary_seed_cache.py covers revision changes, corruption, interrupted downloads, immutable hits, mutable refresh, optional 404 behavior, and invalid JSON.

Custom business layouts are never committed, so Setup 01 cannot download them. Render injects CUSTOM_DICTIONARIES, the SHA-256 of each custom file, and the deploy step upload-custom-dictionaries (deploy/scripts/upload_custom_dictionaries.py) writes those files through the OneLake DFS API to Files/setup/custom-dictionaries/<store_type>/ and reads each one back to compare digests. Setup 01 still downloads _shared from GitHub, takes the custom files from that inbox only when their digests match, and records the digests in the manifest source, so a changed layout never reuses a stale cache. A missing or altered upload fails the notebook. Custom layouts have no optional tags.json.

Fork execution must set RETAIL_SETUP_REPOSITORY_OWNER and RETAIL_SETUP_REPOSITORY_NAME in the notebook runtime environment. Defaults are amattas and retail-demo. The CLI injects the ref but does not auto-detect a fork or automatically forward local environment overrides to Fabric. A fork-only commit must be fetched from the repository that owns it.

The wheel includes dictionaries and all twelve notebook resources under retail_setup/resources/; loaders/rendering can use these outside a checkout. utility/pyproject.toml pins the build backend to hatchling==1.33.0. After generator/template work finishes, rebuild generated notebooks before claiming the packaged/rendered artifact set is current.

items.title: Render targets
items.text:
1. setup-01-seed-dictionaries.ipynb
  2. setup-02-generate-dimensions.ipynb
  3. setup-03-generate-sales.ipynb
  4. setup-04-generate-online-orders.ipynb
  5. setup-05-generate-marketing.ipynb
  6. setup-06-generate-returns-and-promotions.ipynb
  7. setup-07-generate-store-activity.ipynb
  8. setup-08-generate-inventory.ipynb
  9. setup-09-attribute-marketing.ipynb
  10. setup-10-publish-silver.ipynb
  11. setup-11-build-gold.ipynb
  12. stream-events.ipynb

In setup-pipeline, notebooks 02 (dimension validation), 03, 04, and 05 run in parallel after 01. Notebooks 06, 07, and 08 run in parallel after 03; 09 waits for 03 to 06. Each notebook runs its own stages concurrently and passes outputs to later notebooks as gen__* tables in the Silver staging schema.

Setup 10 checks invariants and publishes Silver atomically once 02 to 09 succeed. Setup 11 builds Gold inside ml-required, alongside model training, because both read only Silver.

items.title: Required tokens
items.text:
Token Meaning LAKEHOUSE_NAME Target Lakehouse display name SILVER_DB Silver schema, normally ag GOLD_DB Gold schema, normally au STORE_TYPE Dictionary/profile START_DATE Derived or explicit historical start END_DATE Derived or explicit historical end STORE_COUNT Number of stores TRANSACTIONS_PER_STORE_DAY Historical in-store transactions per store-day; sizes the live stream ONLINE_ORDERS_PER_DAY Historical online orders per day; sizes the live stream SEED Deterministic seed DICTIONARY_REF Git ref used for dictionary content CUSTOM_DICTIONARIES JSON map of custom layout file → SHA-256; {} for presets

stream-events is rendered with the setup notebooks but is staged separately and is not part of the ordered setup pipeline.

items.title: deploy
items.text:
Common flags:

  • --env <name>
  • --skip-terraform
  • --dry-run
  • --yes
  • --recreate
  • --resume

--recreate and --skip-terraform cannot be combined. A non-dry-run deploy loads the environment, validates the current Azure CLI tenant where applicable, detects an existing workspace for interactive reset, executes the deployment plan, and deploys the task flow where selected.

setup-pipeline includes only setup notebooks 01 through 11. For profiles that publish Reporting, deploy then runs ml-required with terminal polling. Its six producers (demand forecast, customer segmentation, churn, stockout, market-basket mining, and promotion/elasticity analysis) feed 15-validate-required-ml-contract; only exact-run success allows a second publication phase to stage the semantic model and report. full-demo runs ml-optional and ml-experimental afterward.

After those pipelines, deployment synchronizes Lakehouse SQL endpoint metadata. This makes newly written tables visible to SQL and Power BI clients. The step is optional because readiness independently fails closed when a required table is unavailable.

The deployment artifact build also consumes the render manifest and rewrites the staged Power BI report date filters to the month containing end_date. The committed Power BI Project (PBIP) remains an authoring template, while each deployed report opens on the latest month generated by that setup, including custom months or explicit date ranges.

Terraform apply consumes the saved, validated plan. --yes pre-confirms Terraform apply but does not skip the destructive-change guard, required pipeline gates or live tenant/capacity preflight. Full-demo's capability preflight needs no prompt when the required tenant switches and capacity are valid. Disabled settings and invalid capacity fail before Fabric changes, with instructions for correcting the problem. --skip-terraform rejects missing, placeholder, incomplete, or wrong-workspace Terraform outputs before publication. --recreate polls for workspace-name release for up to 180 seconds between destroy and apply.

--resume reuses only the contiguous succeeded prefix of an incomplete journal with matching targets and source/config/plan fingerprint. Pending apply or publication consumers refresh their plan or staged inputs before retry. Legacy journals missing the new compatibility fields are not resumable. The prior journal is archived before a different resumed/new run becomes latest. See the deployment specification for compatibility and recreate restrictions.

For standard and full-demo, deployment finishes with a read-only live readiness verification. It never triggers an additional pipeline. Required failed/unknown evidence fails deployment, while optional failed/unknown evidence records a degraded run.

For full-demo, deployment automatically checks for the stable ontology. When it is absent, the orchestrator runs the deployed 30-create-ontology notebook, waits for the item, publishes both Data Agents, deploys all selected task-flow references, and verifies the graph after persistence. The retail-setup post-ontology --env <name> command remains as an idempotent repair path. Optional stream freshness can leave either path DEGRADED without failing required ontology/task-flow publication.

items.title: verify
items.text:
retail-setup verify --env <name> queries profile-selected live items, definitions, task flow, KQL objects, schedules, pipeline jobs, and freshness signals. It writes deploy/.generated/<env>/readiness-report.json atomically and returns 0 for success, 1 for required failure/unknown, 2 for usage, or 3 for optional degradation.

The default is read-only. --run-pipeline is the only mutating verifier flag; it explicitly starts and waits for the profile-required post-publish pipeline. It is rejected for profiles without that pipeline and does not start streaming or other workloads.

items.title: Output behavior
items.text: CLI output is linear plain text with ASCII separators. Required command failures propagate from the plan. Task-flow and pipeline gate/failure behavior is documented in the deployment specification and operations runbook.

items.title: Evidence
items.text:
• utility/src/retail_setup/cli/main.py
  • utility/src/retail_setup/notebooks/inject.py
  • utility/src/retail_setup/config/generation.py
  • utility/tests/test_cli_configure.py
  • utility/tests/test_cli_render.py
  • utility/tests/test_cli_deploy.py

items.title: Runtime
items.text:
stream-events.ipynb is rendered from utility/notebooks/templates/driver-05-stream.py. It is an optional, long-running Fabric Spark Structured Streaming driver.

Supported sinks:

  • eventhouse: direct typed writes through the Spark Kusto connector;
  • delta: development/validation landing table.

The current path does not require Kafka, Event Hubs, or a Fabric Eventstream.

Before emitting events, the driver requires readable, nonempty Silver dim_stores, dim_customers, dim_products, dim_distribution_centers, and dim_trucks. Product/store attribute reads provide prices and tax data. Missing/empty dimensions, a store without a tax_rate, or failed attribute reads stop startup rather than substituting arbitrary ID ranges or synthetic attribute frames. Complete historical setup before starting the stream.

Foreign keys come only from IDs that exist. The driver numbers each dimension's IDs and picks one per row with a seeded hash, through a broadcast join, so gaps in the IDs (a custom layout or a filtered publish) are safe. Baskets, and therefore inventory, stockout and reorder events, use only products whose LaunchDate is on or before the checkpoint's catalog date. A dimension with contiguous IDs 1..n gets the same IDs as the earlier 1..count draw.

items.title: History handoff
items.text:
History ends yesterday in store-local time, so the newest Silver fact_receipts.event_ts is normally less than a day before the stream starts. At startup the driver compares the two (both UTC):

Condition New checkpoint Resumed checkpoint Gap of one day or less Starts Starts History ends up to 14 hours after the start (store time zones) Starts, logs the overlap Starts Gap over one day, overlap over 14 hours, or no receipts Fails Warns

Set the notebook parameter allow_history_gap = True to start a new stream anyway. A resumed checkpoint only warns, because its own downtime is an expected gap (see the catch-up cap below).

items.title: Time and shared vocabulary
items.text:
Every timestamp the stream writes is UTC; the stream never assumes store-local time. Historical Silver uses the same convention (see the historical data contract), and fact_receipts.local_hour gives the store-local hour for both producers.

Tenders, zones, ID formats, marketing channels and devices, promotions, and the decline model come from retail_setup.generation.vocabulary, which the build inlines into the notebook, so live values match history: MOBILE_PAY, base-36 BLE IDs padded to six characters, BEACON_%03d_<zone> and SENSOR_%03d_<zone> IDs, upper-case devices, CAMP<yyyyMMdd><NN> campaign IDs, and padded AdIds. Online orders use the same fulfillment mix, online tenders, decline model, cancellation and backorder rates, promo codes and stage delays (vocabulary.ONLINE_*) as history. No known gap is left; new ones are listed in utility/tests/generation/test_vocabulary.py, which fails when a listed gap closes, so the list only shrinks.

items.title: Volume, hours and customers
items.text:
The live stream reuses the historical models (stream_calendar, stream_events), so its volume, time of day and customer mix continue the history:

  • Rate. source_rows_per_second = 0 (the default) derives the rate-source rate from the store count, the historical transactions_per_store_day (rendered into the notebook), online_orders_per_day, and the marketing volume: the smallest whole rate that covers every lane at its peak. Each row goes to one lane (store visits, online orders, marketing) and is kept with that lane's calendar weight, so a larger explicit rate adds resolution, not volume. volume_scale multiplies every calibrated volume. Inventory and truck events have no lane: they follow from the purchases (below).
  • Store visits. A visit picks a store weighted by daily_traffic_multiplier and is kept with the profile's hourly, daily and monthly weights evaluated in the store's local time (dim_stores.TimeZone, daylight saving included), history's holiday factor for the store type's class and the geography's weather on the local day (stream_calendar). The weight is zero while the store is closed, on Christmas Day and, except for grocers, on Thanksgiving, so no live receipt is outside opening hours. Visits are drawn at transactions_per_store_day / 0.225 per store-day and convert with the same store/day/hour conversion as history (about 22%).
  • Customers. As in history (generation/customers.py), about 45% of visits are anonymous. The rest pick a customer from the store's home-customer pool (85%) or another store's, weighted by visit tickets, and keep them only while they are signed up and not churned on the visit's local day; live churn continues from the history's lifecycle (rendered start, end, churn rate and anonymous share). Online orders take the first of four tries that is active that day.
  • Visit path. A visit walks from the store type's entrance zone through one to three of its department zones (profile.zones, upper-cased) in random order, passes CHECKOUT when it buys and leaves through EXIT when the store type has one (vocabulary.visit_zone_path, the path history uses). Each zone has a dwell time in its range and a customer_entered event as the visitor enters it: foot-traffic sensors count zone passages, so the entrance zone counts visitors and checkout counts buyers (customer_count is 1, dwell_time the zone's dwell). Beacons detect the phone of a quarter of visits (BLE_DETECTED_SHARE, buyers and non-buyers): those emit two to five BLE pings per zone and a zone change on arrival. 30% of detected visits carry the customer's dim_customers.BLEId; the rest are ANON-<store>-<n>, as in history. The receipt, lines and promotions are emitted halfway through checkout and the payment after the tender's processing time. A visit that would run past closing time is compressed to end before it.
  • Purchases. Baskets (complementary products and merged repeated SKUs, generation/baskets.py), shelf prices of the incarnation's catalog date (generation/pricing.py, the same price schedule as history), one basket-level promotion priced over the lines the store could fill, the 40/30/20/10 tender mix and the 2.5% base decline model are the batch helpers. As in history, a declined first tender is retried on another tender 80% of the time (a DECLINED payment at the purchase, then the APPROVED one; the receipt carries the approved tender); otherwise the sale is voided and the visit leaves without buying. One promotion_applied is emitted per receipt and promo code, so at most one per receipt. Visit and online volume follow history's year-over-year trend (annual_volume_growth from the anchor date).
  • Store operations. store_opened and store_closed (lower-case opened/closed, like history) are emitted exactly at each store's local opening and closing time, one pair per open day (none on the store type's closed holidays). A 24-hour store closes at 23:59 and reopens at midnight.
  • Marketing. Background impressions follow the historical campaigns (archetype channels, CAMP IDs on the same campaign windows, flash sales on about one day in seven), cost bands by channel and device, padded AdIds, and a 5% CRM match, at store_count / 86 of the archetype volumes.

items.title: Store inventory
items.text:
stream_supply keeps a running on-hand balance per store and product and replays, in time order, everything that changes it in a micro-batch:

  • Sales. Every receipt line, and every line of a ship-from-store or BOPIS online order (at order time), takes its quantity from the store: inventory_updated with reason = SALE, source = CUSTOMER_PURCHASE or ONLINE_ORDER, a negative quantity_delta and the demand in requested_quantity. Ship-from-DC lines draw on the DC, which, as in history, is an unconstrained supplier.
  • Lost sales. A line the store cannot fill whole becomes reason = LOST_SALE with quantity_delta = 0, like history's policy: the line is left off its receipt or order (and its totals), and a purchase with no line left emits nothing. Balances never go negative.
  • Stockouts. A sale that takes the balance below calibration.STOCKOUT_QUANTITY_THRESHOLD (to zero) emits stockout_detected with the stock it took (last_known_quantity), once per store, product and UTC day, the crossing fact_stockouts records in history.
  • Reorders. After each sale or lost sale the shared replenishment policy (inventory_policy: smoothed daily demand, reorder point of 4 days, order-up-to target of 8 days, 12-unit case pack, URGENT when the shelf is empty, HIGH below two days of demand) compares the position (on hand plus inbound) with the reorder point and emits reorder_triggered.
  • Receipts of stock. A truck unload adds its units: reason = INBOUND_SHIPMENT, source = the shipment ID.
  • DC stock. Each DC keeps its own stock with the historical DC policy (inventory_policy DC functions): supplier orders at the reorder point, received after the product's 3-7 day lead time (short during a supplier short-ship), truck loads, and ship-from-DC online lines when the order is placed (expedited when the DC lacks units). These moves are inventory_updated events with no store_id and reason INBOUND_SHIPMENT, OUTBOUND_SHIPMENT (requested_quantity is what the load asked for; less moved means a short-ship), ONLINE_SHIPMENT or EXPEDITED_RECEIPT. Silver routes them to fact_dc_inventory_txn. A DC reaching zero is a stockout_detected with no store_id. DC entries start from the latest Silver DC balance as of the incarnation start, else from history's DC opening stock.

Every inventory, stockout and reorder event carries the store's DC (dc_id), assigned as in the historical inventory chain (network.assign_dcs: same state, else region, least loaded). A store and product the stream has not touched yet starts from its latest Silver fact_store_inventory_txn balance as of the incarnation start (never below zero) and the mean daily demand of the 7 days before it; one Silver has never seen starts from history's opening stock. The seed time is kept in the meta state, so a restart seeds the same way. History's shipments that were still on the road when history ended are not carried over; the policy reorders that stock.

items.title: Trucks
items.text: A reorder joins its store's pending load at the DC. Each store takes one consolidated delivery a day. The load's schedule comes from incidents.plan_delivery, as in history: the store's next delivery slot (the minute of the store-local day its delivery route gives it, network.plan_routes) whose arrival day the store is open, held to the next slot after a DC outage, loaded late under holiday capacity limits. When it is due, the next free truck of the DC's fleet (dim_trucks.DCID; pool trucks only for a DC with none) loads what the DC has of the pending load for TRUCK_LOAD_MINUTES, drives the lane (a stable 1-4 hour draw per DC and store), and arrives. planned_arrival_time is the plan of the load's oldest reorder; the actual arrival is the planned time plus delay_minutes, and delay_reason names the largest cause (DC_OUTAGE, HOLIDAY_CAPACITY, LANE_DELAY, WEATHER, TRAFFIC, or TRUCK_AVAILABILITY when the load waited for a free truck). SupplyBatch.held_dcs can still hold a DC by hand. The unload takes TRUCK_UNLOAD_BASE_MINUTES plus the load at TRUCK_UNLOAD_UNITS_PER_MINUTE, scaled by a per-store dock factor and the store-local hour (slower 11:00-19:00, quicker 22:00-06:00), plus a 10-minute door wait for a truck 30 or more minutes late and a few minutes of noise, capped at TRUCK_UNLOAD_MINUTES_MAX (network.unload_minutes, shared with history; estimated_unload_duration is the plan, the departure's actual_unload_duration the outcome). A typical load unloads inside the normal 30-75 minute range; an unusually large one can breach the 90-minute SLA. The truck departs when the unload is done, which restocks the store, and drives back. A truck carries one shipment at a time, so it is never in two places at once, and truck_arrived and truck_departed are emitted only once their time has passed.

items.title: Online orders
items.text:
Online orders arrive at online_orders_per_day (by default derived so online orders are the profile's online_order_share of all orders), shaped by the profile's monthly weights, the online holiday factors (Cyber Monday, Black Friday, ...) and the online hourly curve (vocabulary.ONLINE_HOURLY_WEIGHTS, UTC, peaking in the US evening; history uses the same curve). The customer comes from a home-store pool, as in history. Each order has one fulfillment mode and node, drawn by the historical mix (60% ship from a DC, 30% ship from a store, 10% BOPIS): the customer's home store for ship-from-store and BOPIS, the DC that supplies that store for ship-from-DC. Repeated SKUs merge into one line. Its lifecycle runs over hours and days:

Event When online_order_created and one online_order_line_added per line order time payment_processed (order_id, no store) after the online tender's processing time online_order_picked 30-240 minutes later (BOPIS: 4-24 hours, ready for pickup) online_order_shipped 2-4 hours after picking (backorders: 3-14 days more); never for BOPIS online_order_delivered 1-3 days after shipping; BOPIS: 1-24 hours after picking, when the customer collects it

2% of orders are cancelled at once: zero totals, zero line amounts, no payment and no fulfillment. 8% of shippable orders are backordered: they wait 3-14 days for stock before they ship, then deliver as usual. Payments use the online tenders (no cash) and the shared decline model: a declined order is retried on another tender (a DECLINED payment a second after the order, then the APPROVED one) or voided, which cancels it, as in history. Lines carry history's online promo codes, and tax is the fulfilling store's rate for store-fulfilled orders and the customer's destination rate (mean store rate of their geography) for DC shipments. Orders still in progress live in the order state.

items.title: Stream state
items.text:
Events that span micro-batches need state. A visit's and an online order's later events are emitted in the batch whose time they fall in, the store hours need each store's open/closed state, and stock and trucks carry over between batches. The state lives in Lakehouse Delta tables in the Silver schema:

Table Key Contents _stream_state_stores store ID Open or closed, and when it last changed. _stream_state_visits visit (rate row) Visits whose last event is still in the future, with their lost-sale lines. _stream_state_orders order (rate row) Online orders whose last stage is still in the future, with their lost-sale lines. _stream_state_inventory inv:<store>:<product> On hand, inbound, smoothed daily demand and the last stockout day of each store and product the stream has touched. _stream_state_logistics pending:<store>, shipment:<id>, truck:<id> Loads waiting at the DC, shipments on the road and where each truck is. _stream_state_meta clock, seed The time of the last micro-batch, and the inventory seed time.

Each row also carries the checkpoint incarnation (stream ID and nonce), batch_id, the JSON payload and a deleted flag. Micro-batch N reads, per entity, the latest version written before N, and writes its changes with batch_id = N using a Delta replaceWhere on batch_id >= N. A replay of N therefore reads the same state, regenerates the same events, and replaces its own versions: nothing is applied twice. Store inventory is read only for the store-products a batch touches. Superseded versions are deleted every 60 batches. A new incarnation has no rows; at startup it seeds each store from its last Silver fact_store_ops row (or its hours) as batch_id = -1. Rows of an earlier incarnation are ignored and can be deleted.

items.title: Envelope
items.text:
Every event contains:

  • event_type
  • trace_id
  • ingest_timestamp
  • schema_version
  • source
  • correlation_id
  • partition_key
  • session_id
  • parent_event_id

Payload fields are event-specific and mapped by EVENT_PAYLOADS.

items.title: Business event types
items.text:
1. receipt_created
  2. receipt_line_added
  3. payment_processed
  4. inventory_updated
  5. stockout_detected
  6. reorder_triggered
  7. customer_entered
  8. customer_zone_changed
  9. ble_ping_detected
  10. truck_arrived
  11. truck_departed
  12. store_opened
  13. store_closed
  14. ad_impression
  15. promotion_applied
  16. online_order_created
  17. online_order_picked
  18. online_order_shipped
  19. online_order_line_added
  20. online_order_delivered
  21. logistics_incident_started
  22. logistics_incident_resolved

The stream emits all twenty-two. Incidents are sporadic (a few per DC and year), so readiness does not expect fresh incident rows (stream_control.SPORADIC_EVENT_TYPES).

  • logistics_incident_started carries incident_id, incident_type (DC_OUTAGE, LANE_DELAY, WEATHER, HOLIDAY_CAPACITY, SUPPLIER_SHORT_SHIP), dc_id, store_id (the lane's store of a lane delay, else null), started_at, severity, affected_store_count, description, and affected_store_ids (every affected store). logistics_incident_resolved carries the same identity and resolved_at. The stream plans incidents exactly as history does (incidents.plan_incidents with the severe-weather days of the stores' geographies), so the same seed opens the same incident IDs on the same days. With the history's last day (END_DATE) it also plans the end-of-history DC outage that history leaves open (see the data contract), so the first batch starts it and the stream resolves it at its planned end. Each start and resolution is emitted once, in the batch whose window holds it (stream_supply.incident_transitions); the first batch of an incarnation starts the incidents already open. Silver keeps one fact_logistics_incidents row per incident: the start inserts it and the resolution sets resolved_at once (Delta MERGE), and fact_logistics_incident_stores gets one row per affected store. A resolution whose start has aged out of Bronze only updates existing rows.
  • online_order_line_added carries the order line (line_number, product_id, quantity, prices, promo_code) and its fulfillment node; it lands in fact_online_order_lines with status PENDING. Each Silver run then moves recent live lines with their order: PICKED, SHIPPED, DELIVERED (with the stage timestamps), or CANCELLED when the order's header has zero totals.
  • online_order_delivered adds a DELIVERED row to the streaming-only fact_online_order_status table, like picked and shipped.
  • inventory_updated.requested_quantity is the customer's demand of a SALE or LOST_SALE (0 for stock receipts). Silver writes it to requested_quantity and, for a lost sale, to unfulfilled_quantity. The KQL script restates the table with .alter table so the column sits before the envelope, as the positional writes need.
  • A live store stockout keeps DCID NULL in Silver fact_stockouts, as history does; the event's dc_id names the store's DC.

KQL defines an additional unknown_event catch-all table. It is not a generated business event. The current notebook rejects unmapped event types before committing the micro-batch checkpoint. The catch-all is an operational queued-ingestion boundary, not an active direct-writer DLQ. Here DLQ means dead-letter queue: a place to preserve messages that could not be processed.

items.title: Eventhouse writes
items.text:
Each micro-batch is generated inside foreachBatch: the notebook reads the state as of the previous batch, builds the batch's events, writes them, and only then commits the new state. For the Eventhouse sink, the notebook:

  1. Persists the batch.
  2. Finds present mapped event types.
  3. Resolves one notebook runtime token.
  4. Maps JSON to typed envelope/payload columns.
  5. Writes event types concurrently to their same-named KQL tables, one coalesced partition (one blob, one extent, one tag) per table.
  6. Uses FailIfNotExist.
  7. Sets flushImmediately=true.
  8. Unpersists the batch.

Each table write retries transient errors (throttling, HTTP 401/408/429/5xx, timeouts, dropped connections, an expired token) up to five attempts with exponential backoff (2, 4, 8, 16 seconds) and a fresh token. Permanent errors, such as a missing table or a type mismatch, are not retried.

If kusto_uri is blank, the notebook resolves the KQL database queryServiceUri by display name in the current workspace.

The event tables carry an extent_tags_retention policy that drops ingest-by: tags after seven days. They set no streaming-ingestion or ingestion-batching policy: the connector's transactional writes are queued ingestion with flushImmediately, which bypasses batching, and nothing streams into these tables. Eventhouses created by earlier versions keep those policies; they are inert. The unknown_event catch-all keeps both for queued ingestion.

items.title: Trigger, catch-up and restarts
items.text:
Parameter Default Meaning source_rows_per_second 0 0 derives the rate from the store count and historical volume; a larger value adds resolution, not volume. volume_scale 1.0 Multiplies every calibrated live volume. run_seconds 0 0 runs until cancelled; a positive value is a bounded (smoke) run. trigger_seconds 60 Live micro-batch interval. Bounded runs use at most 10 seconds. max_lag_seconds 600 After a stop, rate rows older than this behind the batch time are dropped. max_restarts 5 Supervised restarts of a failed live query. allow_history_gap False Start a new stream despite a history gap or overlap.

Spark's rate source emits every second of downtime in the next micro-batch; a 12-hour stop used to produce about a million events in one batch. The driver keeps only rows within max_lag_seconds of the batch time, so a resumed stream continues from about now and leaves a gap for the downtime. The batch time comes from Spark's offset log, so a replayed batch keeps exactly the same rows. The newer rate-micro-batch source was not used: its timestamps advance per batch, not with the clock, so after a stop every event would stay backdated.

A live query that fails with a transient error restarts from its checkpoint after 30, 60, 120 ... seconds (at most 10 minutes), up to max_restarts times. The count resets after an hour of healthy running. A permanent failure, or one beyond the budget, ends the notebook with the error.

items.title: Checkpoints and incarnations
items.text:
Checkpoints live under Files/setup/stream/checkpoint:

Path Contents _metadata/stream_id The logical stream ID, shared by every sink checkpoint. eventhouse-live/, delta-live/ Spark checkpoint of an unbounded run. eventhouse-smoke/, delta-smoke/ Spark checkpoint of a bounded run, so smoke tests never share offsets with the live stream. _metadata/<checkpoint>.json The checkpoint's incarnation record: an 8-hex nonce and the catalog date.

Earlier versions used eventhouse/ and delta/; they are no longer read and can be deleted.

The incarnation nonce is part of every ingest tag (retail-demo:<stream_id>:<incarnation>:<event_type>:<batch_id>), trace ID, and business ID (RCP-<stream_id>-<incarnation>-<n>). Spark restarts batch IDs at 0 when its checkpoint is deleted. Without the nonce, those batches would reuse tags Kusto still holds, and the connector would silently skip the writes.

At startup the driver compares the record with the Spark offsets and commits logs:

State Result No record, no Spark log New incarnation; the record is written just before the query starts. Record and offsets, last batch committed Resume; the catalog date moves to today, so new launches are sold. Record and offsets, last batch not committed Resume; the pending batch replays with the recorded catalog date, so it regenerates the same baskets, IDs, and tags. Record without offsets Refused: the Spark checkpoint was reset or never ran a batch. Offsets without a record, commits past the offsets, or a record for another stream Refused.

The error names the files to delete. To start a new incarnation, delete the Spark checkpoint folder and its record together. To start a new stream ID, delete the whole checkpoint root.

items.title: Duplicate and failure behavior
items.text:
• Generated business IDs and trace_id include the persisted stream ID and the checkpoint incarnation.
  • Eventhouse writes use the connector's transactional mode, deterministic request IDs, duplicate-blob protection, and matching ingest-by/check tags for each stream, incarnation, event type, and Spark micro-batch.
  • Unmapped event types and any required table-write failure (after retries) raise from foreachBatch, so Spark does not commit that batch's checkpoint.
  • A replayed batch rebuilds the same rows, catalog, state, and tags, so tables that already succeeded are skipped and the rest are written once. The state write replaces the batch's own versions.
  • Silver transforms remove exact duplicate candidates, reject conflicting rows with the same identity, and use Delta MERGE before advancing watermarks.
  • Gold tables are rebuilt with overwrite semantics from duplicate-safe Silver inputs, so reruns do not accumulate aggregate rows.

These controls make expected retries idempotent and are covered by injected failure/replay contracts. tests/test_streaming_dedup_contract.py executes the actual foreachBatch sink function with mocked connector operations, including partial table-write, transient-retry, unmapped-event, and credential failures. utility/tests/generation/test_stream_control.py covers the backlog cap, retries, supervised restarts, incarnation records over a temporary directory, the history handoff, and ID sampling. These tests do not establish live Spark/Kusto transactional behavior. The readiness adapter checks live ingestion and checkpoint tags. The remaining IMP-013 evidence includes a recent bounded run of the intentionally manual stream and live execution of the bounded receipt/inventory/sales reconciliation query.

items.title: Cross-layer ownership
items.text:
The exact KQL table shape is in 01-create-tables.kql. JSON ingestion mappings in 02-create-ingestion-mappings.kql support queued raw-JSON ingestion but are not used by the direct typed live path.

Silver mappings are separately implemented in fabric/lakehouse/03-streaming-to-silver.ipynb. Their current divergence from the historical contract is documented in Fabric analytics.

contracts/retail-demo.json declares one stable path ID per emitted event and one derived attribution path. It stores keys, UTC event-time semantics, targets, terminals, and named exceptions, but never copies physical field or type inventories. python scripts/check_data_contracts.py derives those inventories from the driver, KQL, schemas.py, notebooks, and active TMDL.

items.title: Truck lifecycle
items.text:
truck_arrived and truck_departed share truck_id, dc_id, store_id, and shipment_id. The departure is emitted when the unload completes, after the arrival and never ahead of the stream clock; the dwell follows the load-size and dock model under Trucks. Its parameters come from utility/src/retail_setup/generation/calibration.py, the same module the rules, anomaly functions, and semantic model are checked against.

truck_arrived also carries planned_arrival_time, delay_minutes, delay_reason and load_units (see Trucks). Silver copies them to fact_truck_moves. The KQL script restates the table with .alter table so an existing Eventhouse takes the declared column order, which the positional Spark Kusto writes rely on.

Silver joins the two event tables on all four lifecycle keys and writes one completed fact_truck_moves row. Eventhouse and Gold expose dwell in minutes with STORE_<id> / DC_<id> site labels.

tests/test_truck_dwell_contract.py verifies the generator, rendered stream notebook, KQL table/function contract, Silver join, Gold aggregation, queryset, dashboard template, and 90-minute rule. A live Fabric smoke run remains the deployment verification gate.

items.title: Marketing attribution
items.text:
Approved store and online purchases with a customer are selected for a journey at the rate that makes the attributed net revenue about attribution.TARGET_ROAS (4x) the live impression spend (attribution.live_journey_rate, from the lane volumes, identified buyers and the pre-tax ticket), as history converts impressions. A journey (attribution.with_journey_plan) has one journey ID and one to three ad_impression touches 1 minute to 7 days before the purchase, each on an archetype drawn by impression volume, in the campaign window of its own time, with a creative from the campaign's pool, a CPM cost, a device and a CRM-matched customer_id exactly like background impressions; their impression IDs have the background format. The purchase carries the last touch's campaign_id and impression_id. The existing envelope correlation_id carries attribution_journey_id through impressions, receipt/order creation, promotion, payment, and online status events.

Touches arrive with the purchase: their ingest_timestamp is the purchase time, and the payload's impression_time says when they were shown (background impressions have both equal). Notebook 03 dates fact_marketing rows by impression_time but tracks its watermark and replay window on ingest_timestamp, the arrival time, so touches are never older than the replay window and are not left to the daily deep reconciliation. Kusto's ingestion_time() is not visible through the OneLake shortcut notebook 03 reads; ingest_timestamp stays deterministic from the rate-source time, so replays are identical, and is within one trigger interval of it. KQL fn_marketing_attribution() and fn_campaign_performance() use coalesce(impression_time, ingest_timestamp) as the touch time.

The contract is deterministic last-touch within an inclusive seven-day window, ordered by touch timestamp and impression ID. Silver writes one fact_marketing_attribution row after purchase, promotion, and approved payment reconcile; attributed rows additionally require a valid selected touch, while purchases without a journey are marked UNATTRIBUTED_NO_JOURNEY.

Money remains integer cents:

gross_subtotal_cents - discount_cents = net_subtotal_cents
net_subtotal_cents + tax_cents = total_cents
approved payment_cents = total_cents
attributed_revenue_cents = net_subtotal_cents

Eventhouse exposes reconciliation diagnostics through fn_marketing_attribution(). Consumer-facing fn_attribution() and fn_attribution_window() return only reconciled ATTRIBUTED purchases after future and out-of-window touches are removed and the latest valid touch is selected. fn_campaign_performance() uses that reconciled set. Its spend is the cost of impressions shown in the window; the cost of the impressions behind the window's conversions, shown up to seven days earlier, is reported separately as converted_spend_cents. Gold publishes campaign_performance_daily, and the Direct Lake model exposes both the audit fact and campaign KPIs. Contract tests cover batch determinism, live payload/KQL mappings, Silver/Gold wiring, semantic measures, and all cent equations. A live Fabric smoke run remains the deployment verification gate.

items.title: Contract evidence and live boundary
items.text:
Eight fixture scenarios cover all 22 declared types plus nullable and unknown-event variants. The parameterized matrix validates the nine-field envelope, KQL DDL/mappings, UTC values, business/dedupe keys, Silver/Gold routes, and either an active semantic terminal or the named streaming-only exception.

Repository acceptance for IMP-005 is complete. A live Fabric staging run through Eventhouse, the optional Silver/Gold projection, and Direct Lake remains required external evidence. The static check does not prove tenant-level execution.

items.title: Guides
items.text:
Choose a guide for the task at hand. You can start with setup, a workspace tour, presentation steps, or operations; there is no required reading order.

If Fabric terminology is new to you, keep the plain-language glossary open while you work.

For exact schemas, interfaces, or acceptance criteria, see Design documentation.

items.title: CIO walkthrough
items.text:
Use this walkthrough to show a CIO and their leadership team how Power BI, chat, and two operations agents use the same Fabric retail data. Allow about 15 minutes for the main path or 25 minutes with the additional questions. Start with the report, ask questions in chat, then review a replenishment proposal and a retention campaign draft.

Rehearse against the selected environment and read its readiness report first. This guide is not a live acceptance record. Replay uses synthetic fixtures, and approvals create local demo state, not production orders or campaigns. The app attempts to send action telemetry to Eventhouse, but delivery is not guaranteed.

items.title: Before we start: what's deployed, and why it's useful
items.text:
The data platform is organized in one Fabric workspace. The local app, operator browser, identity provider, and optional router are additional trust and cost boundaries. Four data capabilities share that Fabric foundation:

Layer Fabric component Questions it supports Historical analytics Semantic model (Direct Lake over the Gold Lakehouse) Totals, rankings, and trends Relationships Ontology (graph of business entities) Connections between named entities Real-time Eventhouse (KQL) and streaming Recent sales and operational events Prediction ML models (Gold tables) Forecasts, risk estimates, and pricing recommendations

The same Gold tables feed the report, agents, and models. Eventhouse holds live sales events and any agent telemetry that the app successfully delivers.

Use the semantic model for aggregates such as net sales by region. Use the ontology to connect a named synthetic customer's profile with their segment and churn prediction. Broad aggregations and deep scans generally belong on the semantic model; verify that the selected graph lookup works before the presentation.

See Agentic application for the architecture and service boundaries.

items.title: The interface: what's on screen
items.text:
The Dashboard page places the Power BI report beside the Ask-your-data chat, using about 70% and 30% of the space, respectively. The orchestrator routes each question without asking the presenter to choose a data source.

The Agent Operations page shows an approval funnel from the Eventhouse agent_actions table and refreshes every few seconds.

Expand how I reached this below an answer to inspect the source, router model, call, and result preview. Operations-agent traces include the DAX. Fabric MCP services do not return their generated query text.

items.title: The walkthrough: see it, ask it, act on it
Act 1: See it (Power BI, ~3 min)
items.text:
Open Dashboard, let the report load, then expand these visuals:

  1. Executive sales and margin: show net sales, gross margin %, and channel mix.
  2. Inventory and stockout risk: identify stores to revisit in the replenishment example.
  3. Customer and churn: identify segments to revisit in the retention example.

Suggested narration: "The report shows the selected period's sales and risk signals. Now let's ask a question about the same data."

items.title: Act 2: Ask it (chat, ~5 min)
items.text:
Ask these in order. Expand how I reached this after each answer to show which source answered and why.

# Ask this Source the agent uses Why this question 1 "What were total net sales and gross margin company-wide?" Semantic model Compare chat with the report for the same period 2 "What are the top products by revenue last month, and each one's gross margin %?" Semantic model Check a ranked list with a second measure 3 Ask for the segment and churn probability of an observed loyalty card Ontology Use an authorized synthetic key present in this environment 4 "How many customers are predicted to churn, and what is their total lifetime value?" Semantic model over the ML churn table Inspect model estimates alongside historical value 5 "What were the top-selling products in the last 15 minutes?" Live-sales shortcut; inspect the trace Check freshness, time window, and whether the result is at product or store grain

Suggested narration: "The trace shows which source answered and why. We can compare its result with the report or underlying data."

items.title: Act 3: Act on it (operations agents, ~6 min)
items.text:
Ask a question that requests a decision. The orchestrator hands it to an operations agent, which reads the deployed synthetic data, applies business rules, and drafts a proposal for review.

For Inventory & Replenishment, ask: "What products are at risk of stockout, and what should we do about it?"

Inspect the exposure count and assumptions from the actual response, then the trace: stockout risk → covering reorders → product prices → coverage rule. Review the recommendation card's evidence before approving one local draft. Do not repeat counts or dollar amounts from an older workspace.

For Customer Retention, ask: "Customer churn is rising. What can we do to retain customers?"

Use the current response's cohort count and modeled lifetime-value estimate; these are synthetic risk indicators, not guaranteed recoverable revenue. The trace should show the ML churn read, the join to customer_segments for lifetime value (LTV), cohort selection, and cross-sell suggestions from the market-basket model. Review the draft campaign's Approve and Dismiss controls.

Suggested narration: "Each agent proposes a specific action and shows its evidence. Approval records a local decision; it does not execute an order or campaign."

items.title: Validate it: close the loop
items.text:
Inspect whether each expected draft/decision reached agent_actions. The app attempts Eventhouse logging asynchronously and can lose events without failing the chat or approval. Local approval success is not proof of telemetry delivery or an immutable audit record.

Switch to Agent Operations after Act 3. Check the proposed and approved action counts, estimated replenishment value, and churn LTV associated with the proposals. Confirm actual delivery time rather than promising a fixed latency. Query the ingested events with KQL:

agent_actions
| summarize actions = count(), ltv_at_risk = sum(ltv_at_risk) by agent, action_status
| order by agent asc

These events can support an operations dashboard. Their presence does not establish a complete or immutable approval audit.

items.title: Appendix: deep-cut questions (if time allows)
items.text:
Use these questions to explore combined metrics and model outputs:

  • "What is the total modeled lifetime value of high-churn-risk customers?" Inspect the estimate's limitations before reviewing a local campaign draft.
  • "For products at high stockout risk, estimate the at-risk daily sales." Review the assumptions before approving a local reorder draft.
  • "For each underperforming store, list its top stockout risk, churn-risk customers, and recommended cross-sell." Present this composed action list as a proposal, not a current capability.

items.title: Appendix: pre-flight checklist
items.text:
• Fabric capacity is Active; check the environment's actual pause policy.
  • Local app on loopback; signed in as an operator with only necessary permissions.
  • Streaming notebook running so "last 15 minutes" returns fresh data.
  • Preserve prior telemetry and proposal evidence; do not clear shared state merely to make presentation counters start at zero.
  • Run the Inventory and Retention questions once before presenting; initial DAX reads can take a few seconds.

items.title: Report-to-chat handoff and fallback
items.text:
Use Executive, Sales, Supply Chain, store/product drillthrough, Omnichannel, and Operations/Marketing pages to identify the period, store, product, or cohort before asking. A report slicer is not automatically chat context: include the observed key/name and period in the question. Do not invent a loyalty-card field on report pages that do not expose one.

Prefer named-entity, single-relationship graph questions. Break broad multi-hop/event traversals into smaller questions or use semantic-model aggregation. Inspect source, grain, window, fallback, and empty/error results; the current live-sales shortcut has a fixed store-sales window and does not prove arbitrary product/window answers. See routing.

If a service stalls, show a previously validated report view or explicitly labeled replay, and retain the failure for follow-up. Use the evaluation question bank to explore broader prompts; do not reuse old results as current evidence. Pricing, logistics, merchandising, and composed per-store actions remain proposals.

items.title: Presenter demo script
items.text:
Audience: Retail operations, analytics, and technology stakeholders Duration: 15-20 minutes Data: Synthetic

For a browser-first tour of the deployed workspace, use the deployed solution walkthrough.

For a standalone 5-7 minute persona walkthrough, use the presenter journeys for retail operations, merchandising, or executive/analytics audiences.

items.title: Before the audience arrives
items.text:
1. Complete the getting-started guide.
  2. Confirm the required KQL tables and ag/au Lakehouse tables exist.
  3. Open the Eventhouse query editor, Power BI report, and the streaming notebook.
  4. Check whether the dashboard, ontology, agents, and ML outputs are ready. Skip any feature whose source, permission, or capability checks have failed.
  5. Keep the operations guide open for recovery.

items.title: 1. Frame the architecture
items.text:
Open the architecture overview.

Talk track:

  • Setup notebooks create repeatable historical data. Silver is the cleaned, detailed layer; Gold is the business-ready summary layer.
  • stream-events.ipynb writes twenty-two live event types directly to Eventhouse, including sporadic logistics incidents (DC outages, lane delays, weather, holiday capacity, supplier short-ships).
  • History always ends inside an open DC outage at the busiest DC. Its stores have had no deliveries for three days, so some fast movers are nearly out: the Operations Agent has real cases to act on, and the live stream resolves the outage shortly after it starts.
  • KQL (Kusto Query Language) answers recent event questions; Lakehouse stores durable history and summaries.
  • Power BI uses Direct Lake, which reads Lakehouse data without importing a second copy.
  • Optional ontology and agents add business context after their capability and binding checks pass.

items.title: 2. Start live data
items.text:
In stream-events.ipynb, select the Eventhouse sink and run a bounded stream. Show a recent row:

receipt_created
| where ingest_timestamp > ago(10m)
| take 10

Then show live sales aggregation:

mv_store_sales_minute
| where ts > ago(10m)
| summarize sales = sum(total_sales) by store_id
| order by sales desc

Suggested talk track:

Each generated business event says what happened and when. A unique trace identifier connects related receipt, line-item, promotion, and payment events, so we can follow one synthetic transaction across the process. The payload also identifies the store or order used to keep related events together. Eventhouse records when it received each event, which lets us prove that the optional stream is currently active.

items.title: 3. Ask operational questions
items.text:
Choose a supported path from the presenter journeys, or use checked-in queryset tabs for:

  • Recent sales and top products.
  • Inventory movements and stockout detections.
  • Omnichannel order creation and fulfillment events.
  • Store presence and zone dwell.

Be precise: recent stockout detections are not the same as unresolved current stockout state. Truck dwell is implemented and covered by cross-layer contract tests, but present it only after a bounded live run produces recent fn_truck_sla() rows in the selected workspace.

items.title: 4. Show durable history
items.text:
Run or show the last successful streaming-to-Silver/Gold pipeline. In the Lakehouse:

  • inspect ag.fact_receipts or another mapped fact;
  • inspect a Gold aggregate such as au.sales_minute_store;
  • show run or watermark evidence rather than relying on visual freshness alone.

items.title: 5. Show Power BI
items.text:
Open the Power BI Project (PBIP) report and demonstrate historical and operational pages backed by the Direct Lake model. Use explicit measures and current data periods.

Deployment saves each date filter to the month containing the configured history end date. State that month before showing a number. If the report was rerendered with a different history window, its default month changes with the data.

If required ML tables have not been generated and validated, do not present predictive pages as supported output.

items.title: 6. Close with actions and roadmap
items.text:
If a pricing approval or alert scenario has been validated, show it as an optional action. In full-demo, you can also open the Merchandising & Replenishment Fabric App (retail-approvals): filter to items needing attention, select Propose on one to draft a replenishment proposal from its stock evidence, then show a different reviewer recording an append-only decision under Replenishment approvals. The app does not place orders. RTI dashboards and Activator rules are checked in as design and reference material, not deployed items. Otherwise, describe the action story from the owning backlog:

  • RTI dashboards and Activator
  • Closed-loop pricing

items.title: Do not overclaim
items.text:
Keep these qualifications in the presentation:

  • Truck dwell behavior is owned by the event contract; do not present it as live-validated until a Fabric smoke run has been recorded.
  • Marketing attribution and return on ad spend (ROAS) are implemented and contract-tested. State the seven-day last-touch rule and selected data period before presenting a result.
  • Required ML publication has been exercised live and remains fail-closed. Still check the current readiness report before presenting predictions, because model evidence is time-bounded.

items.title: Deployed walkthrough: analytics and AI
items.text:
Allow 10-15 minutes to show retail and analytics teams the ontology, Data Agents, and Power BI report over synthetic data. Start with the walkthrough overview.

Optional surfaces

Ontology and Data Agents require valid source bindings, permissions, and capability support. Skip a feature that has not passed its preflight checks.

items.title: 1. Show business context in the ontology
items.text:
An ontology is a business map that connects concepts such as Store, Product, Customer, and Receipt to the underlying data. Show this section only after deployment confirmed that the ontology exists and points to the intended Lakehouse and Eventhouse sources.

  1. Open the Ontologies folder.
  2. Open RetailOntology_AutoGen.
  3. Select the Store entity type in Explorer.
  4. Select Relationship to show only the entities connected to Store.

The Relationship view shows Store connected to Geography, Receipt, Promotion, and the machine-learning StockoutRisk entity.

The ontology maps business concepts to existing Lakehouse Silver and Gold data. It is historical-only: Eventhouse event bindings are disabled, so it does not show live stream events. It does not replace the physical schema or copy the source data.

items.title: 2. Test a grounded data-agent answer
items.text:
If the semantic-model agent passed its source and permission checks:

  1. Open the Agents folder.
  2. Open retail-semantic-model-agent.
  3. Select Test data agent.
  4. Ask for net sales and gross margin for a complete month, for example: "What were total net sales and gross margin % for September 2026? Name the measures used."

The data agent answers from the Net Sales and Gross Margin % measures and states the date range, so the result can be checked against the report.

The agent can use every table in retail_model, including the receipt-level fact tables. Ask about a complete month: the latest month is usually partial, so month-over-month and year-over-year figures for it look artificially low. If you compare with the report, set the report's date filter to the same month first. Check each generated answer against measures, query output, and source timestamps.

Skip an agent when it has no selected data sources, returns an error, or has not passed its capability and access checks. The ontology graph can still be shown independently when its bindings are valid.

items.title: 3. Close with the Power BI outcome
items.text:
1. Open the Reports folder.
  2. Open the retail_model report.
  3. Start on Executive Cockpit.
  4. Continue to Sales, Supply Chain Control Tower, Omnichannel Fulfillment, or Operations & Marketing when the audience wants more detail.

The Executive Cockpit combines omnichannel performance, store comparisons, ML risk signals, and an AI-generated narrative over the Direct Lake semantic model.

Direct Lake is the Power BI connection mode that reads Lakehouse tables directly without importing another data copy. The report opens on the latest month generated by this deployment, not a hard-coded month shared by every workspace.

State the selected data period before discussing a value. All values are synthetic, and an AI-generated narrative can contain inaccuracies. Use the underlying measures and source timestamps as evidence.

items.title: Report page gallery
items.text:
SalesSupply chainOmnichannelOperations and marketing

Sales Performance combines revenue, growth, margin, department mix, and customer-lifetime-value signals.

The control tower combines inventory position, replenishment, and ML-predicted stockout risk.

Omnichannel Fulfillment combines store and online revenue with payment mix and demand forecasting.

Operations and Marketing combines campaign spend, churn risk, foot traffic, store operations, and payment-decline context.

items.title: 4. Optional full-demo extensions
items.text:
Show these surfaces only when deployment and readiness confirmed them in the target workspace.

Surface Where to find it What to say Connected operational twins retail-twins report in the Reports folder A separate report over the same governed data; it is not a page of retail_model. Post-Reporting extended ML ml-optional and ml-experimental pipelines Journey analysis (journey_patterns), delivery prediction (dwell_predictions), and experimental dynamic pricing (pricing_recommendations) run after Reporting and are not Reporting prerequisites. Replenishment case preparation prepare-replenishment-case notebook Prepares a human-reviewed replenishment draft from availability signals derived from required ML outputs. Retail Operations Fabric Apps retail-approvals (titled Merchandising & Replenishment) and retail-promotions in the Fabric Apps folder Two standalone apps. Merchandising & Replenishment shows item trends, in-stock rate, and days of cover over a synthetic sample catalog; Propose on an item drafts a replenishment proposal from that evidence, and a different reviewer records an append-only decision under Replenishment approvals. The promotion studio models discount and break-even what-ifs. The apps do not change prices, place orders, or execute transfers.

items.title: Fabric Apps gallery
items.text:
Each app opens from the Fabric Apps folder and requires Fabric sign-in. These screenshots use the apps' synthetic sample data.

MerchandisingPromotion studioReplenishment approvals

Sales, gross profit, in-stock rate, and items needing attention, with a this-period versus previous-period trend and private saved views. Propose on an item opens a replenishment proposal pre-filled from its on-hand units, days of cover, and in-stock rate.

A discount and assumed uplift produce promoted price, revenue, gross profit, and the uplift needed to break even; saved scenarios compare side by side.

Pending proposals wait for a reviewer other than the submitter; decisions are append-only and a rejection needs a reason.

items.title: Connect from VS Code (MCP)
items.text:
The Data Agent and Ontology expose streamable-HTTP Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. Call them from Copilot's agent-mode chat in VS Code to test questions before connecting them to the agentic application. Each call is a JSON-RPC POST authenticated with a Fabric bearer token.

The endpoint URLs follow these shapes (substitute your workspace, data-agent, and ontology-item GUIDs):

# Data Agent (semantic model)
https://api.fabric.microsoft.com/v1/mcp/workspaces/{workspaceId}/dataagents/{dataAgentId}/agent

# Ontology (business graph)
https://api.fabric.microsoft.com/v1/mcp/dataPlane/workspaces/{workspaceId}/items/{ontologyItemId}/ontologyEndpoint

1. Sign in to the tenant that owns the workspace:

az login

2. Obtain a Fabric token and copy the output. Tokens are valid for about 60-75 minutes:

az account get-access-token --resource https://api.fabric.microsoft.com --query accessToken -o tsv

3. Add .vscode/mcp.json (the .vscode/ folder is gitignored). VS Code prompts for the token once per session and passes it in the Authorization header:

{
  "inputs": [
    {
      "type": "promptString",
      "id": "fabric-token",
      "description": "Fabric bearer token (az account get-access-token --resource https://api.fabric.microsoft.com --query accessToken -o tsv)",
      "password": true
    }
  ],
  "servers": {
    "retail-data-agent": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://api.fabric.microsoft.com/v1/mcp/workspaces/{workspaceId}/dataagents/{dataAgentId}/agent",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${input:fabric-token}" }
    },
    "retail-ontology": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://api.fabric.microsoft.com/v1/mcp/dataPlane/workspaces/{workspaceId}/items/{ontologyItemId}/ontologyEndpoint",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${input:fabric-token}" }
    }
  }
}

4. Start the servers. Select Start above each server in .vscode/mcp.json, or run MCP: List Servers from the Command Palette. Paste the token, then open Copilot Chat in Agent mode and confirm both tools are enabled.

The Data Agent advertises one tool (DataAgent_<name>); the Ontology advertises list_ontology_entity_types and search_ontology. If calls return 401 because the token expired, repeat step 2, then use MCP: List Servers to restart the servers.

Which one to ask

Use the Data Agent for aggregates, rankings, and trends, such as the top 10 products by revenue last quarter. Use the Ontology for a named entity's related data, such as a loyalty member's segment and churn probability. Deep multi-hop scans can fail.

items.title: Analytics and AI validation
items.text:
Interaction Expected result Select the ontology Store entity Related business entities and relationship names appear in the graph. Ask the semantic-model agent for a complete month's net sales The answer names the Net Sales and Gross Margin % measures and the date range, and matches the report for the same month. Open Executive Cockpit Report visuals load for the selected data period without model or binding errors.

Return to the walkthrough overview or use a focused presenter journey.

items.title: Deployed walkthrough: data platform
items.text:
Allow 10-15 minutes to show data engineering, analytics, and technology teams how Fabric loads, transforms, stores, and queries the synthetic retail data. Start with the walkthrough overview.

Representative screenshots

A deployed workspace can lag behind the repository. Use the current checked-in notebooks and schema contracts as the authority for exact behavior and field names.

items.title: 1. Show pipeline orchestration
items.text:
Open the Pipelines folder. Use the deployed pipelines to explain how notebooks are grouped into repeatable operations:

  • historical-data-load loads historical data into the Lakehouse.
  • streaming-data-load runs Silver transformation before Gold aggregation and persists anomaly alerts alongside them.
  • daily-maintenance compacts Delta tables, reruns the demand-forecast and stockout models, and refreshes the Operations Agent's signals.
  • ml-required runs the six Reporting producers (including market-basket mining and promotion/elasticity analysis) and contract validator.
  • ml-optional and ml-experimental isolate full-demo extensions after Reporting.
Streaming transformsMachine learning

The streaming pipeline sequences 03-streaming-to-silver before 04-streaming-to-gold.

ml-required builds Gold with setup-11-build-gold, runs the six Reporting producers in parallel, and finishes with 15-validate-required-ml-contract.

ml-optional and ml-experimental are separate pipelines, so extended-model failures cannot block Reporting.

The pipeline canvas shows orchestration order. Use the Run history and activity output to confirm execution; a green dependency arrow only shows the intended order.

items.title: 2. Inspect a transformation notebook
items.text:
Open the Spark Notebooks folder, then open 03-streaming-to-silver.

The notebook moves new Eventhouse rows into Silver tables and uses a watermark to track the last processed event. Column names use snake_case.

Use the notebook header to explain the transform without scrolling through implementation details. Do not run the notebook until its Lakehouse binding and source tables have been verified.

The optional Eventhouse projection is prepared during deployment when streaming_shortcuts.enabled is true. For retail-demo, the deployment provisions OneLake mirroring with historical backfill and creates or verifies the shortcuts under Tables/cusn/ after KQL publication. The selected five-minute mirroring latency favors demo freshness but can produce smaller Parquet files; do not treat it as a production tuning recommendation.

items.title: 3. Inspect durable Lakehouse history
items.text:
1. Open retail_lakehouse.
  2. Expand Tables, then the ag schema.
  3. Select fact_receipts.

The Lakehouse explorer shows the Silver ag.fact_receipts table and a row preview from the generated historical dataset.

Point out:

  • ag contains cleaned, typed Silver dimensions and facts.
  • au contains business-ready Gold summaries used for analytics.
  • fact_receipts stores historical data with one row per receipt.
  • The preview demonstrates shape and content, not current operational freshness.

Use the authoritative historical data contract when explaining table ownership and columns.

items.title: 4. Inspect the Eventhouse hot path
items.text:
1. Open the retail_querysets KQL (Kusto Query Language) queryset.
  2. Confirm that retail_eventhouse appears in Explorer with the typed event tables.
  3. Select the q_receipts_minute_by_store tab. It reads the mv_store_sales_minute materialized view, which aggregates recent store sales.
  4. Select Run. If no stream has run in the last hour, widen lookback (for example to 7d) to show the most recent results.

The queryset reads per-minute store sales from the mv_store_sales_minute materialized view. This capture uses a seven-day lookback.

The materialized views are created by the numbered scripts in fabric/kql_database/ during deployment; the queryset holds the saved operational queries.

For live evidence, run a read-only query against a recent window:

receipt_created
| where ingest_timestamp > ago(10m)
| project ingest_timestamp, store_id, receipt_id, total
| order by ingest_timestamp desc
| take 10

Recent rows prove that Eventhouse ingestion is active. If the query is empty, show the schema and last known data timestamp, then follow the operations guide instead of claiming that the stream is live. Do not run the numbered deployment scripts during a presentation.

items.title: Data-platform validation
items.text:
Interaction Expected result Open streaming-data-load The Silver notebook precedes the Gold notebook in the pipeline canvas. Open 03-streaming-to-silver The notebook identifies Eventhouse sources, Silver targets, and watermark-based processing. Select ag.fact_receipts The Lakehouse explorer shows the table schema and a row preview after historical setup. Run the recent receipt query Rows have recent ingest_timestamp values when the optional stream is active. Run q_receipts_minute_by_store Per-minute store sales from mv_store_sales_minute return without errors (widen lookback if no recent stream ran).

Continue with Analytics and AI.

items.title: Deployed solution walkthrough
items.text:
Use this browser tour to introduce a deployed workspace to retail, analytics, and technology teams. Allow 3-5 minutes for orientation or 15-25 minutes for the full walkthrough. All data is synthetic. The presenter demo provides a detailed talk track and limits on what to claim.

Representative screenshots

The screenshots show a representative deployment. Fabric navigation, generated values, item counts, and data timestamps can vary by deployment and run date. Validate freshness before presenting any value as current.

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
1. Complete Getting started.
  2. Open the deployed Fabric workspace.
  3. Confirm that retail_lakehouse, retail_eventhouse, the KQL queryset, retail_model, the pipelines and notebooks, and any optional ontology or agent items you plan to show are available.
  4. Run the historical setup notebooks. Run stream-events.ipynb only when the walkthrough needs recent Eventhouse data.

items.title: 1. Orient the audience in the workspace
items.text:
Open the workspace task flow and select the Retail Demo flow.

Task flow is a full-demo experience

The task flow is published only after the full-demo ontology step is complete. If the workspace uses core or standard, skip this step and open the workspace item list. You can still follow the historical, live, and Reporting paths described below.

The task flow maps ingestion, transformation, storage, the semantic model, ontology, ML, agents, case preparation, and Fabric Apps. Required ML feeds the Semantic Model; optional and experimental ML follows Reporting.

Explain the paths through the flow:

  • Load and transform deterministic retail history into the Lakehouse.
  • Send typed live events to Eventhouse and optionally project them into Lakehouse tables.
  • Make curated data available through the semantic model, Power BI, ontology, and Data Agents.

The task flow is a navigation aid. It does not prove that a notebook, pipeline, or stream completed successfully.

items.title: Continue the walkthrough
items.text:
Choose the page that matches the audience:

Walkthrough Use it for Data platform Pipelines, Spark notebooks, Lakehouse history, and Eventhouse/KQL Analytics and AI Ontology, grounded data-agent answers, and the Power BI report

For the complete demo, present the data platform first and finish with analytics and AI. For a business audience, use this overview and go directly to Analytics and AI.

items.title: Shared support boundaries
items.text:
• Screenshots show a representative deployment; item counts, values, and timestamps vary.
  • A task-flow node or pipeline canvas is navigation context, not execution evidence.
  • Validate the selected data period before discussing any value.
  • Skip optional ontology, agent, ML, or live-streaming features that have not passed their source, permission, and capability checks.

For a timed presentation, continue with the presenter demo or a focused presenter journey.

items.title: Deployment
items.text:
Use retail-setup deploy to provision, publish, update, or recover a demo workspace. Complete Getting started first if you have not configured the repository and rendered its notebooks.

This guide is for operators, developers, and support engineers. Business analysts can start with deployment outcome and troubleshooting, skipping the advanced authentication details.

See the plain-language glossary for terms such as Terraform, preflight, terminal success, Direct Lake, and DEGRADED.

The deployment framework specification defines exact command order and failure behavior.

Confirm the target

--recreate destroys the configured workspace and every item in it. The deploy polls Fabric until the workspace name is absent and fails before apply if deletion times out or pagination is incomplete. Use recreate only for a disposable demo workspace after confirming the tenant, environment, workspace name, and Terraform state.

items.title: Deployment outcome
items.text:
Every deployment resolves deployment.profile from contracts/retail-demo.json. The manifest selects stable logical asset IDs, existing notebook groups, existing pipeline folders, and existing KQL scripts. It does not redefine physical items or schemas: deploy/config/deploy.yml, deploy/scripts/build_artifacts.py, and the source folders remain authoritative for those definitions.

The current deploy plan:

  1. resolves the exact profile inventory;
  2. runs local and live tenant/capacity preflight before Terraform destroy/apply, publication, or KQL;
  3. generates profile-aware Terraform and fabric-cicd inputs;
  4. initializes Terraform, saves and validates a plan, then applies that exact plan after confirmation unless Terraform is skipped;
  5. captures the selected Terraform-owned identifiers;
  6. stages and publishes infrastructure without Reporting;
  7. executes only the selected ordered KQL scripts and validates infrastructure;
  8. for gated profiles, waits for setup, then runs the six independent required ML producers concurrently and waits for their shared validator;
  9. stages and publishes Reporting only after required ML terminal success;
  10. runs selected optional/experimental ML through a single Spark lane while independent Reporting validation and API publication branches run through a bounded non-Spark worker pool;
  11. tells the Lakehouse SQL endpoint about newly created tables so Power BI and readiness queries can find them;
  12. for full-demo, runs the deployed ontology notebook to create or revalidate the target ontology and its derived graph;
  13. publishes both Data Agents and the complete task flow (14 tasks, 62 item references, 14 edges), then reads the graph back and compares every task, item binding, and edge;
  14. runs read-only readiness verification over the complete selected profile.

Each live run atomically updates deploy/.generated/<env>/deploy-run.json. This journal records target names, the manifest version/hash, profile support and expected counts/folders, core/optional/preview/manual boundaries, exact asset/group/pipeline/KQL inventory, required/optional classification, any failed step, its exit code, and the final SUCCEEDED, DEGRADED, or FAILED status. Artifact build steps link phase-specific artifact-inventory-<phase>.json evidence. Credential-like error text is redacted and raw subprocess output is not stored.

The final journal status is:

  • SUCCEEDED: every selected required and optional check passed.
  • DEGRADED: required capabilities passed, but at least one optional capability has failed, stale, or missing evidence. The required demo path is usable; inspect the linked report before presenting the affected optional feature.
  • FAILED: a required capability failed or could not provide evidence. Do not present the workspace as ready.

items.title: Native Operations Agent and Planning
items.text:
The availability decision pack is separate from fabric-cicd publication. Its Operations Agent deploys by default with every Reporting profile (standard or full-demo, the default) after Reporting; core cannot select it. If Fabric rejects agent creation, the deploy step and readiness report a warning and the rest of the deployment continues. Native Planning stays excluded (include_plan: false) unless you explicitly include it.

Before publication, use a non-trial Fabric capacity, provide an Eventhouse or ontology (plus its KQL database when using Eventhouse), and ensure the creator has a Teams account. A Fabric administrator must enable Operations Agent, Copilot, and Azure OpenAI permissions. The API publisher uses a user identity with Contributor-or-higher workspace access and Item.ReadWrite.All; service principals and managed identities aren't supported for Operations Agent creation. If the capacity is outside the US/EU, enable the documented Azure OpenAI cross-geo processing/storage settings as well. The current tenant settings index has no separate Operations Agent creation toggle; its Operations Agent observability and insights settings are optional.

The deployment preflight checks the configured capacity and the Copilot/Azure OpenAI tenant settings it can inspect. It does not prove that a Teams account exists or that the Operations Agent preview is enabled for the creator's tenant/security group. The publisher creates the Agent stopped with its KQL source and instructions. The public definition API rejects FabricJobAction, so publication then uses the same OA workload endpoint as the Fabric UI to bind prepare-replenishment-case and requires exact source/action readback. It omits an empty playbook because Fabric rejects it with No rule definitions available. Saving that configuration makes Fabric generate the playbook (the agent's rules) from its instructions, which takes a few minutes. By default the publisher then starts the agent: it waits for a playbook with at least one rule and requires an Active state readback. Set operations_planning.activate_agent: false to leave the agent stopped for review. A failed start leaves the agent stopped, records activation_warning in the report, and does not fail the deployment.

The default selection deploys only the Operations Agent and leaves the existing model's SSO binding untouched. It is equivalent to:

operations_planning:
